div.p: TOIL TIT'S WEDDING DAY. Two little torn tits, Sitting on a tree. Suddenly bethought themselves How pleasant it would he, If, instead of living all their lives, As sister and as brother, They billed and cooed like other birds, And married one another. When somebody is bridegroom, And somebody is bride, Of course the proper thing to do Is 'flyaway and hide. - So they crept beneath-a telt of leaves And cottoned close together, And talked about their little selves,: The sunshine and the weather.

JACK MIDDY. A TRUE INCIDENT OF TEE RAIL. Brave Jack Chiddyl Oh, well you may sneer, For the name isn't one that sounds nice in the ear; But a name is a sound—nothing moie—deeds are beet, And Jack had the soul of a man in his breast.

But the story? you say. Well, fm coming to that. Though I wander a little—now, where was I at ? Let me see. Can you catch, shining round and clear, The mouth of the Breslington tunnel from here? You see it? Well, right on the bank at the top, When stacking some blocks, all at owe, down he slope A huge slab of stone from, the rest shore its way. And fell down on the updiint of metals and lay. , One sharp cry of terror burst from us all, As we saw the huge mass topple over and fall. We stood as if bound to the spot, dumb of speech, Beading horror and doubt In the faces of each. Then one of our mates snatched a glance at his watch. Gave a start and a look that made each of us catch At our breath, then a cry, that tlarilyd our hearts through— .. Goa the *Flying Dutchman is overdue!" Hark, straight from over the hill we could hear A dull, dead sound coming faint to the ear, Then a short, sharp whistle that told with its blast That the Dutchman" was into the tunnel at last. And there on the rail lay that huge mass of stone, • And the "Dutchman" behind coming thundiring on; bra minute or less he would come on with a dash. Anda hundred lives would be lost in -the crash. "Now, for your life, Jack I" for Chiddy had flown Down the bank, and three leaps brought him close to the stone. Not of his own life, for wife and child's sake. Thought he, but the hundreds that now were at stake. "Twas the work of a moment. With terrible strength And a heave oPthe shoulder the slab moved at 16ngth— Slipp'd clear of the rail—when, half-muffled in smoke, From the mouth of the tunnel the "Dutchman" broke." Tere was one sharp whistle, a roar, and a crash Of wheels running clear on the rail, and a flash 'Of coiling smoke, and a glitter and gleam Of iron and steel and then down fell the steam. Not a breath could we draw, but stood blank with dismay As the train tore along, making up for delay; Till at last from us all burst a out and a cheer, When we knew that the "Dutchman" had pass'd and was clear' And Chiddy ? Ah me! you will pardon these tears, For he was my mate on the rails many years, When we found him, one look was enough to reveal - That Jack's life-blood was red on the engine-wheel. Brave Jack Chiddy ! Now you don't sneer At the name which I own is but harsh to the ear ; But a name is a sound—nothing more—deeds are best, And Jack had the soul of a Man in his breast. —ALExaNniin ANDERSON, in " Good Words."

NAUTICAL.—Husband (jokingly) : Oh, I'm the mainstay of the family—Wife: Yes, and the jib-boom and the—and the—Small Boy (from experience) : And the spanker, too, mamma. (Applause.) TEE Press.—A piper in a Northumbrian town was once asked if he could play "Within a mile o' Edinbro' Toon." "Within a mile!" he exclaimed, " wey, man, an could play within ten yards on't." Science enumerates 588 species of organic forms in the air we breathe. Just think of it! Every time you draw in a breath, a whole zoological garden slips down your windpipe, and no free ticket. .NErram.oras—A girl who resided near flexham was ill lately, and a neighbour asked the ailing woman's sister what was the nature of her complaint. " Wey," was the answer, "she tyuk teeth wark, then it torned te tic, and DOO it's knowledge in the heed !" The cold that came with the first cold snap of the season blocked up some neighbonrhoods completely. In one of these localities a business man telegraphed to the office of his firm in town, "I shall not be in the office to-day, as I have not got home yesterday yet." An American editor thus retorts upon a critic We are sorry you don't like this paper. We publish it simply to please yon. We should ask you to come to the office and edit it, only if we did, some iniquitous idiot might write and tell how much better he could do it himself, and that would annoy a nervous person like you." A doctor in Scotland made a nerve and bone all-healing salve, and thought he would experiment a little with it. He at first cut off his dog's tail, and applied some of the salve to the stump. A new tail grew out immediately. He teen applied Some to the tail which he had cut off, and a new dog grew out. He did not know which dog was which. Dr. Emmons, the able New England divine, met a Pan- theistical physician at the house of a sick parishioner. It -was no place for a dispute; but the abrupt question of the Pantheist was," Mr. Emmons, how old are you?" "Sixty, sir; and how out are you?" "As old as creation," was the triumphant response. "Then you are of the same age with Adam and Eve ?" "Certainly. I was in the garden when they were." "I have always heard that there was a third party in the garden with them, but I never knew before that it was you," rejoined the divine. THE END OF TEE WORLD.—Two women in the neigh- bourhood of the Felling were conversing about the thuwier the ether night, when one of them was heard to remark, " Ah ! aa's shure it's sumthing dreadful; an' they say the wand's comin' tiv an end this yer, and we shall aall be horned up!" " Ah!" replied the other, "it's eneuf te frighten onv yen te think about it; ae' wheat a pity it'll be for yor Jack, poor lad, just gettin' married, and te hey his nice new fornitnre anti borned up !" " Woe," replied the mother, a it's a blessing it'll not be a loss te him, for he's just gettent insured!" Barcormei.—A Galveston Irishman has a very bright boy, who reads the papers. The other morning the old man asked Patrick junior why he didn't return the change from the marketing. There was no answer except that the boy muttered, "The toirant." "Have you fed the pig,Patrick?" A stony stare was the only reply. Then for about fifteen minutes there was a vision of a son closely pursued by a bare-headed father revolving around the house, until the former overtook the latter and yanked him over a water- barrel. "I was only thrying Boycott on yea, feyther ; for the sake of ould Ireland, lave me alone." Its a boy caught ye are," panted the old man. "I'll tache yer to thrifle wid a Home Ruler," and he reached out and gathered a barrel. stove. The application of coercive measures could be heard four blocks off. A GOOD STORY OF AN ENTHUSIASTIC CURLER.—Poor Wattle, an Ayrshire weaver, was a most enthusiastic lover of the game—he was a keen curler, and threw always a " guid stane." No one could beat him on the icy board, but at the social hoard he was barely a match for the gentle- men. This was his sore point. He liked to stand his own Mame of the liquor "when the crack was gui.d." But how was this to be done? He was a failing man. Week after week he came in from the "pays" and tossed his money into the wife's lap with a sigh. "Twa scobs in the weft, Jean," he would say—a Rob meaning a bad piece, for which there was the penalty of sixpence. Week after week was the story repeated, Jean sighing to herself, as she counted over ' the silver, that her man was sair failing, and raising a hope in her heart as she glanced around that her family might yet be grown up in time to assist her should Wattle get completely helpless at the weaving. And so she mourned till one quiet Sunday forenoon in August, when a neebor's I bairn came round asking for the loan of a cage in which to store a captive blackbird." "Lend ye a cage! That I wull, my laddie," said Wattle's guidwife, jumping upon a chair and unhanging an empty one. "We have had nae use for this since oor canary deiti," she said. "Let that cage alane, emidewife," shouted Wattie, who was lying in his bed with his clothes half on, no doubt thinking of " Inwick4 and outwicks and roaring Manes" for the coming winter. "Pit that doon directly, guidwife " he shouted again, making a spring to catch it. Ere she could obey his orders, how- ever, the seed box slipped to the floor, and from it rolled over 30 sixpences—the missing scobs in the weft which Wattle had so carefully prepared for the winter's campaign. It is needless to state that they were forfeited, but poor Wattle's story was always, after its first recital, considered sufficient excuse for his not standing his gill at his turn.— Ayrshire A ryta. How Toccuwoon BECAME A BARoNET.--Wellington's men having worn out their shoes, by constant pursuit of the enemy, our Government took measures to prepare to shoe them, by the time they had learned to march barefoot. Joseph Totschwood got the contract; his beef had been found of such durable texture, that the hides, ha all reason, must last for ever. The order was placed in Northampton; the shoes were made in a jiffy, and came to Plymouth, two- and-twenty thousand of them, all of a size, not in pairs, but polygamous; being shaped so admirably as to fit either human foot alike. They passed a triumphant examination, and were happily shipped to a Spanish port, which fell into the hands of Marshal Soult, on the very day of their arrival.

How nu TREATED a HORSE.—It was necessa^y on acer- tain occasion in court, to compel a witness to testify as to the way in which a Mr. Smith treated his horse. "Well, sir" said the lawyer, with a sweet and winning smile—a sm9ile intended to drown all suspicion as to the ulterior pur- pose.—" how does Mr. Smith generally ride a horse Z" The witness looked up innocently and replied, "Generally a straddle, sir, I believe." The lawyer asked again, "But, sit; what gait does he ride?" The imperturbable witness answered, 'He never rides any gate at all, but I've seen his boys ride every gate on the farm." The lawyer saw that he was on the track of a Tartar, and his next question was very insinuating. "How does Mr. Smith ride When he is in corn- I pany with others? I demand a clear answer." "Well, sir," said the witness, a he keeps up with the rest, if his horse is able to, and if not befalls behind." lhe lawyer was by this time almost beside himself, and asked, "How does he ride when he is alone ?" "I don't knoas was the reply," I was never with him when he. was alone," and there the case dropped.—Detroit Free Press. Ore CERTAINTY IN THE DOCTRINE OF THE APOSTLES. The most decisive method of testing the Apostle& claim to be the teachers of certainty is for the individual to subject the mind candidly to the influence of their writings. Let., each Mali who has made the lifelong experiment declare the result. For myself, I can only confess that I have found there a.spirit which assures me that it is the merest trifling With moral evidence to confound these men with the vulgar potenders of heathenism or of Islam. They were naani- testily intelligent, serious, and therefore enftlejent witne.sses of the resurrection of Christ; men Who 'ciritnot be set aside as dreamers or fanatics. I find in their writings a spirit which corresponds' with the transcendent claim which they make to inspiration of God. It awes me like the sound of many waters. As none works so none speaks like the Lord of all. In the Old Testament I hear the dread sound of the storm and the eaithquake. But Jehovah li not in the tempest. These are but the heralds of that "still small voice" of Infinite Love in which onward comes the Lord. There is in the New Testament an authority, an earnestness, a sincerity, a simplicity, a purity,a tenderness, a dignity, a depth and a loftiness of, thought, which breathe on the soul with an immortal energy: I could as soon think of ques- tioning the Divine hand in the sunrise as the Divine source of the writings of St. Paul and St. John. They reach something deeper than the intellect. They commend them- selves to every man's conscience in the sight of God. And when I hear these holy pAges read, they compel me to listen, as if a choir of angels filled the firmament with their songs. Their theme is "Peace on earth, Good-will to men." It is the voice of the Eternal Love reaching me through its hnman messengers. I recognise the tone of the Eternal Mercy, and I rest in the faith of the resurrection of the dead, and the hope of the life to come.—The Tone and Teach- ing of the New Testament on Certainty in Religion. Being the Merchants' Lecture for October, 1880. By Ect,card White. ELECTRICAL Snanows.—Some curious phenomena— electrical shadows so-called—have been lately described by Herr Holtz to the Uriittingen Academy. They are bat et' by fixing to one discharge rod of a Holtz machine a large concave disc with a piece of silk without wrinkles' adhering to it by electric action; at the point of the other roer, Placed opposite, appears, when the machine is worked, a small, feeble, luminous star, and on the disc a luminous girds, and the shadows appear on the latter when objects are inter- hiosed. That they are not optical shadows is proved, inter 1 alia, by the fact that not all objects give them. They are, produced in general only by conductors or semi-conductors; insulating bodies, when small, give no shadow; when large they may give some shadow at first, but this gradually goes out as the action of the machine is continued. It makes no ' difference whether the conducting bodies are connected with the earth or insulated. The shadow-forming power is to be measured not only by the darkness of the image, hut by the magnification. Herr Holtz tried pasteboard, ebonite, silk, linen, knitting-needles, and glass rods or tubes; the former he used in the form of strips, crosses, and rings. The size and form of the shadows are affected by various things. The shadow is larger or smaller according as the body ap- proaches the point or the large surface. It enlarges, too, outwards from the centre of the disc, so that the shadow of a strip of uniform width is narrowed in the middle. It is further notable that, to a certain limit, a strip gives the same shadow, whether it is placed with its broad side or its nat.' row edge towards the disc. A system of strips, placed edge- ways, gives the same shadow as a homogenous piece. Various instructive experiments may be contrived : thus, a moss of pasteboard and ebonite gives only the shadow of the pasteboard, but by breathing on the cross a full cross-shadow momentarily appears. A glass rod with one end made con- ducting by -heat gives a partial shadow, which gradually dis- appears on cooling; and so on. Herr Holtz does not at this stage say much as to what the phenomena means. FROTOMSTRICAL STANDARDS.—SeveraI attempts are now being made to construct a standard photometer, or rather a standard sensitometer, as it is rather barbarously termed, since the attempts referred to are being made by photo- graphers, and are for the purpose of measuring the actinism of any light, rather than the actual amount of the lightlte self. One of these is by Mr. Warnerke, and a brief descrip- tion of it is given in a recent number of the Journal of Photography. Mr. Warnerke proposes to employ different varieties of luminous paint for the purpose. It has been ascertained that the different metallic sulphides employed for this purpose are sensjtive in different degrees to the dif- ferent parts-of the spectrum, and it is further said that a similar difference is found in different specimens of the same sulphide. The Journal of Photography states that from the most generally-used sulphide, calcium sulphide, "it is possible to prepare different materials so as to give off a phosphorescent light, varying very greatly in colour, from violet and blue to red." It is not stated precisely how Mr. Warnerke applies these principles; but supposing it to be possible to produce a 'material of standard sensitiveness, it is not difficult to imagine that it might be possible to con- struct both a standard unit of light—that is to say, a sur- face of given area covered with a material which might be yosensitiveto allsot sorts tr coonsf light, aa se andwnos iutlodmsehtoewr, , merely which equally amount—and d al show the amount of blue and red rays in any given light, and consequently the actinism of the light. M. Leon Vidal has also recently brought a selenium photometer be- fore the Paris Photograpical Society. From the description given, it does not really differ from the "selenium eye" of Dr. Siemens. The British Journal of Photography gives a description of a selenium cell mounted on the top of a pho- tographic studio, and arranged so as to show on a galvano- meter within the amount of light falling on the selenium at any moment, so as to enable a photographer to judge the amount of exposure necessary for his plate. It is hardly possible to doubt that this arrangement is at present purely imaginary, as is also the suggestion that an automatic ar- rangement should be attached to the camera which should expose the photographic plate a varying length of time, according to the amount of actinism in the light. Al. Vidal states that he has not found his selenium subject to the "fatigue" which has been so commonly noted by all who have had the slightest experience of the action of selenium previously. He further states that, whatever be the colour of the light thrown on the selenium, it appears to make no difference. Here again he is entirely at variance with the authorities in this country. THE GERM THEORY AND HYDROPHOBIA.—At the last meeting of the French Academy of Medicine some experi- ments by Messrs. Maurice Raynaud and Lanneloegue on inoculation with the virus of hydrophobia formed the sub- ject of an interesting discussion. The researches were undertaken to ascertain whether the disease can be commu- nicated from the human subject to animals, and subse- quently transmitted from one animal to another. One prac- tical result which, it is suggested, may accrue from these researches is the discovery of a method of attenuating the virus so that it may serve as a vaccine with which to in- noculate dogs, and possibly human being., in order to pro- tect them from the more severe form of the disease. Such a possibility is obviously suggested by M. Pasteur's recent discovery of a method of robbing the virus of fowl's cholera of its fatal character. In any case the experiments tend to .a more complete knowledge of the microphyte which, it is suspected, may be present in rabies, as in other diseases in which definite periods of incubation are apparently pre- sented. The experiments described by M. Raynaud were made on rabbits. Three groups Were inoculated; the first with saliva and blood taken from a living but rabid human subject, the second with mucus taken from -varions organs (including the brain) of the same subject after death, and the third with matter taken from the inoculated rabbits after death. Of thirty-eight rabbits thus inoculati-dtwenty- six died, a sufficiently large proportion to indicate the pres- ence of a specific disease. But the question arose, was .the disease which killed the rabbits really rabies? and on this point thera was a keen discussion ,It has been proved that a rabbit-bay he inobnlated from a Mild dog, and that in such a case the period of incubation is seventeen days. But M. Raynaud's rabbita,aidd also an inocutated ape, died within periods varying from twenty to forty-eight hours onle. M. Colin contended that death was caused by ordinary septi- cemia, dlie to.inoculation with putrid matter; N. NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CU.LTU MANURING AND IMPROVI SOIL.—At no time can the removal of manure and soil be conducteekeo expeditiously and economically as during frosty weathbr; aims, perinftl ting. Whether the matter is to be removed is done by carte or wheelbarrows the results are the same, and much more work is accomplished in a given time, and with less of exer- tion to man and horse than when the roads, walks,and lands are in a soft condition. On well-managed farms this prin- title is always acted on; but it is not by any means gene- rally-applied in the gardens of amateurs, nor, somewhat strangely, in all those belonging to farmers. An idea some- what widely prevails that spring is soon enough for coit-' naencing "gardening," forgetting that by doing certain Work in winter, under specially favourable conditions, ISA only is the ipring work greatly facilitated, but it is done !tter, because done= good time, and there is a great saving labour, and better crops into the bargain. Whenever the mind is hard and dry, manure should be placed on all ots requiring it, ready for digging in when the ground rives in proper condition. Nothing is more unsatisfactory an to see the land soft and dry waiting for the spade, and manure over soft walks and gropnda jrtenst.afentge engaged in he welhoeseelofga_term of frost. Before this work of dreparing for digging is completed, rain often falls, and the ground cannot be worked under favourable conditions. Time it then lost, and crops suffer simply because the eight work, applying manure, rkc., in frosty weather, was not done at the right time. It is well to remember that farm-yard manure is not the best application for -all soils and all crops. Some old gardens are so light and rich that further manuring , would be the reverse of beneficial, especi. ally where potat. • and other root crops are inteeded to be grown. To sue! land applications of fresh soil„sach as the trimmings of ditches and roadsides whuld be far more profitably employed than rich manure. Fresh soil of any kind, and got from anywhere, when used in conjunction with a heavy dressing of lime, has often contributed immensely to the productive power of gardens that have been long under a course of manuring and cropping. For potatoes especially, the prac- tice indicated cannot fail to be advantageous in nearly all its, and the richer manure can be reserved for such green crops as require it—celery, cauliflowers, lettuce, strawber- ries, and the surface dressing of raspberries. , Tim FARMERS' CLUB.—When his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales took the step which he recently did of be- coming a member of the Farmers' Club, that venerable body was not unfairly viewed as having taken a newlease of life, and made one more step forward. Despite the gloom of all agricultural prospects, many of its members augured a coming season of good work in the Way of practical instruc- tion to British farmers. The bill of fare issued for the year is certainly a full and varied one, while it is clear certain subjects of special interest and moment will engage the at- tention of the farmers and others who frequent the Inns of Court Hotel on the first Mondays of the coming months. Mr. Duckham take the chair under very good auspices, and he seems disposed to make the office no sinecure, for he volunteers ere the season closes' and despite Parliamentary claims on his time, to deliver alecture on the effect of land being owned by corporate bodies. The Club have succeeded in obtaining the services of an expert, Mr. Bailey Denton, in dealing with the vexed but just now very timely question of the manageraent'of rivers—a subject set down for discus- sion-'at the February meeting, on the evening before the day when the legislative proposals submitted to ParFament, with a view to improve river management, will be discussed'l by the Central and Associated Chambers of Agriculture. Mr. Aveling is also opportune in proposing to enlighten the Club on the 7th of March on Vtlies, ordinary and extra- 'ordinary i for although Mr. Inderifick's little bill on the last-named subject standofor elioesid .reading 'a good way in the session, the corn returns measure introduced by Col. Berne, and which so closely affects and so largely alters the tithe settlement of 1335, occupies a first place on the notice paper of,the Douse of Commons on Wednesday, 9th March For April we are promised It paper that cannot fail to be in- structive from the pen of Mr. Thomas Belt, on the teaching of the Agricultural Returns for 1880, so that, with the fol- lowing list, we may may a good deal of souad information in likely to be elicited on Very weighty and appropriate ques- tions :—On May 2nd, "The effect of land being owned by corporate bodies," Mr. T. Duck barn, M.P., Bayeham Court, Ross, Herefordshire ; on November 7th, "Dairying," Mr. G. M. Allender, St. Petersburgh-place, Bayswater, W.; OD December sth, "Agricultural experiments; how to conduct them," Pr. Voeicker, 11, Salisbury-square, El), ......_ SELLING CATTLE BY LIVE WEIGHT. Mr. William Anderson, farmer, Wellhouse, .Alford, Aber- deenshire, writes s—" I am very glad to see from the news- papers that the farmers in the Tarves district have been taking steps for erecting a weigh-bridge for the selling of fat stock by live weight. r regret to see also that the use of the weigh-bridge has not been A 1311CCess at Turriff. I can well enough understand bow sellers and buyers who do not rare for honest business are opposed to the use of the weigh-. big machine in the buying and selling of cattle, but I am sure that honest and honourable men, both among buyers and sellers' if the weigh-bridge were introduced into use, would be glad to be assisted by it in the conduct of their business. The use of the weigh-bridge would put an end to the 'leap in the dark' character of the trade, and also to that hiegling about weights and prices which ought not to ' be tolerated, and which would not be tolerated in any well- conducted business. Those who are opposed to the selling of fat stock by live weight and the use of the weigh-bridge can only be so from prejudice, or on the principle that they love darkness rather than light in doing business, and thus would keep an open door for dishonest dealing for those who are inclined to it. Local agricultnral societies could hardly do a greater service to agriculture at present than by taking active steps to get weigh-bridges erected, aad thus to en- courage the selling of fat cattln by live weight. The use of the weigh-bridge and the selling of fat cattle by live weight would effect an important reform in the meat trade, but I think it is the case that the Aberdeenshire meat trade will not be placed on a satisfactory footing in the interests of farmers, until they take the London trade largely, if not entirely, into their own hands. I think it important, then, for the interests of both the producers and the consumers of that meat, that there should be special stands and special salesmen in the London live stock and dead meat markets, and even in special localities, special depots and shops for the sale and retail of Aberdeenshire meat. Is it not worth the consideration of the agriculturists of Aberdeenshire and , the north, both landlords and tenants, whether the meat 1 trade could not be better managed, in their interests and that i of the vonsutners of their meat, by means of an 'Aberdeen • Meat Supply Company, Limited, which could make special arrangements and appoint special agencies for the sale of genuine 'Prime Scots wherever there is a market for it. I know this, however, if my brother agriculturists of Aber- deenshire apply their clear, vigorous, practical fieads and strong common sense to the consideration of whether the present mode of conducting the meat trade is the beet that can be, I have no doubt they will Bee the need of reform as clearly sal do, and I think they will also see that reform in the meat trade is almost as much needed in the interests of farmers as attention to scientific farming." Mr. G. Waken Waterside, of Forbes, Aberdeenshire, al- ludes to the above subject as follows:—" The sooner the farmers in Aberdeenshire unite in some way, not only to se- cure the best price for their beef, but also to pievent its de- preciation in the London and other markets, it will be the better for their own interests. Mr. Anderson 'suggests the formation of a 'Meat Supply Association,' which I believe to be quite practicable, and do not see that there would be any particular difficulty in managing -such, if only a suf- ficient number of feeders of cattle would sup& the meat. If a regular supply were arranged for, there is no doubt an Aberdeen alley in the Islington _ hive, and a stall in the Metropolitan Dead Meat Markets would Command both steady sales and good prices, and they could be managed at little expense compared to the present system. About this time last year I visited the Chicago, New Jersey, and New York stock-yards, and was astonished at the celerity and simplicity of the arrangements for carrying on the extensive transactions in cattle, hogs, and sheep compared with our large meat markets on this side, and to my mini the great simplifier of transactions on the American side is ' the scales.' By them there is no haggling, the greatest element of differences' in this country; weight, is Boon settled with- out any chance of dispute or Thjustice either to buyer or 1 seller. 'I carefully watched the transactions of one of the I largest firms in the Chicago stock-yards for some hours, 1 and the greatest difference I heard between offerer and seller was 5c., or 20. per 1001 b. live weight, and seldom more than 2c. S.H. crosses, or grade cattle as they are termed all over America, take the place of the best Scotch in Lon- don—i.e., command the highest prices in America; and, as a rule, Texan steers kill most dead meat compared with the live weight. I saw two pens of the former, forty each, sold in less time than it takes me to write these two lines. The top price of the day was quoted at 4d015.83c. per 1001 b. live weight. The seller asked that price. The offerer said 4dols. 82c. Answer—' No use.' Offerer—' Very well, I take them.' The scales ten minutes afterwards settled the transaction. I met a Liverpool salesman in the Chicago stockyards, and asked him the question, 'Gould the same business be done in Liverpool or London by our system by the same number of salesmen?' His answer was, 'Not by a great deal.' The number of cattle the day I was there was over the usual number 'Minn. great Christmas market (Chicago market is held on every day of the week), and the business was mostly over by twelve o'clock. Cattle, hogs, and sheep weighed, and off to the killing shops, and all goes on with clock-like regularity, selling its cattle, hogs, and sheep by the million yearly, and all by live weight. This year I again visited the great London Christmas market, and could not help contrasting the quickjimple, and safe form on the other side of the Atlantic with the haphazard prices and haggling on this side, the business in London being con- 'ducted in much the same style as in MIT markets at homk ; and I was told by many consumers in London that it did not matter much to them whether the farmers get a good or badio)ir niracy. eupAor nor nnifbeedbee Anderson, rseashfsiani sntcawa st thioeaisaaoauaettntltehtdclni haieemt presentmgaret nspghusatelrieksemodhetev. wepboeslneocf; improvement fenthryyneedeesomtesrit only scalesoeei lianmeNiaysraeosetlgsnnhhewui sceetflieteasolinslsl sellingqt.enfdlaouyaot t hi tini tatnhtethngoaredeaatiabreiwteuctessencaopiwatghtptthfithtehei:rere:. , in nhs oesutefhlladleri selling ffagererhmcitbse yrafaigrstttlic, and too often has only the chance of one buyer in a market, , the other offerers being simply spokes of a wheel kept going by the dealer with the cash. Besides, what chance has a farmer to learn to judge weight correctly, who is only sell- ing a few animals now .aid again, with the dealer, buying, killing, and testing his 'judgment by Wetght every day. TRADE NOTES.

The engineers of Jarrow resolved, on Saturday, to apply for an advance of 15 per cent. The employers at about 80 collieries in North Stafford- shire have received notices from the miners for an advance of 15 per cent. ke miners of Northumberland have, by a narrow majority, decided to abide by the Employers' Liability Act, the nego- tia,ons :Jr a compromise having failed. The colliers of North Wales have given notice requiring weekly payments instead'of the present mode of payment, and ask for their employers' decision en or before the 12th instant.
- At a meeting of Oldham cotton employers, on Tuesday Hizht, it was resolved to support those employers whose workmen were out on strike. Over 100,000 spinners are

ihe Hoyland Silkstone Colliery Company have offered their colliers an advance of 7i per cent, in wages, but this the men hare at a meeting decided to decline, and refuse to return to work unless they receive the 10 per cent. asked.

At a conference of miners' delegates at Glasgow, on Mon- day, it was agreed that the men should insist upon an adTance of 6 per cent., and that the conference should meet on the 14th inst. to receive the report and consider subse- quent action. The South Yorkshire Miners' Association have resolved that all pits where the notices given for an advance of 10 per cent, in wages expire this week, the men shall leave work unless it be granted in full ; and.that where notices have not been given the men will give them. About 8,000 men will therefore come out this week, but it is expected that corns of the owners will give the advance. . _

A conference of South. Staffordshire ironworkers was held on Monday, to discuss an insurance scheme submitted by the iroutnasters' section of the Wages Board. The adoption of the scheme was advocated on the ground of the certainty of the benefits obtainable from it as against the uncertainty tif benefits to be obtained from the Act, and because all suf- ferers from accidonts, whether fatal or not, and whether caused by negligence of the employers or not, would get compensAtion under the scheme. The discussion was ad- journed for a fortnight.

Several persons were injured, on Monday, during the hearing of a long-firm case in the Central Criminal & ourt, by the falling of a considerable portion of the ceiling in the old court. An order in council was issued on Monday, by the Lord-Lieutenant, prohibiting, from the let to the 28th of February, the importation of cattle into Ireland from Eng- land, owing to the prevalence of foot-and-mouth disease in England,

Mr. Morgan Lloyd has brought in a bill, the principal objects of which are to prohibit canvassing and the use of public-houses as committee-rooms at parliamentary eled- tions. The bill is also backed by Mr. Dillwyn, Mr. Rath- bone, and Mr. Cohen. At the Chester Assizes, on Monday, Enoch Thomas Fry, a groom, was sentenced to seven years' penal ooryitude for forging a doctor's certificate for the purpose of defrauding the Chohnondlay Court of Foresters, Knutsford, of a weekly allowance for sick pay. At the same Assizes, William Thomas Phnblott (17), a laborer, was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude for a criminal assault on Mary Maria Clark at Macclesfield. A destructive fire occurred at Eldon Colliery, Bishop Auckland, on Sunday, which resulted in the destruction of the engine house and machinery. Two hundred and fifty men are thrown out of employment, and the damage is esti- mated at £4,000 or £5,000. At Liverpool, on Saturday, an auctioneer and cattle dealer named Robert Burnside, of Darlington, was ined £2O for exhibiting for sale at Cabbage Hall a number of cows in contravention of the order of the Privy Council respecting the holding of market. and fairs. Amongst the names of those gentlemen who have recently been placed on the commissiem of the peace for the borough of Preptou we notice the following :—Mr. George Toulnun, proprietor of the Preston Guardian, and Mr. Henry E. Sowerbutts, cotton manufacturer of Preston. Macclesfield Election Commission inquiry was resumed on Monday. A large mass of evidence was given as to the employment of sham canvassers and . bribery. It is expected that the Commissioners will hold a sitting in Lon- don, at which Mr. Chadwiek will be further examined.

The iron viaduct across the Solway was seriously damaged on Sunday by drifting ice. Many pillars have 'eon carried away. Fortunately the line is closod on Sundays, so th.d no accidents occurred. The bridge is a mile and a quarter in length, and some time must elapse before tratth: can be resumed.

Between Saturday night and Sunday morning a daring burglary was committed in Aberdeen. The premises of Messrs. George Jamieson and Son, the principal jewellers, were entered, and watches, zings, lockets. seals, and brace- lets, to the value of £2,000, were stolen. Access to the shop had been obtained through empty offices in the upper flat, a hole having been cut in the floor,through which the burglars had passed and carried away their booty. The Cornmitsioners ,appointed to enquire into the, exist- ence of corrupt practices in Can'erbury state, in their report, that ;.to. evidence given before them has led them to the Opinion that the constituency is not now arlsa whole corrupt. Out of 3,000 voter,, perhaps 500 or 600 are at all times accessib'e to bribery. The Commissioners find that corrupt practices extensively prevailed at the elections of 1879 and 1 18 0. Schedules are appended giving the names of persons guilty of bribery and of persons who accepted bribes. The Royal Commission appointed in 1879 to inquire into the cause of accidents in mines have concluded the taking of evidence. The attention of the Commission is now directed to a series of experiments as to the explosive nature of coal dust, as to the best kind of safety lamp, and as to : other matters designed to elucidate the causes of explosions. It is proposed that some experiments shalt take place to test the efficacy of the electric light as an illuminating power in miles. Two years ago, Sir Henry Havelock was left a valuable estate, now yielding £lO,OOO a year, 012 condition that he assumed the testator's name of Allan; but he was not-to , op, the estate until his children had attained their majo- rity. the income in the meantime to accumulate. Sir Henry appealed to the Cllancery Division for an allowance from the eetate, to enable him to educate his sons in a manner to qualify them 1,.1 their future position, Yi-VilillIcC1!9I Matins on Saturday granieu oun x.ztoo a year. Atthe Stafford Assizes, on Monday, James Williams (24), tailor, wee sentenced to death for the wilful murder of his sweetheart, Elizabeth Bagn ill, at Great Haywood, Stafford- shire. The prisoner and the deceased girl had been during the day at Stafford servants' fair together, and going home at night passed along the canal towing-path. Later on Williams arrived at Haywood in an excited condition, and declared he had pushed his sweetheart into the canal, where the police subsequently found the girl's body. He said she had wanted to saddle him with an illegitimate child. Lord Roseberv, presiding at the annual meeting of the East and North of Scotland Liberal Association in Edin- burgh, on Saturday, said the people of Midlothian did not expect when they returned MrS. Gladstone as their member that unclouded times would accompany his accession to the Ministry. They knew that there must be storms and there must be tumults, but they knew that they had a great states- man at the helm. They knew that they had a man in whom they could trust. They felt that to be the case now, and as long as that is the case they had no reason to fear the result. _ .

A correspondent sends to the 4aity News the following I letter addressed to him by Mr. Bright in 1868:—" Rochdale, March 4, 1861.—Dear Sir,—l thank you for kind letter and for your pamphlet. I cannot agree with your recommends- Eons. Depend upon it, is not benevolence or charity that is wanted in Ireland, butaust law. I hope we may soon see changes which will soften the bitter feeling towards ling- land which now prevails in Ireland. But England is a slow learner, and our Parliament never learns at all, except under the presence of some great calamity.-lam, very truly yours, JOHN BRIGHT." There are few knots that a skilful tar is unable to untie, but there is one that may give him more than ordinary trouble. On Saturday, a sailor, who a short time ago had tied the I matrimonial knot, applied at the Thames Street Pollee [Court to have it cut asunder, or, in other words,for a divorce. I Poll had been unfaithful and Jack wished to get rid of her, but looked very crestfalleu when the magistrates told him that he would have to apply to the Divorce Court for the severance from his apogee which he sought for. "If I'd a knowed," said tke sailor, "it was so much trouble to get un- tied I'd be blowed if I'd a-got spliced at all." Having made this sorrowful assertion poor Jack left the court. Some severe strictures on the rapacity of money-lenders as a class passed by Vice-Chancellor Malice during the hear- ing of an ex pane application, made in the Chancery Divi- sion of the High Court of Justice, for an injunction restrain- ing the defendant from selling certain goods under a bill of sale given as security for money advanced. His lordship, in granting the injunction to extend over next motion day, said that he wished it was his power to suppress all such dealings, and to prescribe an adequate punishment for them. The terrorism practised by loan offices and money-lenders was worse than the terrorism practised in another place, and their conduct and voracity outraged every feeling of humanity. The arrivals at Liverpool of live stock and fresh meat from the United States and Canada last week show a large decrease in both live stock and fresh meat. As regards live stock there was only one steamer arrived, which was the Pembroke, with 230 cattle and no sheep. The steamers which arrived with fresh meat were as follow: The City of Brussels, with 814 quarters of beef, 425 carcases of mutton, and 2,018 dead pigs; the Polynesian, with 934 quarters of beef; the Indiana, with 804 quarters of beef and 150 carcases ' of mutton; the Germanic, with 640 quarters of beef and 250 carcases of mutton; and the Italy, with 232 quarters of beef, 504 carcases of mutton, and 484 pigs ; making a total of 230 cattle, 3,424 quarters of beef, 1,329 carcases of mutton, and 2,502 carcases of pigs. MR. GLADSTONE AND MR. PARNELL.--The Right Hon. W. E. Forster had addressed the following letter to Mr. Par- nell, M.P. :—" House of Commons, January 29, 1881.—Sir, —As I put in Mr. Gladstone's hands while be was speaking the passage which I supposed to have been spoken by you in Galway on Oct. 25th, to the effect that no man was to ,take a farm from which another had been evicted, no matter what was the cause,--' write to tell you that I find upon examination that this speech was not made by you. It was made at another Land League meeting by a Mr. M‘Donell. The mistake arose from a printer's error in accidentally omit- ting the marginal note of the place of meeting and name of the speaker. I will publicly correct it when I next speak on the Protection Bill, but I take the earliest opportunity of in- forming you.-4 am, sir, your obedient servant, W. E. FORS-TER.—To C. S. Parnell, Esq , M.P." Bishop Fnesust presided on Saturday evening at the annual soirée of the Failsworth Co-operative Society. Alluding to the educational facilities provided by societies of this kind through their libraries, dm., he said that although he had not found time to read more than about two new novels during his ',bishopric, he had succeeded in reading Lord Beaconsfield's " Endymion." He had pernsed this fanciful novel with a good deal of amusement and interest, and though the novel was not very satisfying to his mind, he was enabled to pick out of it two sentiments which seemed to he the best in the book, one of which described horse-racing as the most demoralising pastime of the people of this country, whilst the second sentiment, as expressed in a discussion by a gentleman who was supposed to repre- sent the Young England of the future, was to the effect that co-operation was destined to work a vast good for the great mass of the people of England. An important case under the Burials Act came on before fie Queen's Bench Division on Saturday, the judges holding that A clergyman had no discretion to refuse burial in an old but unclosed churchyard by reason of their hdving been another burial ground provided for the parish. The case, known as the "Kingston Burial Scandal," was one in which the vicar of St. Mary's, Teddington, had for some time de- clined to allow the interment of the body of a child, due notice having been given under the Act. The rev, gentle- man was sued for the expenses of the funeral, which were not allowed. The case was decided in his favour in the county court, but has now been sent back for re-trial. The Lord Chief Justice, correcting a mistaken but very prevalent impression, remarked in the course of the arguments, that in the strict sense of the word a clergyman had not a right in the freehold of his churchyard, and, as to the rights be did possess, they also belonged co-equally to his parishioners. div.head: FENIAN SCARE.
div.p: THE FENIAN SCARE.

Another al.irming Fenian rumour was current in Man- chester on Saturday. It was to the effect that a plot had been discovered for blowing up a number of public buildings and poisoning the water supply. Whether the rumour bad any foundation in fact or not, it had the effect of making the authorities take extra precautionary measures, and strong guards of military and police were stationed at various points said to be threatened. The recent explosion in the Salford Barracks no doubt justified these precautions, but it is doubtful whether there was any basis of truth in the rumours which gave rise to them. It is very improb- able that if the Fenians at Manchester or elsewhere contem- plated mischief they would be so considerate as to inform the public as to what they were about to do. A London contemporary says: That the Government are taking unusual precautions to protect the Government pro- pAdy is quite evident; but the barracks and arsenals that are generally well pretected may feel pretty secure under tins head. There is, however, another kind of property easily accessible, but which cannot be so easily protected. The telegraph system of the country is the property of the Government, and any line of that system is at the mercy of anyone whe feels destructively inclined. Have the Govern- ment well considered this weak point in their harness ; and and are they provided with any system of adequate protec- tion?

THE AGITATION IN IRELAND. At a meeting, on Monday, at the Tußemote branch of the Land League, it was stated that the wife of a prominent Irish member of Parliament was assisting in the formation of a Ladies' Land League. The object of the movement, in view of contemplated repressive measures, is to have ladies to take the place of the Land League executive should the latter be arrested, and assist in distributing relief to evicted tenants. Miss Anna Parnell is understood to be the president of the Ladies' League. ‘syerat lidieA in Tlorco !n PellItf!" Is if an_ .s expected the MoVe- ' P.lBbi will IA4 totulally organised next Tuesday, when the central league nieete, The Land Leaguers in Cone have resolved, in the event of the League being suppressed by the Government, to form secret societies. On Saturday they unanimously deter- mined to call upon Messrs. Shaw and Colthurst to resign, expressed regret that Mr. Bright had become a "turncoat," and one of the speakers—a Mr. Harrington—made the dread- ful announcement that if Mr. Parnell sent a message to Ire- land telling the people not to touch anything that was manufaltured in England it would be acted upon. A Westport telegram states that the steward of Mr. Mit- chell Henry was fired at on his way to Kylemore Castle, but he escaped unhurt. Several landlords in the Balla district have refused to pay income tax on the ground of their not having received any rent during the past year. At Boyle Borough Court, Colonel King-Herman on Mon- day fined two farmers £1 each for cheering in the street, and anncunced that others brought up for the same offence would get seven days imprisonment without the option of a fine. Mr. Cowen, M.P., in acknowledging a vote of thanks from the Newcastle branch of the Land League, promises to resist to the full all attempts to apply coercion to the Irish people. He fears resistance will be unavailing, but the necessity for opposing such hateful legislation is none the lees urgent on all Radicals. RnonGANtskriox OF THE LAND LEAGUE —The London correspondent of the Leeds Mercury says :—Obstruction, in the House of Commone is carried on with the following pur- pose :—As soon as the Government Coercive Bill becomes law, the Land League, as at present constituted, will be powerless. The scoundrels to whom Mr. Forster referred, and who are most active and unscrupulous members, will be either in prison or beyond the sea. In view of this con.tin- gency, Mr. Devitt is now engaged in organising the society on a different basis, so that the Land Leaguers will be able to continue their policy without any person being held .e- -sponsible for it. The scheme in question will occupy several weeks, and it is calculated that if the discussion of the bills can be made to last for six weeks, Mr. Davitt will have everything in order. As an illustration of the terrorism which the Land League now exercises in some parts of Ireland, it was rnentioued, in the course of proce dings in the Dublin Queen's Bench Court on Monday, that no process-server would venture to serve writs in the Tulle district. At Cloghan, King's County, a land meeting was held on Monday, at which a noticeable feature was the presence of 500 horsemen. Some dlys ago a shot as fired through the shop window of a tradesman in Crossmolina, county Mayo. The bullet lodged in the ceiling. The object of the offender is believed to have been to frighten the occupants. The troopship Himalaya left Portsmouth on Wednesday with twa steam pinnaces. each armed with a Gatling gun, for coastguard service in the Shannon with her Majesty's ship Valiant"' Several more Irish landlords, including Mr. Patrick Foley, of Donaile, and Mr. John Culligan, Kneckerra, have accepted rents at Griffith's valuation. At Gorlor, Mayo, on Wednesday, an inquest was held on a man who died from fracture of the skull. He was examined by a magistrate before his death, but refused to reveal who had inflicted the injury.
VACCINATION AND RE-VACCINATION,

The Local Government Board have issued a circular, dated the 26th January, to boards of guardians, directing attention to the necessity, in view of the present prevalence of small-pox, of special measures being taken for the pro- motion of vaccination and re-vaccination. The board re- commend that special inquiries, if necessary from house to house, should be made by vaccination officers in order to detect all children who are illegally unvaccinated, an I that means should be taken to make known the advantages of re-vaccination. It is stated that, generally speaking, the best time of life for re-vaccination is when growth is com- pleting itself, or between the age of 15 and 18; but tke board advises that when small-pox becomes epidemic, not only should all persons above 15 years of age, who have hitherto neglected to have themselves re-vaccinated, be care- ful to neglect it no longer, but in cases where there is like- lihood of infection, even ;he age of 15 should not be waited for, especially by those 'whose marks of original vaccina- tion are unsatisfactory. It is further stated that re-vaccina- tion, once properly and successfully performed, does not appear ever to require a repetition. The nurses and other servants of the London Smallpox Hospital, when they enter the service, unless it be certain that they have already had small-pox, are invariably submitted to vaccination, which in their case generally is re-vaccination, and is never after- wards repeated, and so perfect is the protection, that though the muses live in the closest and most constant attendance on small-pox patients, and though, also, the other servants are in various ways exposed to special chances of infection, the resident surgeon of the hospital, during his 41 years of office there, has never knownamall-pox to affect any one of these nurses or servants. To this experience is added that of the Metropolitan Asylums Board, which shows that of the numerous nurses employed by the managers in their large hospitals, although such nurses inevitably come in cbntact with cases of small-pox of the most malignant type, not one has ever died from that disease, and in the three cif four instances in which they have contracted it it has shown itself in a very modified form. It has been the practice to re-vaccinate these nurses en their entering upon their duties, but not to repeat the operation; and thus, so far as this very extensive experience goes, it shows that re-vaccination, properly performed, affords almost absolute protection from small-pox, and entire immunity from fatal attacks of that disease. The board further point out that re-vaccination is now performed by all public vaccinators at their respective vaccination stations; and, so far as is not inconsistent with ptletersmonorcennilminpgerwaittihvienctlhaeimtserinfosr npfritthnearryegvnalactciin.nnastimona,37tohlyne applying to the public station of the district in whichornedfecriernecue- lar, dated the 27th of January, has beeresides, obtain re-vaccination free of con sti. Assued e to ate children born in workhouses and poor-law infirmaries, most of whom have hitherto escaped vaccination in Conse- quence of the difficulty of tracing them after the diqcharge of their mothers. THE ST. HELENS GLOBE ALKALI WORKS STRIKE. ,fikesßke at Nee chemical works, an account of which was published in the Examiner a few weeks ago, seems to be as far off alisettlement as it formerly was. The men, to the number of 300, it will be remembered, struck against a reduc- tion from Sc. a ton for the making of salt cake to 2s. 6d. a top. A statement having been published that the wages were the same as those at Widnes, the men have desired us to state that the lowest wages in Widnes are 2s. 10d. and 2s. lid.; and as much as 3s. in the majority of the works there. It was also said that the men could earn as much as £1 17s. 6d. a week, and this they contradict, and say that the earnings of each salt cake furnace man averages about 288., and had to be earned by the sweat of the brow, and by breathing large quantities of gas. There are: • about thirteen chemical Works in St. Helens, the Globe Alkali Company being the only one to reduce the wages, and some of the other firms have actually raised the wages of their men. The price through- out the town is 3s. a ton, and in some works 3s. 44. We understand, on good authority, that; the Globe Alkali Co. have been endeavouring to import men from Newcastle, but having been made aware of the condition of affairs by the strike comenittee in St. Helens, the Newcastle men have decided not to come, and have written expressing sympathy with those who are out on strike. The firm say that their furnaees are of quite modern construction, and were erected at considerable cost. This the men admit, but say they are not as perfect as they might be. and they consider that the reduction is more unjustifiable, as other firms in the town have made advances in the wages of their employes. The men on strike desire to express their thanks for the support they have received in Widnes as well as in St. Helens, and hope that the strike will soon be at an end. MINERS' STRIKE AT ST. HELENS. The strike in St:' Helens and immediate neighbourhood during the past week has furnished but very little to write about, but the miners apparently are as firm as ever to re- main out until their demands have been conceded. St. Helens has been exceedingly fortunate in being free from riot and lawlessness. The sympathies of the public are with the miners, and one tradesman, Mr. Peter MoKinley, hal taken a very active part in the struggle, and presided at several of the miners' meetings. It was rumoered on Satur- day that a disturbance was likely to take place at the Ashton Green's Colliery, but nothing of the nature of a breach of the peace *occurred. Nearly 200 colliers ptesented them- selves for payment of four days' wages alleged to be due to thorn. It was said that the money would not be paid, and Superintendent Johnston, with a good force . of men, went to the place to be in readiness should a disturbance ensue. During the after- noon the manager announced that the wages would be paid on the following Monday, and the men went quietly away: The men were paid onlitionday according to promise. Many thousands of men went from St. Helens on Monday to at- tend a mass meeting on Newton Common, Mr. P. McKinley presiding. It was then resolved to remain out on strike until their demands were granted. On Thursday afternoon a large`ineeting of. miners assembled on the Fair thouod. having been called together by the bell-man. Mr. P. ale Kinky. presided. Mr. Cross complained that soaie of the colliers in Rainford had gone to their masters to ask to be allowed to return to work although they had only a ftw days previously expressed themselves determined to remain out. He believed St. Helena was the last to come out, and if the other miners in the district had been AS honourable, nothing would have been found to say against them. He believed St. Helens would be the lasi to go in. Although the masters cou d very well afford to give them what they asked for, yet they did not like to be considered defeated, and they were willing to lose £lO,OOO in one way or another before they would give in. One firm near Wigaii had said they had 30,000 tons of coal yet, and they would give the advance when that was used up, and only one colliery in Wisan lesd offered the advance. He complained that the newspapers had not given them a fair representatioti, but had said that certain collieries were commencing' work, when nothing of the sort was the case. Some of the masters had saidia' You are not united ; we will starve you out, as you have, no money." No doubt it was hard when they had five or six children, bat What did they do in former days ? They even died by the roadside and starve 4 in the fight for liberty, No country ever got its liberty without struggling and fighting for it. They had made the masters give up the Liability-Bill, had made them promise weekly pays, and it was now for them to say whether they would make them give the advance. - Mr. Cron concluded by moving that a deputation of men wait on Friday upon the masters to see if they would give the advance, and that the report be.lodged the same evening at nine o'clock at the George Inn. • The motion was seconded. Mr. DOWNES then addressed the meeting, and said those miners who had had the advance offered might go in if they. liked, but he could tell them that if they did so the battle would be lest—(hear, hear)—for if they did that it would be far more difficult for the others to remain out until they got theirs, and if they were not able to remain out and had to go in at the same wages, bow long, in the nadir of common sense, would the other masters continue to pay' 10 percent. more than their friends. If part of the men did go in at an advanced rate the battle would be lost to everyone of them. (Cheers.) He would move, as an amendment, "-that the men do not wait upon the masters until they are sent for. (Laughter and cheers.) The CHAIRMAN then put the amendment, at the same time advising everyone to vote as he thought fit, and nearly every hand was held up in favour of the amendment. About seven voted for the original motion, and the amend- ment was declared carried. A mass meeting of the miners is arranged to be held an Newton Common on Monday, when the question will be further discussed. The meeting on the Fair Ground was very orderly, and the men quietly dispersed. MASS MEETING ON NEWTON COMMON. On Monday afternoon a large meeting of miners was held on Newton Common. It was apprehended that disturbancei might arise, and special precautions were taken by the authorities. Shortly after noon largo bodies of men made their way to the common from Ashton, Haydock, St. Helens, Wigan, Leigh, Tyldeslev, and Hindley. The number present was variously estimated at from 5,000 to 8,000. During the meeting a carriage containing Colonel hPCorquodale, and Messrs. J. Pearson, R. Houghton, and F. S. Gerard, county magistrates, and Mr. E. H. Woodcock, clerk to the justices, drove past and stayed awhile watching the proceedings, which on the whole were most peaceable. Mr. Peter M`Kinley, St. Helens, who was called upon to preside, said the men were met that day to assert their righti, and to try and get a fair day's wage for a fair day's work. (Hear, hear.) Was there anything wrong in that (Cries of "No.") Then he maintained that the colliers' rights were no rean's wrong. He was happy to see that in that district they had so far conducted themselves like gentlemen, and he had no doubt they could still assemble to maintain their rights, and behave as became them. (Cheers.) Any man who did not fight for his wife and family would be a coward. (Cheers.) He felt sure that this question of an advance of wages would sooner or later come to be decided in favour of the men, because they had been working for such a length of time at very low wages, so that it had come to be almost impossible for them to keep body and soul together. (Cheers.) The men were determined not to submit to the present state of things any longer, and he maintained that they were right. (Cheers.) They were only asserting their rights and .he was certain these rights must prevail in the end. (Cheers.) Mr. John Houghton, a Medley miner, said they did not intend to fight as before—one part working and the other on strike. They were unanimous in their demands. The men must not be afraid of the battle. He had a wife and six children, and not a penny coming in, but he would stand till he died in the street rather than give in. The masters thought because they were poor they could grind them down still lower, but they would see. Mr. John Cross (St. Helens) said wages had got so low now that the men could barely keep soul and body together, and yet the masters said they could not give any advance. He could tell the masters that many a Oilier was now in a better position than when he was working; because hundreds of men had often to go home from their work and see the agonies of their starving wives and children. (Cheers.) He maintained that it would have been impossible to have got such unanimity among the men if they lead not had great grievances to redress. Referring to the present prices of coal and slack, the speaker said the colliery proprietors ought to raise the price of slack from 4s. to 6s. a ton, because at the former price they were selling it at aloes, whereas the latter figure would enable them to give the men the advance they sought. (Cheers.) He advised the men to stick together until they got their demands,'because .f they surrendered to the masters, they might depend upon it that their position would be worse than ever it had been before. He concluded by urging the men to go into the other counties, and try to persuade their bretheren there not to send up another ton of coal until the masters acceded to their demands. (Cheers.) Mr. If. Stringfellow (Wigan) urged the men when they went to work to join a strong union, founded on sound and practical principles, and to work together for the good of all. A resolution to the effect that those present pledged them- selves to remain out on strike until the masters conceded their demands as to an advance or wages and also to the weekly payment of wages was carried with acclamation. A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the meeting, and the assembly then dispersed. FAVOURABLE ASPECT OF AFFAIES. The secretary of the Coal Owners! Association of South - We... Lancashire wrote to Mr. Pickard, the miners' agent at Wigan' on Tuesday, informing him that as soon as the men return to work a committee of the masters will meet an authorised deputation of the 'nen on the question of a slidieg scale and weekly pay. The district on Taesday was very quiet. At several pits the men have returned to work under protection.

THE ST. HELENS TRAMWAYS.—A special general meeting of the St. Helens Tramways Company was held at the Fleece Hotel, St. Helens, on. Monday afternoon, in °ln' iance with the s Standing orders of the House of Commens. Thi local Tramway Bill was passed in 1878, and provided that in two Tears the undertaking should be completed. If it were not so, the powers to continue the work would cease. It has been fon - -n- .n3possible to finish in July nest, and an e/tention of time is sought. The meeting confirmed the action taken in Parliament. Regarding the Prescot section, it was loped to be finished in a short time. The weather, the chairman stated, had prevented operations but as soon as the ground was in a fit state to be worked upon, the *Ma- , tractor Would commence again.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
• HOUSE OF LORDS.—MoNneY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at five o'clock. .

THE Tnassuar,.—The Earl of KIMBERLEY, replying to a question on the subject, said the Government had received no further information as to the position-of affairs in the Transvaal beyond that already published. THE RIVERS CONSERVANCY BILL.—Lord SPENCER moved the second reading of the Bill for the Prevention of Floods, and explained its provisions at considerable length. It was proposed to proceed by provisional orders, to be applied for by conservancy bodies, sanitary authorities, or owners and occupiers of lands to a certain value. The taxation neces- sary under the bill would be divided among lands separated into three classes—uplt nd, midlands, and lowlands—the up- lands not to be rated to more than one-sixth the extent of the highest rate in the district. The objects of the bill were four—namely, to give protection from injury by floods, to facilitate arterial drainage, and to provide ter the storage of water and the irrigation of land. On application fo the Local Government Board, conservancy boards may be ap- pointed with power to execute the necessary works, pro- vision being made for protecting the rights of the owners. The general purposes of the Act were the protection of land from injury by floods, the arterial drainage of land, the storage of water for drinking and other purposes, and the irrigation of land. The board would have power to cleanse, repair, and maintain watercourses and ontfalls for water, to embank and improve watercourses by the removal of darns and other obstructions, and to make new watercourses or outfalls. Ample powers were also given for awarding com- pensation to ptivate individuals, to acq.-ire lands, and to borrow money.—After some discussiOn, the bill n/as read a second time. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Trasray.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 5-0. METROPOLITAN WATER TRUST.—The Earl Of CAMPER- DOWN asked whether, considering the present condition of public business, it was not advisable to introduce in the House of Lords the bill providing for the creation of a Metropolitan Water Trust. The noble Earl remarked that it was highly probable if this course were not taken the session would pass without this important measure becoming law. The measure was one with which their Lordships were peculiarly fitted to deal, and he hoped the Govern- ment would initiate it in this House in order to give their Lordships something to do.—The Earl of DALHOUSIE said that bill was under the consideration of the Secretary of State, but he had as yet come to no decision with regard to it. On the part of the Government he assured his noble friend that his suggestion should have careful consideratien. The House adjourned at 5-25. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The SPEAKER took the chair at four o'clock.

.NOTICES.—Mr. STANHOPE gave notice that on an early day he would call attention to the policy of the Govern- ment in Afghanistan and move a resolution.—Amid some laughter, Colonel MARINI; gave notice that he will consult with the Chief Commissioner of Works as to the conveni- ence, in view of the prevalence of daylight sittings, of having a flag flying from the Clock Tower at hours when the light which pow indicates that the House is sitting is no longer visible. BRITISH REPRESENTATION IN AFOHANISTAN.—In reply to Sir Henry Tyler, Lord RARTINGTON said it was thought desirable that the Indian Government should hare a repre- sentative at CAUL PARLIAMENTARY OBSTRUCTION.—RepIying to Mr. Baxter, Mr. CriADSTOzen bclioved that a feeling of dissatis- faction did exist in the 12.i.ge consittuencei Conierliience of the fiioOrpti.th of the attention of the House by Irish aftaltA; and, he added, amid loud cheers, "the feeling will probably grow." At present, all he would say was that the subject had by no means escaped the attention of the Government, who would be ready to take any steps that might appear desirable for dealing with the matter. TURKEY AND GREECIL—Sir CHARLES DILKE, in reply to questions, said there was now no question of a Conference at Constantinople, it having been arranged that negotiations touching the Greek frontier question should be carried on by representatives of the Great Powers at Constantinople acting individually. There was no question of isolated action, and it was trusted that the negotiations now in pro- gress would have a satisfactory termination. Mr. Goschen would leave for Constantinople in a fevrdays. THE WAR IN Tin& TRANSVAAL—RepIying to questions from several members, Mr. CHILDERS gave an account of the means which had been adopted to secure a prompt and adequate supply of reinforcements to Sir George Colley in the Transvaal. When the insurrection broke out the force at his command numbered 4,100, scattered over Natal and the Transvaal, and now 2,554 additional troops had been des- patched to his aid. On the question of the belligerent rights of the Boers, he said that whilst surprised there could be any doubt that they would be treated according to the ordinary laws of war, he had, to avoid possible mis- apprehension, telegraphed to Sir George Colley instructions that the Boers should be treated in accordance with the recognised rules of ordinary warfare, including the exchange of prisoners. Within sixteen hours, a remarkable evidence of telegraphic facilities, he had received a reply to the effect that, whilst avoiding the questien of belligerent right, Sir George Colley had maintained relations of courtesy with the Boer commanders. "They were," the telegram stated, "acting with courtesy and humanity in the matter of our wounded." THE PUBLICATION OF THE COERCION BILL..— Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL introducing the subject of the accidentally premature publication of the Coercion Bill, Mr. FORSTER said he was as much surprised as any one, but the fault lay entirely with the printers. There was, he added, no substantial difference between the text of the Bill and the statement he had made when introducing it. THE PROTECTION OF PROPERTY AND PERSON IN IRELAND.

div.p: ANOTHER EXTRAORDINARY SITTING: THE LONGEST ON RECORD.

THE HOME RULERS MARCH OUT IN A BODY. Mr. GLADSTONE took an opportunity of stating, amid loud cheers from both sides of the House, that the second read- ing of the Protection Bill would be taken at the sitting after the first reading was agreed to, and it was expected that the division on the first reading would be taken at the currenb sitting.—'The debate on the first reading was resumed by Mr. CHARLES Law's, who was followed by Mr. C. RUSSELL. The hen. and learned member, in a long speech, delivered under the disadvantage of an almost empty House, strongly opposed the Bill. The discussion was maintained with the unwonted assistance of some English members, Mr. HOP- WOOD and Mr. Rnoarintinwr speaking as Radicals in favour of the Bill, which was supported on totally differentgrounds by Mr. NEWDEGATE, Who involuntarily created some amuse- ment by rising before Mr. T. D. SULLIVAN, who preceded him, bad concluded his speech. So impressed was Mr. Newdegate with the conviction that by this time the hon. member must have brought his remarks to a conclusion that he insisted upon commencing his speech, and for several scconds gentlemen near him failed to bring home to him the fact that Mr. Sullivan was yet in possession of the House. At 11 o'clock Mr. A. M. SULLIVAN rose and succeeded in drawing something like "a House" whilst he defended the Land League, and, as alate corner from Ireland, ridiculed the notion that outrages existed in that country, or that alarm prevailed, except in the columns of "landlord-terror journals."—Whilst hon. members have apparently had enough of a discussion that practically has lasted over three weeks, the interest of the public, as represented in the gal- leries facing the Speaker, is rather on the increase. Night after night long lines of strangers sit or stand in St. Stephen's Hall, waiting for the remote chance of gaining admission to the galleries. On Monday night, as on all earlier nights of the Session, the galleries were crowded to the fullest ex- tent. A remarkable feature in this now familiar aspect was the presence of a large number of peers, prominent among them being Earl Spencer. Just before midnight Mr. Daw- eon commenced a speech which, with the assistance of many documents, carried the House far into the next day. When he resumed his seat there were loud cries for a division. These were answered by a motion for the adjournment moved, by Mr. Gabbett. Mr. Gladstone, without waste of words, announced, amid loud cheers, that the Government would jloownrinn resist the motion. The debate was then resumed, and the question of ad- gmeenact each other er in incessantly s u ticseeslls succession—Mr. Irish members .171m.e.lrisbtreLs vf AO :N. advocated the adjournment on the ground that Mr. Parnell had not had an opportunity of making his speech on the main question.—The Marquis of HARTINGTON, Mr. Glad- stone having left the House, asked, amid general cheering, what there had been to prevent Mr. Parnell from speaking at any hour of the evening. It was, he said, rather too much to expect the House to protract the debate for 24 hours because it had not pleased Mr. Parnell to reply to a speech shade last Friday. The noble lord further pointed out that it had not always been thought necessary that every member of a party should speak on a question, and that a much larger party than that of the lionae Rulers had often been satisfied with less discassion than had taken place on the introduction of this bill. It was for the Irish members, he significantly observed, to determine what atnount of resistance they would offer, and, it was for the majority to decide how much endurance they would exer- cise Finally, he declared, amid loud cheering, that the time for compromise was ahnost past, and that a discussion of four nights, following seven nighta of precisely similar debate on the Address, was discussion enough for any subject whatever. At this time there was a full House, and the Strange's' Galleries were filled.— Mr. T. P. O'Corn•ron followed Lord Hartington, whom he ce bl aa nr ggeeda wt bi teh t ehv na e ienfg t, bbsyd et hbaet ec3hnaerta cf t3errt beef fihrisst itni int eer v. enTtny, had, he said, exchanged Don Quixote for Sancho Penn. This betise, which was supposed to indicate M Gladstone and Lord Hartington, excited Only A further irrelevent reference to the nbobl fla t tg laughter.d tet ianr the hon. member to be called to ordermarquis caused the h Speaker; and he then urged that time was wanted for an appeal to the working men of England against the policy oftheGovern- nient. A remark ,calling in quention the freedom of the liberal members to vote as they pleased, brought up e Mr. HUSSEY VIVIAN with a request for the intervention of the Speaker, who observed that if the hon. member charged any hon. member with being influenced by improper motive, he was out of order "—a meanieg which Mr. O'CoNxon at once disclaimed, stating that he had merely accused hon. members of being under the influence of party ties—Mr. MITCILEL Hmertv admitting that he was one of the small minority of Irish members who were contending against an enormous majority in opposing the Bill, asked the minority Whether it was wise in them to fight d outrance. They I would want all their resources for the later stages and he I Pathetically inquired if it was worth while to sit up all night, destroying their constitutions, in order to settle the question whether the Bill should be introduced then or a little later.
