div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEI3RUARY 5, 1881.

He requested Irish members to fight on some intelligible ground, and reconmended them to allow the Bill "in all its deformity and wickedness " to come before the country as soon as posible At half-past three there was a fair attendance of members on the Ministerial and Irish benches, the solitary Conserva- tive who kept guard on the Opposition front ranks being Mr. Alderman White. The Government was represented by Mr. Mundella, Mr. Courtney, and the Solicitor-General for Ire- land, while Mr. O'DONNELL remained in undisputed posses- sion of the floor, declaring the bill turned the House into a registry chamber for the new cases of the despotic Irish Secretary, whom a little further on he styled a lay figure without the least weight. He was called to order several times by the Speaker for going wide of his subject. Shortly before four o'clock Lord Sandon, Colonel Stanley, Lord Crichton, and Sir 11. Gifford, who had been away about an hour, resumed their seats on the front Opposition bench, and were joined a little later by Mr. W. H. Smith.—Mr. BIG-GAR was by this time the orator of the moment. He went on steadily for some time, but finding it necessary to refer to his notes, was greeted with shouts of "Divide." One member, however, said in a tone of resignation, "Go on," the advice which Mr. Biggar followed, amidst great laughter. Presently Mr. Biggar woke his hearers up by declaring that the Irish members were being persecuted by the two parth s following the Government in the vilest conspiracies. This raised shouts of "withdraw," but the member for County Cavan explained it as the conspiracy of an Irish landlord to mislead the Government and the public. Mr. Biggaes I eloquence flowed on for over half-an-hour, when he gave place to Mr. SEXTON, whose rising at ten minutes to five served as a signal to the Speaker to retire. Dr. Mayfair having taken the chair as Deputy-Speaker, Mr. Sexton I argued that though the Marquis of Hartington might be a very great personage in the State—an ironical remark which was cheered in earnest by the House—Mr. Parnell was not bound to consult his convenience, and that the debate, if allowed to conclude without Mr. Parnell having been heard, would be re- garded in Ireland as incomplete and even frag- mentary. Several other Irish members also, including him- self, had not yet found an opportunity of addressing the Heinle on the main question. He held that the Govern- ment feared delay lest they should lose their hold on public opinion in England.—During the delivery of Mr. Sexton's speech, which last for half an hour, the House presented much the same appearance as before, save that the strangers interested in the proceedings showed signs of waning. The last lingerers in the Ladies' Gallery had but lately left. The Solicitor-General for Ireland snatched fitful dozes on the Treasury bench, and Mr. O'Donnell, enveloped in an immense overcoat, slept on his bench in a posture which was an impartial compromise between sitting and lying. Mr. Warton, who had remained in his place for several hours before this period, and had not left th 3 House several hours later' was alert and vigorous, snuff-box ia hand. The Fourth Party had from an early hour been nnrepresented, and the places usually occupied by two of its leaders were now, oddly enough, filled by Mr. Herbert Gladstone and Mr. Molloy.— Mr. LEAMY introduced a little liveliness into the otherwise dreary debate by his mirth-provoking manner of stating his case. "It has been said," he exclaimed, "that Irish mem- bers have taken up to mueh time." Such an epportunity could not be resisted, and sympathetic cries of "No, no ; certainly not," reached him from the Liberal benches, "It has been said," he continued, "that Irish members have obstructed debate," and again a chorus of comic cendolence was uttered by the Liberal members. "It is said that English feeling is rising against us?" exclaimed the unfortunate nvember, inviting a derisive Volley of "Oh no, not at all." —A reminder from the DEPUTY-SPIAXER that the st.bjeet before the House was th, -djournment, hastened the conclu- sion of Mr. Leamy's short ch.—Mr. T.. D. SULLIVAN— who began by observing that there was no hurry, and ended with the judicious advice to the House. "to sleep over it," —and Mr. BYRNE, who was called to order for not keeping to the question, having disposed of fifteen minutes between them.—Mr. NELSON rose at a quarter to six and spoke for nearly half an hour, amid a shower of calls to order. En- tering upon the subject of the seven hundred years of English oppression, he was informed by the DEPUTY- SPEAKER that the question was a very limited one; and tHn Mr. BIGGAR rose to older, and was promptly ruled to be out of order.—Mr. NELSON next took up. Mr. C. Lewis's speech, and spoke of ,the "audacity" of the hon. and learned gentleman, but, as the word was ob- jected to by a member of the Opposition, Mr. NELSON obligingly substituted for it what he termed the " milder " expression "truculence." Ultimately he was called to order, and being condemned by the chair found a defender in Mr. A. M. SULLIVAN, who moved that the House disagreed with the rulings of the chair. This I produced a scene, Mr. Sullivan standing silent on the floor amid general shouts of "Divide !"—Mr. SAMUELSON, rising, said he had heard Mr. Sullivan remark to members behind hint, "This will do as well as anything else."—The DEPUTY SPEAKER did not think this a.",-grave offence; whereupon Mr. Sullivan expressed satisfaction at being protected from eavesdroppers. Hue was a fresh effence, and, amidst a stormy scene, Mr. Sullivan sat down. _ .

There was considerable confusion, the chair calling en Mr. Nelson to speak, which he did with considerable ve- hemence. His emphatic assertions that he did not mean to obstruct was met with prolonged "Oh, oh," which Mr. Nelson plaintively declared meant that he was telling lies Being greeted with peristent cries of question he at last re- sumed his seat, exclaiming that he really did not know what the question was. At a quarter to seven the House divided: —For the amer.dment 27, against it 148. A result which was greeted with loud cheers, and the sitting went on. At seven o'clock the grey dawn of day struggled to make itself apparent to the legislators' chamber, and nothing could be more dreary and dismal than the revelation it made—the House itself untidy in the extreme, members lolling in every stage of weariness, some slumbering, and others strug- gling gamely to keep their eyes open. By this time the number of strangers had diminished to 50.

As soon as the numbers had been declared, Mr. HEALY expressed his desire to offer a few observations on the general question, and this he did from about seven o'clock till a quarter past nine. Sir T. Erskine May, who had been absent from the Hauge for a time, resumed his place at the ' table at nin• o'clock. Mr. Healy in the course of his ad- dress contributed t new flower of speech to the Parliamen- tary phrase book, namely, the expression "up to snuff." lie was twice ruled out of order, once for baying spoken of Mr. Justice Fitzgerald as a "thorough old crocodile whose proper place would be on the banks of the Nile. On other occasions Mr. Healy was called to order by Sir C. REED (one of the earliest arrivals of the relay okmembers due at eight o'clock), Sir J. Lußßocit, and Mr. MORGAN LLOYD, and though ruled by the DEPIITY-SPBAKER to be technically in order. he was at last advised that he was trying the patience of the House. During Mr. Healy's speech, Sir W. Harcourt, Mr. Childers, and Mr. Forster severally arrived, and were heartily cheered. Mr. Dodson, Mr. Ilibbert, Mr. Shaw Lefevre, Mr. Osborne Morgan, Mr. Trevelyan, and the Lord Advocate also reinforced the Treasury Bench. Sir Stafford Northcote anti Lord John Manners came to do duty for the Opposition. As the fresh men of the rank and lie arrived, the tired watchers on both sides, with a few exceptions (Mr. Warton being one), went away to bed. The curtains were drawn back from the windows, and the scanty daylight of a misty morning then struggled in. Mr. Healy concluded his speech by moving the adjournment of the House, and the motion was seconded by The O'GonerAN MAHON, who had sat through the night, and who, it may be remarked, was in Parliament half a century ago.—Mr. DALY having made a short speech, as to which he was ad- vised from the Chair that it wag difficult to see the bearing of his remarks on the question beford the House, the DEPPTY-SPEAKER, at twenty minutes to ten, retired for a short time for needful refreshments, and on his return the day's sittin may. be said to have commenced.— Calling to order seemed the order of the day.—Sir HARRY VERNEY came in for it, and suddenly collapsed; and Mr. O'Sullivan, who followed, was called to order three times, the third occasion jumping up Mr. A. M. SuLLITAN, who proceeded to discourse upon Parliamentary practice from the days cf Lord Palmerston downwards.—Mr. O'StiLLlvear, finding himself unable to speak to the motion, quietly sub- sided.—Mr. Dimon. discoursed on infernal machines, poisoned water, drc., and was promptly calleed to order by hon. members. He kept on for half an hour.—Mr. O'SHAUGHWESSY next unburdened himself, but being called twice to order in the space of sixty seconds, the hon. mem- ber for Meath took up the cudgels, having been awakened from apparently troubled slumbers, and a terrible combat ensued between him and Sir Henry Tyler on a point of order.—Mr. SaLLIvAN having possession of the house, reverted to the practices of the house from the time of Lord Palmerston, a'subject which the hon. member had evidently carefully studied. He was in good form, and gave an amusing description of obstruction, at the same time advis- ing the Irish members to persevere, feeling sure that the English people would be with them in the end.—Mr. BIGGAR followed, and the discussion ingloriously fell several degrees.—Mr. GLADSTONE entered the house at a quarter past eleven, but members seemed too dispirited to cheer.— Mr. Labouchere and Mr. Afacliver also took their seats, "smiling," as Mr. Healy mournfully phrased it, " under the refreshing influence of clean shirts."—Mr. Benny supported the motion for adjournment, Lord Randolph Churchill entering the house during the hon. gentleman's speech, to all appearance sleepy, and yawning alarmingly, although, as Mr. Sullivan pointed out, he had only been conspicuous by his absence from the all - night sitting. Mr. FINIGAN charged both the Premier and the Irish Secre- tary with having made mis-statements to mislead the House; but although called to order by Sir R. Coss, the House was apparently too languid or indifferent to resent the allegations. Later, Mr. Gregory called the hon. mem- ber to order—an iutertnption which Mr. Finigan described as impertinent. He was then called to order, and under pressure, withdrev.- the word "impertinent," but Mr. WAR- TON thought it was not done in a sufficiently graceful man- ner, and that the hon. member should have apologised.—Mr. HEALY drew attention to the fact of an hon. member having used the word "disgraceful," but the observation had not reached the Deputy-Speaker's ears.—Mr. THOMPSON (Durham) supported the Irish members, and was greeted with loud cheers from the Obstructionists.—Mr. T. D. Sur, LIVIIN being called to order, promptly gave way to Mr. GILL, who spoke with a deliberation which apparently acted as an irritant upon the nerves and temper of limn. members, and a general buzz of conversation ensued. At this time the occupants of the Treasury bench were the Home Secretary, Mr. Forster, and Mr. Bright. Mr. Gill still continued to Perorate discursively amid cries of question. On his concluding, Dr. Playfair put the question; but, Mr. Lalor interfeting, the interminable discussion took a fresh start.

At four o'clock on Tuesday afternoon the House having been in session 24 hours, there were about 150 members present. The air of the House was hot and heavy, and over all there bung a feeling of lassitude and inanite weariness.

Only Mr. A. M. StmuveN, outshining his earlier exploits of endurance, was on his legs, as he had been for brief intervals during twenty-four hours, and was now with resonant voice and emphatic gesture protesting against "the perverseness of the tlevornment." The galleries over the clock were all full, the stria ng,ers displaying an undying interest in the pro- ceedings. 'Noble lords on their way down to another place had looked in to behold the spectacle of the House of Com- mons still sitting. The question before the House was Mr. Healy's motion for the adjournment made at 8 o'clock in the morning in a speech of two hears and a half duration. The motion was rejected by 225 votes against 21. Mr. DALY then moved the alternate motion for the adjournment of the debate, on which Mr. Suituvetz, following his habit of making a speech on each motion, offered a few remarks. Sir PATRICK O'BRIEN introduced into the proceedings a liveliness long lacking. He proceeded with unusual quietude for some time, till he hit upon the declaration that he "was not a lunatic." This statement, introduced with some measure of abruptness and made in a loud voice, sue- ceded in the now difficult task of amusing the House. The laughter and cheers with which it was received reacted , upon the bon. baronet, who thenceforward in animated style declaimed against his compatriots opposite, whom he ob- scurely accused of "playing a game of spoiled five." The House laughed a good deal whilst Sir Patrick was speaking, hut once it broke into a storm of cheering, when he declared that whatever his faults -as an Irish member might be, he had never touched pne penny of the money of the poor. The SPEAKER finally recalling Sir Patrick's attention to the question before the House, the hon. baronet cleverly excused himself by observing that he had for so I rug listened to the speeches from hon. members opposite that he scarcely knew what the question was. . - _

At half-past four Lord Beaconsfield joined noble lords in the gallery, arriving just in time to hear Mr. o,CoNaton POWER express the hope that the debate woulci_continue as long as Irish members could speak a word or brag ene leg after the other into the division lobby.--It was half-past seven when Mr. Daly's amendment was negatived by 163 against 23.—Mr. FINIGAIY, in a speech extending over an hour and a half, moved the adjournment of the debate.—Mr. 13EALY followed with an occasionally violent speech, and, after being several times called to order, resumed his seat in obedience to a significant warning from the Speaker.—Mr. ARTHUR O'Coanecna attempted to lecture the House and denounce the Government, but was met with a storm of angry cries; and Mr. T. D. &murex 'net with a similar ieception, when Sir R. CROSS, recurring to a standing order passed two years ago, invited the Speaker to declare under it that the Irish members had been guilty of a combination wilfully to obstruct the business of the House.—Mr. PAR- NELL and the SPEAKER rose together, amid a roar ~f cries of "Order," before which Mr. Parnell resumed his seat.—The SPEAKER said if he found there was a distinct and clear combiaation on the part of members wilfully and persis- tently to obStruct the business of the House, he should con- sider that tke standing order would apply. He was bound to say that the course of the debate had brought before him evidence of the existence of such a combination. The right hon. gentleman somewhat unexpectedly concluded by calling upon Mr. Sullivan to proceed.—The SPEAKER then left the chair, it being close on midnight, and Mr.l LYON PLAYFAIR presided in his stead. Half-an-hour later Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTB, referring to the poiat raised by Sir It. Cross, asked the Deputy Speaker at what point the limits would be reached at which the Standing Order might be cleerucci to apply. Havißg. expressed sur- prise that no member of the arovernment nau ;:riaen the question was raised before, Mr. CHILDERS, in the ab- sence of Mr. Gladstone and Lord Hartington, promptly answered the challenge. "If you think fit," he said, "and I Lupe you will think fit, to put a stop to this obstruction, you will have the most cordial support of her Majesty's Go- vernment."—Mr. MCCARTHY entered a spirited protest against what he called "this gigantic innovation."—Mr. O'DONNELL'S remarks, which were followed by Mr. NEW- DEGATE with lively manifestations of interest, thrice led to the interference of the Deputy Speaker, Hereupon there were loud cries of" Three times," and Mr. O'Donnell sat down after one of the shortest speeches he ever delivered since elected to Parliament.—Mr. Donsox made a strong ap• peal to the Irish members not to protract a barren discussion. —Mr. (ions'', amid loud cheers, ridiculed the notion of ap— pealing to them, and called upon the Deputy Speaker to declare any member attempting to protract the debate guilty of obstruction.—The DIIPTITY SPEAKER read the statement the Speaker had earlier made, and said he would carefully watch the conduct of the Irish members —Mr. PARNELL was addressing the House when an extraordinary scene burst forth.—Mr. W. H. SMITH, calling attention to the Standing Order, peremptorily demanded that the Deputy- Speaker should name Mr. Parnell.—Mr. LYON PLATFAIR said he did not think he had yet brought himself within the rule.—Hereupon Sir Stafford Northcote abruptly left the House, accompanied by Sir M. Hicks-Beach and other mem- bers of the late Ministry, with the exception of Sir R. Cross. The example was followed by many gentlemen sitting on the back benches, and by a few from the Liberal side of the House.—Mr. PARNELL continuing, Mr. MILLEANK excitedly rose, and called upon her Majesty's Government to support the Chair.—Mr. PARmsr..r. disputed the floor with him, sad some cries rose from the Irish members.—Mr. MILLBANK rising, with increased energy declared that Mr. Biggar had addressed to him an opproadous epithet.—Mr. O'SuRA, who followed, was greeted with angry cries of "Name, name"; but the Deputy-Speaker still withstood the evident desire of the House that someone should forthwith be offered up a sacrifice to order.—Mr. BRIGHT, rising at a quarter past one, brought the House back to a quieter mood. The Govern- ment, he said, did not shirk their responsibility, but altera- tions of the rules of the House were not to be made at a moment's notice. Mr. Gladstone wonld very shortly make a proposition which would, he believed, whilst preservinz freedom of debate, do something to save the English House of Commons from the discreditable scenes which have e late disgraced it. The House continued to sit throughout the whole of Tuesday night without any prospect of the struggle ending. The Irish members succeeded each other with apparently.

interminable speeches, varied by occasional counts of the House and angry altercations produced by calls to order. Several discreditable scenes °marred, members accusing each other of using disgraceful language, but theseeharges generally fell through the chair not having hcard the epithets referred to. At 3 o'clock, on Wednesday morning, Dr. Comaings addressed the House on the following amend- ment, moved by Dr. Limes:—" That, in the opinion of the House' it is expedient and desirable, and is most fully in accord with the wise and generous exercise of the undis- puted power of this House and the interests of tkeeMpire at large, that remedial legislation on the land question in Ire- land should take precedence over the coercive 'Measures proposed by the Government, and that her Majesty's Ministers be requested to reconsider their decision in this regard." Towards the close of Dr. Committee speech Sir Patrick O'Brien entered the House, and shortly afterwards Dr. Commrs, raising his voice to its highest-tones, shouted to the startled House that the bon. member had declared him to be a "b— humbug."—Sir PATRICK O'BRiror dis- claimed the use of the first word, but admitted that he hid said to a mernber that the arguments of Dr. Commins's -speech were "humbug." He apologised to the House, and the incident terminated; but Sir Patrick afterwards amused the House by frequent Interruptions. • At 3-30 a.m, the debate on the main question was con- tinued in an exceedingly- thin House by Mr. BARRY (who spoke for an hour), Mr. HEALY (who spoke for two hOOrEI and a half), Mr. BEAMS, and Mr. BIGGAR. The latter gentleman was in possession of the chair, when, shortly before nine o'clock, the Speaker returned to the House and took the chair. Mr. Gladstone had entered the House a few minutes before, and most of her Majesty's Ministers were present. As the Speaker entered the House there was a great rush of members to their places on the long-deserted benches.

The SPEAKER said:—The motion for leave to bring in the Protection of Person and Property (Ireland) Bill has now been under discussion for about five days. The present sitting, having commenced on Monday last at four o'clock, has continued until this (Wednesday) morning at nine, a period of not less than forty-one hours, the House having been occupied with the discussion of repeated motions of adjournments. However tedious these discussions, the motions have been supported by small minorities in opposi- tion to the general sense of the House. (Loud cheers). A , erisis has now arisen—(cheers)—which demands the prompt interposition of the chair and of the House. (Renewed cheers.) The usual rules of procedure have been found powerless to ensure orderly and effectual debate. An important measure recommended in Her Majesty's speech nearly a month since, and declared to be urgent in the interests of the State by a decisive majority, is being arrested by the action of an incensiderable minority (cheers) the members of which have resorted to those modes of obstruction which have been recognised by the House as a Parliamentary 'offence. The dignity, credit, and authority of this House are seriously threatened, and it is necessary that they sho aid be vindicated. (Cheers.) Undoubtedly the operation of accustomed rules and Methods of procedure, and the legiti- mate powers of the House are paralysed. A new and excep- tional course is imperatively demanded, and I am satisfied that I shall best carry out the will of the House, and that I I may rely upon its support, if I decline to call upon any more members to speak, and at once proceed to put the several questions to the House. (Loud cheers, and cries of "No " from the Irish benches.) I feel assured that the House will be prepared to exercise all its powers in giving effect to this proceeding. (Renewed cheers.) Future measures for ensuring orderly debate I must leave to the judgment of the House; but I may add that it will be necessary either for the House itself to assume a more effec- tual control over its debates or to entrust greater authority to the chair. (Cheers.) This announcement took the Irish members by surprise and they remained in consultation while the Speaker put the question of Dr. Lyon's amendment to the house. On a division there voted— For the amendment Against

Majority 14.5 The SPEAKER then put the question that leave be given to bring in the bill. Mr. Josris M'Caurrny rose to address the house, but was received with cries of "Chair." The Speaker remained standing, whereupon the Home Rulers rose in their places in a group, shouting "Privilege" at the pitch of their voices. The Speaker still standing to call the house to order, the Irish members, led by Mr. M'Carthy, filed out of the house, turning at the door, and bowing ceremoniously to the Chair. Their somewhat dramatic exit was attended with cheers and laughter from the house. Mr. Callan,who alone of the Irish I members voted in the minority, remained in his place. he Bill was then read a first time. MR. GLADSTONE AND THE FUTURE OF OBSTRUCTION. - Mr, Gladstone gave notice that on Thursday he would move

the following resolution for the better conduct of the House : —"lf upon notice g is-en, a motion be made that the state of the public business is urgeat, and if, on the call of the Speaker, forty members shall support it by rising in their places, the Speaker shall forthwith put the question, no de- bate, amendment, or adjournment beingittloWed ; and if, on the voices beinggiven, he shall without doubt perceive that the 'Noes' have it, his decision shall not be challenged; and if otherwise, a division shall forthwith be taken, and if the question be determined in the affirmative by a majority of not less than three to one, the powers of the House for the regulation of business in the several stages of bills shall be and remain with the Speaker, until the Speaker shall declare that the state of public business is no longer urgent." Mr. Gladstone added :—I shall also propose to follow this motion by a second—namely, that the state of public business io argent. , The House adjourned at hale past nine. Mr. J. G. McMinnies and Mr. Rylands were accidentally shut out at the division and prevented voting with the Government.

WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON.

The Speaker took the chair at twelve o'clock. THE COERCION Bru.,.—Mr. Bruntenort gave notice that he would move the omission of the retrospective clause. INCOME TAX N IRELAND.—Replying to Mr. M'Coan, Mr. GLADSTONE stated that the iscome tax in Ireland was levied upon Griffith's valuation. It had not been so levied for the benefit of the Irish landlords, but with the concurrence and the approval, at the tit-melt was laid on, of all the Irish mem- bers in the hosse.—Mr. A. M. SerLuverr asked if the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer would in future levy the income tax on the full rent drawn by Irish landlords.—Mr. GLADSTONE asked the hon. member to repeat his queSUOR. THE RULES OF DEBATE.—Lord R. CHURCHILL asked whether it was the intention of the Government to proceed with the resolutions relating to the rules of the House with- out first giving notice, and whether it would not be neces- sary to rescind the resolution already taken to give prece- dence to the Bills of which Mr. Forster has charge. The noble lord's anxiety for orderly procedure did not receive any encouragement from Mr. Gladstone; nor was he success- ful on further reference to the Speaker, who ruled that such notice would not be necessary.

THE SPEASES AND THE OBSTRUCTION.—Mr. LADOIICHERE "respectfully asked " the Speaker whether his action in closing the debate earlier in the morning had been taken under any Standing Order, and, if so, which. "I acted upon my own responsibility," said the Speaker, "and from a sense of duty to this House." This was received with loud and prolonged cheering fromboth sides. Mr. PAIIMILL, starting from the question put by Mr. Labsuchere, proposed to submit a resolution declaring that the Speaker, in refus- ing to permit further debate on the motion for leave to in- troduce the Protection Bill, had committed a breach of the privileges of the House. This proposal was greeted with cheers from the Horne Rulers, and loud cries ofdissentfram other parts of the House. The Speaker quietly pointed out that the question was one, not of privilege, but of order, and if it mere brought forward it could only be lone after due notice —The Smarm having dis- posed of Mr. Parnell and The O'Donoghue, Mr. A. M. Sim- Livew came to the front, and was found a mach more per- sistent combatant. At some evident peril, and under repeated warning, he argued the case first with the Speaker and then with the Premier, turning aside from time to time to dispose of interjectory remarks from various parts of the House.—After this had gone on for some time, Mr. GLAD- f'TDNE called upon the Speaker to proclaim Mr. Sullivan's observations As disorderly.—The Speaker did not adopt the suggestion, whereupon Mr. SULLIVAN, rising again, said, "I thank you, sir, for your ruling, and I thank God that the rules of this House are in your hands and not in his"— Pointing, with dramatic gesture, to the Treasury Bench, where Mr. Gladstone sat amid his colleagues. Stormy cries of " Order!' greeted this outburst, but Mr. Sulli- van proceeded at further length. Eventually, amid cries that warned him that he had been cautioned three' times, he concluded with a motion for the adjournment.— It was of course opposed by Mr. Gladstone, and supported by Mr. Cowen, but great surprise was occasioned by the Idriilecthoivoninersey,rnetbcheear recently Lord R. Churchill inclined to the side of the rr t t refusedbearing in longer n lminde many r aSclidrreSs. N°o ul any tob cae influenced by "the Fourth," and threw in his lot with the Government. Mr. Onslow followed the same course, and Mr. Balfour; revolting at last against Lord R. Churchill, went over to the ex-Chancelkr of the Exchequer, Affairs ' became still more mixed when Mr. M. it'enry lectured the Irish memlsers, and was in turn assailed by Mr. Callan for implying that Mr. Parnell's veracity was in some degree open to question. The series of speeches continued without incident until twenty minutes to six. A divison was taken, and the adjournment negatived by 278 against 44. By the time the figures were announced the usual hoar for adjournment on Wednesday was passed, and the debate necessarily stood adjourned. The rest of the orders were run through wider the supervision of Mr. Biggar and Mr. Finnigan, who, having taken their seats on the front Oppo- sition bench, impartially objected to all but two of the Bills I for which formal progress was prolsosed. These were Irish Bills, and in order to avoid invidious distinctions. Mr. Warton, amid much laughter, rose and completed the round of objections by also blocking these. The House adjourned at a few minutes to six. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIIIRSDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 5 o'clock. THE FLOODS PREVENTION 13 IL,L.—Lord SPENCER con- sented to refer this bill to a Select Committee, but pointed oat that as a committee had already inquired into the matter, it would net be necessary to take evidence. The Navv.—Lord NORTRBROOE gave some explanations 9S to the stoppages of pay in the navy, and the formation of a fund for the relief of the widows and families of sea- meP. HOUSE OF CONIMONS.—TIIIMSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. -- TILE FORTHCOMING LAICD BILL.-Mr. GLADSTONE, in re- II)" to Mr. Givan, said he was afraid, though he wished it vere otherwise, there was 'rut one way of safely and usefully presenting to the House en idea of the nature of the Govern- ment Land Bill, and that was by a lengthehed statement accompanied by the laying of the bill on the table. (Cheers.) They were anitious to do so at the earliest opportunity; but it was impossible te say when that would be.

- AN UNPARALLELED SCENE.—MR. PARNELL AND HIS FOLLOWERS SUSPENDED. In answer to Mr. Parnell, the HOME SECRETARY said that Michael Davitt had been arrested uuder his ticket-of-leave, as after consultation with the law officers of the Crown; both he (the Home Secretary)and Mr. Forster were of opinion that Davitt had violated the conditions of his license.— Mr. PARNELL asked which condition had been violated amid cries of "No, no," and Sir William Harcourt making no reply the Irish members, continued in a body to shout with great vehemence " Answer," ' Answer," " Why don't you answer ?"—The SPEAKER thereupon rose and called upon Mr. GrAnaronx, who was received with cheers, and was about to proceed with the introduction of his motion respecting obstruction, Mr. Dlizote, however, was also on his feet, and was greeted with cries of "Order."-The SPEAKER : The right hon. gentleman is in possession of the House.—. Mr. DILLON again rising amid a storm of interruption said • Mr. SPeaker —The SPEAKER rose and there were cries of "Chair," and Mr. Dillon, as is the cuatom of the House, was expected to resume his seat, but he stood defiantly looking at the Speaker, amid a scene of painful excitement.—The SPEAKER, when the clamour had momentarily subsided, said: I call upon the lion member to resume his seat.—Mr. DILLott paid no regard to the command of the Speaker, but stood in a wsition of contemptuous defiance. Shouts of "Name him " were raised from all parts of the House.—Mr. DILLoN : Mr. Speaker, I rise to demand my privileges. (Cries of "Name him," and counter cries from the Irish benches of "A point of order.") This scene of excitement continued for several minutes, the Speaker and Mr. Dillon both standing.— Mr. GLADSTONE then moved the suspension of Mr. Dillon for the remainder of the sitting.—As the House was clearing for the division, Mr. A. M. Sur-uvarr shouted: Mr. Dillon rose to a point of order, and I object to the division.—The cry was taken up by other Irish members, "We object to the division," and they could be heard conjuring one another, "Don't move, don't move ; " and for a time they all kept their seats, as if with the intention of taking no part in the division. Then there was a brief consultation among them, and they went out in a body into the division lobby. The result of the division was—For Mr. Dillon's suspension, 395; against, 33. The SPEAKER called upon Mr. Dillon to withdraw, but that hon. member, regardless of reinonstrances and hisses, "most respectfully" declined to go Out when told by the Speaker. Having brought his defiance to this climax he sat down, and on his again refusing to move he was loudly cheered by the Home Rulers. Meanwhile the vigilant Sergeant-at- Arms had crossed the bar and was ready to advance up the floor. At the command of the SPEAKER be walked towards the gangway to reach Mr. Dillon and had to approach Mr. SoLuvax, who had risen to make a protest, which he sought to enforce by reference to Mr. Bradlaugh's case. No notice of this irregular harangue was taken by the Speaker, and the Sergeant, steadily pursuing his course, passed Mr. Dawson, and making his way along in front of the seco-d bench invited Mr. Dillon to follow him.—Mr. DILLorr did not stir, but, with arms folded, treated the Sergeant with haughty disdain.—Captain GOSSETT, fully equal to the emergency, new as it was, beckoned to his myrmidons waiting expectantly at the bar, and Mr. Hartley, one of the door keepers, together with four other officials, marched in single file up the floor and along the gangway, where they joined the gallsnt Sergeant. Mr. SULLIVAN, in the row above them, was gesticulating violently as he con- tinued his disorderly address, and the wondering House made ready to witness a violent outburst on the part of the incensed Irishmen. Mr. Dru.ow, finding the Sergeant and his small army ready for action, muttered sulkily, "If you use force I will go,' and he rose and walked with the Ser- geant at the head of the troop out of the House, his friends crying "Shame" by way of expressing their sympathy with one whose expulsion was joyfully watched by the rest of the assembly. It was tken open to Mr. SULLIVAN to state his objection, and the SPEAKER easily convinced the House that he had acted with stricu regularity in dealing with the rebellious Mr. Dillo A stormy scene followed, in which Mr. Parnell moved that Mr. Gladstone be not heard. Ultimately the Speaker " named " Mr. Parnell as disregarding the authority of the Chair. Mr. Gladstone moved his suspension during the remainder of the sitting, and this ws- i also agreed to, Mr. Parnell leaving the " I Exactly the same scene was repeated in the Finigan, the numbers in the division ha bi-
against 2. A body of P.unellites ref,' during the division, and their tellers, the the Speaker " flair- - gardo4 the authorit—

were then suspended, amidst the greatest excitement, by 410 against 6 votes. Mr. 01Celly and Mr. O'Donnell were also subsequently suspended.—Order having been restyred, Mr. GLansronn moved his resolution, adding the following words at the end;—" Or until the House shall a. determine upon a motion made after notice given by any member, put without amendment, debate, or adjournment, and decided by the majority." Mr. Gladstone, in an eloquent speech, which was heartily applauded, expressed deep regret that, after nearly forty years experience in the House, he should be compelled to move such a resolution. He could not, he said, long hope to see the operation of it; but he trusted that under it many honourable members might maintain the dignity of Parliament, and save the Housq of Commons from being made the laughing-stock of the world. He de- clared that the question of the adoption of the new rule was not one of honour or dishonour, but of life or death, a remark which was received with loud cheers. The right hon. gentleman paid a graceful tribute on the part of Her Majesty's Government to the conduct of the Opposition for the fidelity and self-sacrifice displayed by them in the interests of the country since Parliament had assembled. He accepted at once Sir S. Northcote's amendment that the Proceedings described in his resolution should only be taken On the motion of a Minister of the Crewn.—Mr. M. HENRY moved as an amendment that the question be adjourned, which was supported by Mr. CALLAN, who was commenting on the suspension of the Irish members, when he was called to order by the Speaker, and eventually this amendment was defeated by a vote of 371 against 228.-14 amendment, moved by Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE, which proposed that the majority giving power to the Speaker should consist of not less than 300 was negatived by a vote of 234 against 150.—Mr. Gransporen suggested that such power should be given by a majority of three to one in a House of 300 members, which was agreed to without a division, and the resolution as amended was then adopted. Mr. GLADSTONE: I have now to move "That the state of public business is urgent," and, in conformity with the terms of the resolution just passed, I, being a Minister of the Crown, declare in toy place that the Bill for the Pro- tection of Life and Property in Ireland now before the House is urgent, and that it is of importance to the public interest that the same should be proceeded with without delay. The resolution was, amid prolonged cheers, carried with- out opposition or discussion. The House adjourned at ten minutes past- two.

It is said to be owing to the assistance given him by Signor Gessi, one of Colonel Gordon's old lieutenants, that Dr. Junker has succeeded in penetrating into the heart of Niam-Niam country, where no traveer has been before. On reaching Dem-Bekir, near the southern borders of Dar-Fertit, he ascertained that the chief Ndoruma was in the neighbour- hood, and desired to learn the objects of his journey and the number of men he had with him. He succeeded in making a favourable impression on him, and this powerful chief re- turned home to prepare a house for Dr. Junker. The latter afterwards moved on Loin Dem-Bekir to Solongo, where he found a large body of porters sent by Ndoruma to accompany him to his town. PRESOOT PETTY SEssione.—These sessions were held on Tuesday before Messrs. Thompson and H. A. Bright. —Paul Hunt, landlord of the Eagle and Child public-house, was charged with unlawfully opening his house for the sal* of intoxicating liquors on the 9th January, being Sunday. —P.S.'s Dingley and Crawford and P.C. Morgan gave evidence to the effect that they saw a man enter the Nouse at five minutes to eight in the morning. Another came and Was admitted. A lad was seen to enter with a bottle, but he shortly came out. In a short time he again entered, and the policeman went to the door, which was not opened for several minutes. One of the sergeants spoke to the lad, who answered that he bad come for six pennyworth of rum; but on the landlord putting the question to him, he replied that he had come for castor oil. When the police- men entered, the landlord was engaged at a barrel, appar- ently tapping it. The bottle which the lad had in his hand smelled strongly of whiskey.—Mr. Swift, who defended, said there was no evidence against the defendant, and called the I lad, who said that he went to the public-house the first time for six pennyworth of whiskey, but the landlord said he did not sell on Sundays. He went the second time for some castor oil, as the landlord's wife promised his aunt Jane some the night previous, eh.' being charwoman for the defendant's wife.—The magistrates dismissed the case, remarking there was not sufficient evidence, although the case was very suspicjous.—John Heap was then charged with being found on the premises for an unlawful purpose I during the time the premises Ought to haVO been closed.— The defence was that he was the companion of a man named , Dutton, who lodged at the house, and he was there simply ' to see his friend, and did not have any liquor.—The officers having stated that there were no appearances of any drink- ing, the case was dismissed.—Paul Hunt WAS charged with being drunk on his own licensed premises on the 22nd Jan. —Sergeant Bull deposed to seeing the prisoner in the front room so drunk as to be utterly unable to manage his business. The house was in a disorderly state, young people were dancing, and two persons were quite drunk.—ln answer to Mr. Swift, witness said defendant walked up and down the stairs without assistance.—Dismiised.

WARRINGTON PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY. The House assembled on Monday evening St the Co- operative Ha 11, the Chairman of Committees (Mr. W. Stirrup) presiding in the absence of the Speaker. There was only a moderate attendance of members, but the "strangers' gallery " was well filled.

IMPLIES. • The FOREIGN Sr-am-ratty, replying to the member for West Cumberland, said he should have thought the records ; of the House would have made it unnecessary for him tio have answered the bon. member's question. The House would remember when he was speaking on the subject of Ireland his time happened to expire, consequently he hadto I finish with a rather awkward observation. After that be • wrote a letter to the then Leader of the Opposition, who read that letter to the House, and it was now a record of ' the House. That letter sufficiently explained his views. • The HOME SECRETARY, in answer to the member for Evesham, said he was rather surprised that the bon. mem- ber should have the rashness to put a question with regard to the London water question, because it was well known that the Liberal party made use of that question to turn out the Tory Government, and, raving made use of that ques- tion, they had dropped it like a red-hot poker. (Oh.) The Fon, member was quite competent to deal with the question himself, and be would receive every cornideration from that side of the House. The WAR SECRETARY, replying to the member for Halifax, said there was little information with regard to the outrage at Salford Barracks beyond the fact that the jury at the in- quest returned a verdict of " wilful murder" against some person unknown, and the Government had offered a sub- stantial reward. As to the second part of the question, he had no knowledge of any other outrage, although precau- tions had been taken to prevent them. The PRIME MINISTER, answering the member for Wolver- hampton, said no clergymen of the Church of England Lad been committed to gaol under the provisions of the Public Worship Regulation Act. (Laughter and Ministerial chee-s.) Probably the hon. member did not seem to understand that the Public Worship Regulation Act did not provide any punishment for contempt of court, for which offence those clergymen we-e sent to prison. Replying. to the rePmber for Mid-Lincoln, the PRIME MINIsTER fork' he should be very sorry to hear that the Land Leawoe wei e foi MIN{ a League in England with the object of that in Ireland. He did not know if that was the case, but if tLey dlti so it would be the duty of the Govern- ment to take not:ce. of L. The COLONIAL S,:cril.rany stated, in answer to the mem- ber for EvubLAln,thatairangements had been made for dis- cottinuing the forced Ltbour ordinance in the island of Cyprus; but he observed that forced labour ordinanceg were by no means confined to that island.

THE ORDER OT BTSINESS. The PRIME Alumna said he was hopeful if the debate on the Queen's speech was concluded that night, that the first business the Government almost felt bound to intro- dnce Was a bill for the prottction of lift and property in IreFuld. (Applause.) As Nam as ever that bill was passed or an opinion of the Hons expressed upon it, the Govern- ment would be ready to give private members it a night. A number of notices of luestions having been given, the House proceeded with

THE ADJOURNED DI PATE ON THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. The hon. member for CARDIFF, in resuming the debate on the address, eemplimented those who had had the getting up of the speech, winch in the matter of composition or pre- -1 paration would compar e very favourably with any speech that they had yet had. He also complimented the mover and seconder of the address: It was gratifying to hear that our relations with i-oreign powers were of a friendly nature. ! Of course. Conservative administrators always bad been on 1 friendly terms with foreign powers—(laughter)—and he hoped they would continue to be. As to the South African colonies, the key note of the whale subject meant repres- sion of insurrection. He was sorry to see that word intro- duced in this emphatic manner, because he believed that our position in the South African colonies at present was one of a very peculiar nature, and that they ought to be I very cautious how they proceeded -with those people whom Iwe had undertaken to :overn. But his opinion as to the repressioa of insurrection, which they were pleased to call it, was not a very high one. Referring to Afghanistan, ho I took it that the action of the Liberal leaders in opposition brought that war to a conclusion, and he supposed the House would be asked to give their thanks to those w'ao had brough& about that conclusion, viz, the Liberal party. (Hear, hear; and "No no," from the Government.) He thought the occupation of Candahar was not necessary for the maintenance of satisfactory relations between this country and Afghanistan. He was pleased to find that the little regatta at Dulcigno, which they were told fp playfully about, was to insist upon the carrying out of the provisions of a treaty which was made under the auspices of the Tory leaders. Adverting to Ireland, the hon. member said he was glad to find that the subject of elementary education in Ire- land was under the consideration of Government, and hoped it would have a very full consideration, and result in a measure which would do something to give an education to the people of Ireland, for it was sadly needed. (Hear, hear.) He Bladuld think it was patent to every one who read the , newspapers that it was desirable measures should be intro- duced to improve the relations between landlords and I tenants in Ireland. He was not going to speak against the Imeature which the Government proposed to bring in for the 1 better protection of life and property in Ire/and. .(Hear, hear.) Measures of repression might be necessary, but what he contended was that mere acts of force and acts ef repres- sion did not constitute real statesmanship. (Hear, hear.) As a citizen of England he felt ashamed at the course which had been adopted towards Ireland; and in a capital perora- tion, called upon the Government to introduce measures which would make Ireland a source of strength instead uf weakness to the country to which it belonged. I 1 The HOMH SECRETARY spoke mainly on the paragraph in the speech referring to Ireland, and maintained that coer- cion would stop outrage, assassination, and crime. He was ashamed that these crimes should have been perpetrated in I Ireland, and should have been spoken of so lightly by some of his countrymen. Some members urged that fresh laws should be made, but he would ask what guarantee had they that those laws would be I enforced? The Coercion Bill that had just been brought in i by the Liberal Government ought to have come four months ago—(" No, no," and hear, hear)—because he believed a \ responsible minister who refused to enforce the law practi- cally set himself above the law. An officer of State had no option but to execute the laws passed by the Imperial House of Parliament; and therefore in exercising discretion the minister was guilty of far greater imperialism than ever , they had under the late Government. (" Oh," and cheers.) I The member for EVESHAM, who complained of insolent ' objection from the Conservative members, hoped the Go- vernment would bring in a bill founded on what were called the three f's. The member for NEWCASTLE defended the Indeperkients from the attack made upon them by the Leader of the Oppo- sition, and maintained that it was the dety of every right thinking man to act as the exigenciss of the case demanded. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the speech, he said there were two or three points in it which struck him. It was terse and business like, it was courteous, and emphatic or pro- nounced in tone, toe pronounced in some portions even for him. Turning to Ireland, he said he did not believe in making new laws for the purpose of pleasing peeple who believed-in setting all law at defiance. The members fo; Westmeath (L), Coleraine (C), and Car- lisle (L) having spoken, The PRIME Mixterm said he had not heard the policy laid down in the speech very-severely criticised. He agreed with the Leader of the Opposition that if men looked at questions from an independent standpoint they were far more likely to vote with the Government that with the Oppo- sition. (Laughter and cheers.) In regard to South Africa . they simply accepted the position as it stood, and finding the Transvaal was At, portion of the Queen's empire they thought it ought to remain such. div.head: AGITATION IN IRELAND.
div.p: THE AGITATION IN IRELAND.
ARREST OF DAVITT.

Dumas, Thursday e—vening.—Michael Davitt was arrested this afternoon for breach of the conditions of his ticket-of- leave as a Fenian convict. He was crossing Carlisle Bridge in company with Mr. Ikennan and Mr. Harris on his way to lunch when the party were met by a member of the Dublin detective force who informed Davitt that his presence was requested at the Lower Castle Yard. Davitt at once parted from his colleagues, and accompanied the detective to the head-quarters of the Executive Govarnirent of Ireland. There two English detectives were in waitilig to receive him, and showed him a warrant for his arrest. This arrest seems not to have been generally expected in Dublin, but it will be remembered that at the Land League meeting, about ten days ago, Davitt expressed his belief that he was about to be arrested, and referred to his statement on th,tt occasion as being probably his farewell speech. One curious result of the vigour and determination exhibited by the Government, in the past week or so, has been that in the streets of Dublin at night, and probably also over the coun- try, there-has been a sudden peacefulness—no noisy voices, no tipsy cheers for "Parnell," or for an "Irish Republic," such as were some time ago qnite common. Another result corresponding to the former is that the Dublin police seem to exhibit by their demeanour greater self-confidence and sense of authority as guardians of loyalty and order. THE LAND LEAGUE IN AMERICA. The Roman Catholic Archbishop and clergy of this diocese have issued an address assuring the Irish people of their moral and material support, and approving of the platform of the Buffalo Land League Convention. While promising sympathy and co-operation with all who are guided by its principles, the address denounces the per- nicious and imfamous conduct of the emissaries of secret societies who seek to infuse into the movement the spirit of injustice and disregard for morality. It concludes with a declaration in favour of peace and civic order. The address will be immediately followed by a contribution to the funds of the Dublin Land League.

div.head: SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 57 1881.
div.p: SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 57 1881.

THE position of Irish affairs is one which peculiarly requires that politicians on this side of the Channel should spare no effort of self-restraint so as to keep their heads Cool, their perceptions of duty clear, and their understandings free from prejudice. The acts of the Land Leaguers in Ireland, and of their spokes. men in the House of Commons, have together suc- ceeded in creating a most acute and dangerous crisis in British constitutional government. It is a crisis not only in the internal administration of Ireland and in the social connection of classes in that country, but also in the political relations betwixt IrelAn4 Engianci, and in the working of representative 'government in the House of Commons. Were it to happen that the statesmen who compose the Queen's Government for the time being proved unequal to the severe exigency, whether through personal lack of address and coin age, or from the absence of adequate visible support from Parliament and the constituencies, very calamitous consequences might ensue—nay, could not be prevented from ensuing. First, the social anarchy which has set in in some parts of Ireland would become general and chronic, for, unless the Government can receive from Parliament the powers it requires to restore and preserve order, disorder must continue. Secondly, the subversion of the existing administration in Ireland must leave that country practically without a Government, a prey to all imaginable excesses and intestine feuds, unless the men who had frustrated the Queen's Government had the power to establish in its stead a recognised and capable Irish Government. Thirdly, the unity of the British Empire would be virtually destroyed, and there would be no prospect before the people consti- tuting that empire but a civil war togiettle the quarrel, and either to close up the schism or to complete the separation. And fourthly—which would be to the English and Scottish sections of the nation the most deplorable event of all—our Parliamentary system of self-government would have broken down utterly under the strain, and would have either to be pain- fully reconstructed, or to give place to a less limited Monarchical Government. Have we not then, every one of us, no matter what may be our political opinions, the utmost interest, as eitizens, in the avoid- ance of this terrible collapse and complicated catas- trophe; and must we not be ready to unite in giving to the Government and our representatives in the House of Commons all the support we can to help them to surmount the enormous difficulties which beset them in dealing with Ireland ? Whether we can realise it or not, the situation of this country as regards the Irish section of the nation is hardly less grave than that of the United States of America was just before the outbreak of the Southern Rebellion about twenty years ago. Sectional enmities are Coming to a head. Desperate counsels prevail amongst the disaffected section. Insurrection is un- disguisedly threatened. The conflict in Parliament between the Irish Parnellite members and the rest of the House is to the full as fierce and bitter as any that was waged in the American House of Repre- sentatives before the secession of the Southern States. There may not be really the same probabilities of civil war as existed in the United States after the election of President Lincoln, but that is not because, the disaffected portion of the Irish people, actuated by their leaders, are not ripe for a revolt, but merely that the odds are so heavy against them, the relative military power and material resources of the British Empire so tremendously greater than those of the Irishmen who want to recede, that the rashest amongst them shrinks from the responsibility of giving the signal for war. If a rebellion should break out this year, it will probably be without premeditation, and arise out of some untoward casual collision betwixt the Queen's troops posted in some part of Ireland and a riotous assemblage of Land Leaguers. We state these matters with no wish to unduly alarm our readers, but to impresss upon their minds the fact that the time is really perilous, and to make them feel that no British elector or taxpayer can reckon that the outcome of the struggle of a combination of Irishmen against the laws and the Government, which has now been transferred from the western counties of Ireland to the floor of the House of Com- mons, is a thing of trifling consequence to himself as , private citizen. Irishmen who dwell in English towns and villages, and witness the solicitude of their English neighbours that Parliament should not succumb to avowed obstruction, and that the Govern- ment may obtain the authority it demands to Put down lawlessness and to punish wrong-doers, should understand that it is no spirit of domination over the people of Ireland that England desires these results, but because we all feel that the very stabty of society throughout the realm, and of every institution we possess, is at stake in the contest. The na laon asks for peace, for security to life, liberty, and pro- perty throughout its borders. ; for order and decency in Parliamentary debate ; for room and i toi. legislative reforms to be considered and shaped it is only when a certain party of Irish men e en beaded by Mr. Parnell, seen's to devote bl, to depriving the country of these desired that its people find themselves in undesigned

It has been whispered that certain gentlemen on the Run- corn Board of Commissioners are opposed to the erection of the proposed infcctious Diseases Hoqpital at Runcorn, and, judging from the terribly slow progress made with the scheme, which I believe has been under consideration several years, one would almost be inclined to believe there was some truth in the report. The committee who have charge of the matter are still "struggling" with the site question ; and it will be somewhat marvellous if they get the founda- tion stone of the building laid before the town is incor- porated, the date of which event is no doubt years away. There is much talk in Runcore about the lucky end of the abduction suit, at least as far as the young man is con- cerned. Many people seem to be of opinion that "the parent" would have acted more wisely if he had not been quite so demonstrative. The judge is evidently determined not to stand in the way of making two lovers happy. Notwithstanding the contradiction given to the statemen made in the Examiner the other week, in regard to the Marquis of Cholmondley having granted permission to the Mersey Salt and Brine Company to pass through his Rock Savage estate, to Runcorn, lam prepared to maintain the correctness of my former assertion. The enemies of the company appear to be very active, but I have good reason to believe that all their efforts will prove utterly futile.
The latest original novelty is on which must have special

interest for the ladies—it is that of "Political valentines." The idea is attributed to my amusing and eccentric friend, Mr. Tracy Turnerelli, but I cannot sax that the idea is a happy one. lam rather inclined to the opinion that most of my readers would prefer that " Valentine's Day " and its pleasant amatory associations should remain untainted by such exciting and frequently passionate matters as politics. Just fancy how exasperating it would be to the feelings of a Liberal maiden to receive, instead of the usual skewered hearts and loving sentiments, which tradi- tion has almost sacredly associated with the 14th of Feb- ruary, a copy of verses enlarging upon the legislative value of the House of Lords, or abusing the present Cabi- net as "Demagogic and Radical "! It is quite possible that Mr. Tracy Turnerelli may be able to say, with Dryden, "Old as I am, for lady's love unfit," but I scarcely think that even that justifies him in trying to trample all our cherished customs in connection with Valentine's day un- derfoot, and thrusting his fiery Toryism into a dominion hitherto consecrated to tender sentiment and "spooning." No, no, Mr. Turnerelli, I know that I shall have all tke young ladies with me when I say that we must keep our love making and billet doux entirely free from politics.

The new postal notes that were introduced at the com- mencement of the year have not as yet proved so success- full as was anticipated. Complaints have been made by provincial banks, that an undue length of time is required by the post office before they are cashed, and that the banks are compelled to incur responsibility in case of any irregu- larity, and tke result is that several banks have declined to receive them to the credit of customers. This is greatly to be regretted, as these postal orders seemed to fulfil a want long felt by the public, but unless they are punctually paid upon presentation at the office on which they are drawn, people will soon get chary of taking them. The idea is without doubt a thoroughly good one if properly carried out, but there is evidently great room for improvement at pre- sent.

The new system of saving small sums by means of postage stamps is, without doubt, appreciated by the public from the success which has already attended it The only objection that I have heard raised against it is that it is likely to encourage petty pilfering by office boys and clerks, who may endeavour to become savings' bank depositors at the expense of their employers. I now learn that a plan has been devised which will render such petty felonies very difficult, if not altogether impossible. Arrangements have been made at certain post offices for the peroration of the initials of any large consumer on the stamps, as recognised and recommended by the pbstal authorities, without extra charge. I have also learnt that other merchants can be supplied in quantities of £5 and upwards on payment sim- ply for the die, or, if preferred, from a general stock die (a cross) without any expense. This is a good idea, as "pre- vention is better that cure."

It woul I appear that there is no limit to the purposes for which glass can be used. I am told that wicks of spun glass are being used in Germany for petroleum and spirit lamps, and that they are considered much superior to the ordinary cotton wicks. This would appear to be almost in- credible, but 'my lady readers will probably be still more surprised when I tell them that the latest novelty in ladies' costumes is a beautiful glass scarf. ram informed that these novelties are now being manufactured in the Midlands, and although I have not had the pleasure of inspecting one myself,! am assured by one who has that they are real works of art. They are composed entirely of fibres of glass, drawn out to a more delicate state of fineness than evea floss silk. Although far surpassing that fabric in brilliance and richness of colour, in texture and appearance the glass scarf somewhat resembles satin, except that it can be folded up without creasing. My informant says that it seemed altogether like the production of some fairy loom, rather than the manufacture of a glass blower, and it required a rather considerable effort to believe that the filmy substance of which the fringe was composed had been made by the rough hand of man out of glass.

I heard of a lamentable accident attributable entirely to the recent severe weather. Passing down one of the princi- pal streets of the town just after a heavy fall of snow, one night, I saw a large crowd congregated around a number of persons engaged in a diligent search for something. On making enquiry, I was informed that one of the "young ladies" taking part in the search had been walking along the slippery thoroughfare when she suddenly stumble and met with - -qident. She did not fall down herself

..et with a suit,' acc; but her fright was so great that she lost several of her teeth ; her very best too. Cost nearly 20s. a piece, I was told, and only fancy that because tke crowd became rather numerous, and some of the bystanders made use of imperti- nent observations, she did not stay long enough to pick them up.

The members of the Runcorn Fire Brigade are becoming quite an important body of men, and they and their doings have given rise to what your last report of the inonthly pro- ceedings of the Commissioners describes as "fiery words between Dr. McDougall and Mr. Shaw." It seems as though the former gentleman had taken the brigade under his especial care, and he bad determined to champion them through evil and through good report. Quite a large amount of money has been spent in adorning these worthies of late too large a sum to meet with the approval of the general body of the ratepayers. Whet with monograms and gold lace, there is ne telling where the expenditure will stop, and if matters are allowed to go on as they have been doing in the past, the firemen and their officers will be as resplendent when they turn out as the finest cavalry regiment. At the meeting referred to Mr. Shaw strongly censured Dr. McDougall, as chairman Of the committee having charge of the matter, for permitting an account for two additional caps to be passed without a resolution. Then the learned doctor became personal, and said "they had heard a great deal of Mr. Shaw on that Board and outside of it, and also of his personal vanity." He also reflected upon that gentleman's knowledge of the English tongue, as if Dr. McDougall himself were competent to reply to the author of "The Queen's English," and in- dite a similar work to that known as "The Deau's English," which at one time created quite a stir in the world of literature. From what I have been privilegol to hear of the harangues of the Doctor, I must say that there is con- siderable roorn for improvement in his language and mode of public address. The constant squabbles witnessed at the meetings of the Commissioners do not add to the dignity of their deliberations, and, if they do not cease in a short time, it will probably be a question with Mr. Meadowcroft, or some of the cooler beads in the chamber, as te whether the cloture ought not to be introduced. SAD Ern) or A WOMAN AN FARNWORTIL—On Wednes- day Mr. Barker held an inquest at the Horns Inn, Farn- worth, on the body of a woman named Jane Unswortb, who was found dead in a cesspool on Monday afternoon. De- ceased was forty-five years of age the wife of a labourer named John Unsworth. On Sunday evening, about ten o'clock, deceased left her home for the purpose of going to the I Horns Inn for some beer, and was at the time somewhat under the influence of drink. In the Horns Inn deceased asked for a glass of beer, and the landlady refused to supply her. She next asked for a gill of rum, which Was supplied her, and. she left. Nothing further was seen or heard of her until Monday afternoon, when her body was discovered In a cesspool by a man named Joseph Grice. She was lying with her face and hands visible. Grice gave information to constable Simpson, and with his assistance the body was recovered. The Jury returned a verdict of "Found dead.

A HALTom Flan! Lamottnau DROWNED.—An inquest was held on Tuesday, by Mr. Wonley, deputy coroner, at the Norton Arms, on the body of Michael Tulley, aged 33, a labourer at the Manor Farm, Norton. On Saturday even- ing the deceased went to Runcorn to purchase provisions, and did not return home. On the following morning, about ten o'clock, as several young men were walking along the canal side, at Halton, they found a hat and a bundle of provisions. As it was supposed some one must have been drowned dragging was commenced, and continued until about three in the afternoon, when deceased's body was found. It is supposed that Tulley crossed the canal in order to get home sooner, and was not aware that the ice had been broken up by the ice-boat. The jury returned an open verdict.

DEATH OF THE REV. T. PENNINGTON, FORMERLY OF RIINCORN.—The death is announced of the Rev. Thomas Pennington, of Walkden. The deceased received a good education and was intended for commercial pursuits, and he entered into the service of the Bridgewater Trustees at Run- corn, for the purpose of learning accounts, etc. His parents were old-fashioned Methodists, and their house formed a centre for Method sm in the district surrounding Worsley. Under these influer ces be was gradually attracted towards the work of the Methodist ministry, and after undergoing the usual probation, was ordained at the Birmingham Con- ference in 1836, his ordination bible containing the signa- tures of men so well known to Methodists of past generatiens as Jabez Buntin4, Robert Newton, Richard Reece, John Burdsall, and James Gill. He travelled to the Runcorn circuit, where he made many friends; aini many of his circuits bear his impress of the erection of new chapels The rev, gentleman retired from the ministry ih 1860, and settled at his native village of Walkden. His death was con- sequent upon a comparatively short illness, and arose from an attack of his chronic complaint of bronchitis. WIDNES AND THE FENIAN Pic.—Much excitement was caused in Widnes, on Sunday morning, upon it being found out that a placard, of which the following is a copy, had been pretty extensively posted in the town:—" Men of Ireland,—The country is now passing through a crisis full of danger to the national cause. The action of the British Government and its eiders and abettors is obviously intended to provoke premature reeistance. Upon you, there- fore, rests the responsibility of averting defeat and humilia- tion. You have grievous cause for revolt, but you are not prepared, and a crushing disaster now would live to the next generation. The task of beginning anew the great work al- ready so far advanced—the salvation of our people—lies in the achievement of national independence alone, butthe time to strike has not yet come. Beware, then, of being misled by false or foolish friends, or goaded by the enemy into fruitless outbreaks. The man who now incites to attempts at insurrection is doing England's work, and must be held guilty of treason to Ireland. The most rigid discipline must be enforced and partial outbreaks prevented. Move only by command of your officers. Our present duty is to prepare, to watch, to wait until the hour of action comes. Let your attitude be one of calm reserve, self-sacrifice, and unshaken confidence in the final triump of our cause.—By erder of the Irish National Directory."—The Central News agency states that a similar bill has been put up at Westport and the neigh- bourhood.

THE DEATH IN A. RUNCORN QUARRY.—On Saturday the inquest on the body of John Dawson, who was killed under circumstances reported in last week's Examiner, was held at the Barlevmow Hotel, Church-street, by Mr. Ridgway' county coroner. Mr. Joseph Roscoe, master of the WorsleY ysid belonging to the trustees, attended to watch the case on behalf of those gentlemen. Samuel Dawson, labourer, Seville-street, said the deceased was his brother, and 47 years of age. He was employed at the Mill Brow quarry, belonging to the Bridgwater trustees, and he (witness) was with him at the time of the accident, which occurred on the previous day at about a quarter-past seven. Deceased, witvess,and a man named Charles Woods were engaged removing a stone weighing about two tons, which was on a wagon, where it had been for a fortnight, from one crane to another. Immediately before they attempted to change the position of the stone, deceased removed the wooden "skids "—pieces of wood by-which it was secured—from underneath it, thus making it liable to slip. He did not know what was the reason which caused him to remove the "skids," unless it was that he might put his back aglinst the stone better. The stone slipped and fell upon deceased, who said his back was broken. They carried him into the smithy, and placed him by the fire; but he only lived five or ten minutes. At the time deceased moved the "skid," he (witness) did cot consider there was any harm in his doing so. In answer to a juryman, the witness said deceased put the stone on the wagon himself, and he bad worked for the firm about 20 years. Mr. Wm. Leach, Albert-street, foreman at the quarry, said he saw the accident, and shouted to the men. He assisted deceased's brother to remove him into the smithy. The Coroner briefly summed up, and the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

SID ACCIDENT AT TILE BIG POOL, RIINCORN.-012 Saturday, Mr. Ridgway, county coroner, held an inquest at the Hai leymow Hotel, Church-street, Runcorn, on the body of Joseph Inglesfield, son of William Inglesfield, labourer, of Heath-road, Mill-blow, who was found by his father under the ice in the Big Pool, quite dead, at about four o'clock the same morning.—William Inglesfield, the father stated that the lad was eight years old. He came home about six o'clock that morning and found that his son, who had been sliding upon the Big Pool on the pre- vious evening, had not returned home. He and his wife, therefore, went round the water and in the neighbourhood, but could not obtain any information about deceased. He then borrowed a boat hook and went to the pool in which he had been told a number of holes had been made by a boatman named Twigg for the purpose of catching snigs. In one of these, in the middle of the pool, he found thel dead body of his son. The man Twigg had been told not to make the holes in the ice, as some one would be getting in. In answer to a juryman, witness stared that the brother of deceased, who was only about four years of age, had been on the ice with him, and, on coming home about four o'clock, he told his mother that the deceased had gone off the ice. Mr. Leach, a foreman at the Bridgewater Trustees' yard, had told him (witness) that he saw Twigg making the holes in the ice, and he should be glad to give evidence to that effect. The pool was very deep, being as much as 12 or 14 feet in some places.—John James Pilling, aged ten years, the son of Joseph Pilling, labourer, Jackson's-lane, deposed that he was with the deceased on the pool most of the day, sliding. The lad knew there was a hole in the middle of the ice on the pool. Sometime about five o'clock in the afternoon, the deceased fell into a hole which was opposite the delph, but succeeded in getting out. He left him about half-an-hour afterwards near the ice. There was no other person there at the time. Deceased told him he was going to the pit on the common.—Mr. Coventry, one of the jury, said it would be much better if a notice was put up to warn people against making holes in the centre of the pool when there was ice on it. Any person might have gone upon the ice not knowing there was a hole there, and fallen in.—Mr. Woodland considered it advisable that the Bridgewater Trustees who belong to the pool, ahould be re- quested, in the case of future frosts, to issuira notice pro- hibiting anyone breaking the ice.—The Coroner said the jury must not forget that the statements made concerning Twigg were not evidence, and, if called, he might altogether deny what had been said. He suggested that it might be worth while to send for Mr. Leach; but the jury thought it was scarcely necessary to delay the inquiry for the purpose of hearing his statement. They returned an open verdict.

SAD ACCIDENT AT MESSES. MIJSPEATT'S, WIDNES.— On Wednesday, au inquest was held by Mr. Barker, deputy county coroner, on the body of John Burke, a labourer, aged 24 years, who, on the previous Sunday, sustained injuries at Messrs. Muspratt's works, that town, from which he died on the following afternoon. Mr. Lewis, manager to Messrs. Muspratt's, was present watching the case on behalf of the firm. Thomas Luskey deposed that on Sunday afternoon, be was in charge of a number of labourers at the works, who were hoisting a hopper, weighing about 28 cwt. Deceased was working under a contractor, who was taking some engines to pieces, and without receiving any instructions to do so, he left his labour and went to assist in the hoisting et the hopper, which was being raised by an engine and blocks. Deceased was on one side of the hopper and he (witness) on the other, upon the scaffolding, when the chain by which it was being hoisted broke. Deceased had hold of the chain, and fell with the hopper, a distance of about nine feet, and injured his' bead. He (witness) had examined the chain on the Sunday morning, and could not perceive the slightest flaw in it, neither was he of opinion that the severity of the frost had damaged it.—ln reply to the Coroner, witness stated that he had told deceased he had no business upon the scaffolding, and that he must come down, but he said he would stop and see the hopper put in its place. Only a few days before the accident, two or three tons had been raised by the chain.—David Evans, also in charge of labourers at the works, stated that he ordered deceased off the scaffolding, and though he went down he returned to his former position four or five minutes afterwards. He again ordered himoff, but he would not go. When raised from the ground, deceased was quite unconscious. He appeared to be perfectly sober. He (witness)examined the chain two days before, and hoisted three tons with it; be thought it was in good order.—ln answer to the Coroner, witness said no one was to blame but deceased.—John Dunn, fore- man bricksetter at Messrs. Muspratt's, said that after the man was hurt a doctor was sent for, and he was taken to the hospital. He heard deceased twice told to go down. In his opinion the chain was of quite sufficient strength for its work. Deceased had had a little drink that day.—The Coroner said it clearly appeared that the deceased had gone upon the scaffolding through his own perversity. —Mr. David Forster, boiler soaker, said he considered the chain quite capable of miring four tons.—Mr. Lewis ob- served that the only theory he could advance, as an engineer, was that the different atmospheric pressure which the chain had lately had to undergo, owing to the severe weather, had caused it to become weak in some part where an examina- tion of it would 'not detect the flaw.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."
