Cooke's paper, subject, "Free Trade," was resumed on Thursday, when the following members took part in the discussion :-Mr. A. White '(chairman), Messrs. R. Greenhalsh, E. Cross, J. Marnley, B. Hobson, and J. Watson. After a debate of about two hours the subject was again adjourned. Pmexlerll BAND "on HOPE.-On Wednesday last a very interesting and well attended meeting in connection with the Band of Hope was held in the Wesleyan School- room, under the presidency of Mr. R. A. Naylor, of Grap- penhall. The Chairman spoke of the evils of intemperance and in favour of temperance, after which a miscellaneous. entertainment was given by several members. The various pieces were rendered in a very creditable manner, and the reading of Mrs. D. Garnett was very effective. , TJterrisie METHODDIT FREE CHURCH, ORMSKIRR- STREET, BAND or HOPE SOCIETY, ST, HELENS-The first of the 1881 series-of meetings of the above society, was held in the schoolroom on Monday. The chair was taken by Mr Forster. A number of recitations and songs were given by the juvenile members, noticeable among these being a duet by Master and Miss Harrison, and a song by Miss Florence Aldridge, who possesses a clear sweet voice. Mr. J. Lindon gave an address, speaking of the sad results accruing from strong drink, and urged the members (juvenile) to stand firm by their pledge, and aid the spread of temperance to the best of their ability. The following adult friends con- tributed to the evening's entertainment. Songs, Mrs. Mel- lors , part song, Mrs. and Miss Lindon. Reading (Lan- cashire dialect), from " Besom Ben," Mr. James Douglas. Recitations, Miss Needs and Mr. J. G. Pickersgill. Votes of thanks being given to the chairman and friends who had assisted, the meeting terminated with the doxology being sung, and the benediction pronounced. ST. HELENS YOUNG MEN'S INSTITUTE.-On Monday • evening the Rev. R. J. Ward read an entertaining and in- structive paper on" Recreations, past and present," befere the members of this Institute, in the Independent School- room. Mr. H. R. Lacey' occupied the chair, and briefly introduced Mr. Ward, who, from ae earliest period traced the history of recreations of every description. He dwelt especially upon recreations in the shape of the theatre, cards, . dancing, dm., and while not wholly condemning them as morally bad, he thought as at present conducted those re- creations in the majority of instances had a damaging effect upon the morals of the people. He urged upon the young men to choose games innocent in their character, and pointed out several means of deriving rational enjoyment in their leisure hours. The Chairman, Messrs. Samuel Glover, C. Sharpies, Drummond, and White (of the Salford Bank) having briefly spoken on the subject, the meeting " closed with the usual votes of thanks.

div.p: F RODSIIAM.

Mr. Albert Henry Walker, son of Mr. Samuel Walker, printer, Frodsham, has successfully passed the preliminary examination qualifying for admission as a candidate for "BA." at the next:university examination. ACCIDENT TO THE ROYAL MAIL.—On Tuesday evening a trap belonging to a Frodsham innkeeper came into colli- sion with the mail cart conveying the mails from Frodsham to Preston Brook. The occupants of both conveyances were much shaken, and the mail cart completely collapsed, and had to be left on the roadside. The accident occurred near Barley Groves, Frodsham Bridge, which it is needless to say is not within the Frodsham lighting district. DARING ArrEmPT AT ROBBERY.—As a Frodsham woman was proceeding to Runcorn last week she was stopped on Runcorn Common by two men, who took hold of her roughly, and demandel money. The woman describes one of the men as having a long beard, which she courageously took hold of and punished the would-be robber severely. Luckily at this juncture assistance was seen approaching, and the men quickly beat a retreat. THE WEATHER AND THE DISTRESS—The thaw has I rendered the canal near Frodsham navigable for the salt trade, but owing to the colliers' strike a large number of men lately employed at the Weston chemical works have been unable to resume work. The Relief Committee have not considered it necessary to commence operations, but a considerable amount of relief has been granted by the liberality of private gentlemen, and has offered unusual facilities for imposition, which has been practised to some extent. The tides in the Weaver have been very high, and the river has been blocked with ice.

FRODSHAM CRICKET CLUB.—A meeting of the members of the Frodsham Cricket. Club, was held on Monday evening in the school room, Church-street, when the Rev. A. P. Reynolds presided, and there were about twenty members pre. sent The lion. Treasurer reported that during the past year £5 lOs. Od. had been contributed by honorary members, and ,Ll 4 12s. Od. by playing members. The expenditure amounted to £l4 leaving a balance in favour of the club of £l3 2s, Od. The following appointments were made for the ensuing season, viz: President, the Rev. Henry B. Blogg, M.A.•, captain, Mr. Frank Hilditch ; sub-captain, Mr. Daniel Ashton; hon. secretary and treasures, Mr. Samuel Davies. A committee was appointed, and Mr. Charles E. Linaker was requested to arrange for a field in Overton, and report to an adjourned meeting.

THE FATAL ACCIDENT, AT FLENWORTH.—On Friday week, an inquest was held at the Griffin Inn, Farnworth, on the body of Thomas Craig, the youth who was killed at the Cheshire Lines goods station, on the previous day, under circumstances fully reported in the last issue of The Examiner. The witnesses examined were Chas. Smethurst and Wm. Goulding.—The jury returned a verdict of" Acci- dental death."

He is suc- ceeded in the title by hie only son, Colonel the Lion. Arthur, Walsh. LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. The House adjourned. • " HOUSE OF COMMONS. —Laer NIGHT. He should preserve freedoin of debate, but at the same time see that business 3vas not unduly interrupted. He, relied on the support of the House in carrying the resolution into effect. (Great cheering.) He intended framing rules in conformity with the resolution. At present he had decided upon limit- ing the power of moving the adjournment of the House. beers.) ( Hume AND Estor.e.la—Sir C. Mute said the statement that mutual engagements hails been entered into between England and Russia, by which Russia hat undertaken not to advance on Mery on condition that Candahar should be given up by England, was untrue. His belief was that Russia was not advancing On Merv. No negotiations were in progress on any such engagement. DIISH PROCLAMATION.—Sir W. HARCOURT said his atten- tion had been called to the proclamation issued by Irish national directory, but he delined stating the steps be pro- posed taking. THE PROTECTION OP PROPERTY AND PERSON (LarrAND) BILL.—Mr. Pons= moved the second reading of this bill amid considerable cheering. He said the explanations he had made rendered any lengthy statement unnecessary. The provisions of the bill would, he contended, in no way inter- fere with the rights of well-disposed people; but it would, he hoped, prove efficient in preventing a continuance of that lawlessness which now unhappily existed in Ireland.l He Pointed out that objection had been raised to the retro- spective action of the bill ; but he asked the House to trust the Government, and rest content with his assurance that the clause was necessary, otherwise it never would have been inserted in the bill.—At this point the Prince of Wales and Duke of Connaught entered the Peers' Gallery. --Mr. FolisTria, continuing, defended the statistics pub- lished regarding outrages, and condemned the systematic manner in which rent was withheld by persons well able to pay. He again referred to the serious condition of affairs, and concluded by saying that if either the House or the Government were now to give way, the unwritten law wquld be the only law obeyed in Ireland.—Mr. Bilaimetraw %wed that the bill be read a second time that day six months, as he believed that no offence had been shown to'exist which ordinary law was not sufficient to meet, and also because he had the greatest objection to the bill being retrospective. „ [LEFT errnwo.] ,

- - ------- TEE Thaw AT Fanant's FEERY.—The river sfensey on Sunday last presented a scene not often witnessed. AbitfUt 11-30 a.m. the tide began to flow very rapidly, and it was remarkable to see it battling with the huge masses of ice, which, being brcken up, floated away until stopped by some obstruction, when they would be thrown one piece upon another. The blocks of ice were hurled with such terrific force as to remove the huge stone wall of the lock belong- ing to the St. Helans canal (some of the stones weighing about 15 cwt.), lifting them bodily on the bank. The tide also lifted the steps on the landing place where passengers cross the river, and canned other damage. The several large blocks of ice lay stranded on the Cheshire side until the following tide floated them away.

ANOTHER RESULT OF THE MINERS' STRIKE, A.T Sr HELENS.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Tuesday, be- fore Mr. R. Pilkington, two respectably dressed men named Joseph Cross, and James Grcenall were charged with begging in Windle-street. P.C. Hamilton stated that he saw the prisoners and others in Windle-street that morning. In his opinion there would be about a dozen. They were all sing- ing hymns, and one of them was playing a harmonium. He brought the two prisoners to the station, and they were locked up.—Mr. Prescott (the magistrate's clerk's assistant) stated that the prisoners were both colliers, and he handed the magistrate a paper which they were taking from door to door. It read as follows:—" Kind friends, we are a few of the miners that are now suffering on account of the strike, and we appeal to your liberality to assist us in our necessity. We represent twelve families composed of 02 persons, and your help will he thankfully received. He that giveth to the poor lendeth to the Lord." The magistrate said that he would dismiss the case if prisoners would promise that that sort of thing should be stopped. He must inform them that they had broken the law and rendered themselves liable to imprisonment. However' as they seemed decent and honest men, if they promised not to offend again they might go. The requisite promise was given, and the prisoners were liberated.

'YEE ATTROTIA BORRALIS. About 6-45 on Monday night this beautiful northern light seemed to be at its brightest, and the form it had assumed was of a long con- tinued streak of light, starting at a point just under the North Pole star, and extending in a south west. rly direction for at least one third of the horizon, terminating in a beauti- ful bow or cupola. The Aurora at that time was, the colour of burnished silver and threw j out as much light as the moon when ' half full. It kept varying in shape, throwing off long streaks of light in a southerly direction until close upon nine o'clock, when it seemed to disappear behind a dark cloud on the , northern horizon. It was remarkable from the fact that it never seemed to change colour. There were none of those ; beautiful roseate streaks:we are accustomed to see in the aurora, but it seemed to vie with the new moon in colour and bright- ness. Another curious feature in the evening was the moon the entire surface of which was clearly visible a halo,seem- I ing to spread itself all roundr the sharp edge of the new moon, bright as silver, being clearly shown against Vie dark body of the moon's surface, and forming a remarkable contrast, whilst below the moon Venus, and above the moon the three forming a straight line, Jupiter and Saturn were glorious in their splendour.

WYCLIFFE SIINYLLY SCHOOL PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.— 1 The distribution of prizes to the scholars attending Wycliffe 1 Sunday school, took place in Wycliffe Hall, on Tuesday evening. The ball was crowded with scholars and their 1 parents and friends. The tea meeting, which in previous 1 years has preceded 'the distribution of prizes, was this ! year deemed advisable to dispense with. The chair was taken by Mr. S. Rigby, J.P., who was supported by theßev. J. Yonge, Rev. D. M. Jenkins (Whitechapel-road, London), Mr. F. W. B. Knott (Manchester), and the secretaries of the school. Suitable addresses were delivered by the Chair- man and Rev. D. M. Jenkins. During the evening several of the scholars cave recitations in a very pleasing manner, and one by Mr. C. H. Mills, entitled "Frank's dream," was much applauded. Hymns were also sung by a choir, under the leadership of Mr. W. H. Wallington. Miss A:Naylor gave "Stars that on your wondrous way," and three of the female scholars sang "A foolish little maiden." Miss M. A. Wallington presided at the harmonium. At intervals, the prizes, to the number of about 180, an increase on any previous year, were distributed by the Chairman, who ad- dressed a few well-chosen remarks to the recipients, many of whom were loudly cheered. At the conclusion of the programme, the Rev. J. Yonge proposed a vote of thanks to all who had assisted in making the arrangements for the meeting, and also to Mr. Rigby for presiding. The motion was carried, and the Chairman having been heartily cheered, the proceedings terminated.—On Wednesday evening the infants met and were entertained in the infant schoolroom, by the Rev. J. Yonge, Mr. G. Wallington, Jun., Mr. J. P. Jones, Jun., and also by a magic lantern, exhibited by Messrs. Mills and Massey. During the proceedings, oranges, biscuits, and sweets were distributed to the children.

- RELIEF TO THE AGED POOR OF WARRINGTO2L—A most unusual occurrence was witnessed at the Warrington Publio Hall. on Tuesday. The committee having the management of the fund for the "treat to the aged poor" announced that through the continued liberality of the sub- scribers they would be enabled to give tickets to the aged poor to relieve them, to some extent, in their distress occa- sioned by the severity of the weather and the colliers' strike. In consequence of this announcement the door way of the Public Hall was crowded for several hours, on the day above named, with applicants for relief tickets. Some idea of the crowd may be g ttbered from the fact that several women who had children with them, when they succeeded in getting to the committee fell to the ground from sheer exhaustion, and had to be removed; and a poor elderly woman, on emerging from the crowd, found her arm bleeding from a wound she had received in the struggle to get to the front. The crush at one time became so great that the committee threatened to cease issuing the tickets, and found it neces- sary to apply to Mr. Hunt (the chief constable) for assis- tance to keep the applicants in order. The Chief Constable accordingly despatched a sergeant and two constables, and the proceedings afterwards were of an orderly character. The gentlemen who distributed the relief were—Messrs. John Pierpoint (president), Thomas Jones (vice-president), J. Smethurst, P. Chrimes, IV. Horton, and T. Sutton (secre- tary); and they were engaged without intermission from ten o'clock in the morning until seven in the evening. The relief administered consisted of orders upon shopkeepers for ne,cessaries. and varied in amount from Is to 3s in ewes of extreme distress. The number of ticketsdisposed of Was 1,028, and a most noticeable feature was the overwhelming number of Irish as compared with English applicants. There were several cases of most abject poverty, the emaciated appearance of the applicants exciting much sympathy, while on the other hand there was a number of cases of in- gratitude, one woman, who thought she had received a ticket for 2s. ed. on discovering that it only represented is. remarking that "it was not worth coming for." The com- mittee refused to relieve able-bodied men, and were success- ful in detecting instances of imposition which were attemp- ted to be practised.

THE HELLTII OF WASZIMON.—The Medical Oficer of Health (Mr. Gornall) reports, for the week ending 29th January, that 25 births and 28 deaths (including seven at the Workhouse) have been registered. On the estimated population, including Latchford, of 40,000, the birth rate was equal to 32.5 in the 1,000, and the death rate 38.4 against 30.9 is the corresponding week of 1880, and 35 1 in 1879. The deaths of persons under five years of age were 5, and under one year 5, and the deaths of persons above 60 years were 14. One death is reoorded as having reached the advanced age of 108 years. The total of 28 deaths in- cludes 1 from measles, 11 from lung diseases, and 16 from other causes. There was, therefore, only one death in the zymetic class, and the proportionate mortality from pre- ventible disease was 7 per cent. Three cases of 'fnfections disease kave been reported during the week—two of enteric fever and one of malignant scarlet fever. The two former sere removed to the Fever Hospital; he latter was mori- bund when reported. The high death rate is undoubtedly due to the stress of weather producing an increved mor- tality from diseases of the respiratory organs. "

If there is a bit of land to be let, no matter what the rent is, there are hundreds for it, proposing rent to any amount, thinking they can work larder and fare worse than those who left it, or, I should say, were turned out of it, as very few leave a farm in Ireland except death or the bailiffs interfere. Thus undue advanfage is is often taken by the landlord of this competition in land, and the people are powerless, as they have no other means of getting a living. The land is known to be rack rented from north to south and east to west, generally one-third to a half over Griffith's, or Government, valuation, which in Ireland is considered a fair valuation. I will here state that the Land- lord takes no interest in his tenants or their improvements ; he neither builds, fences, drains, nor reclaims; so that if a tenant's house tumbles down he may live in t'oe garden for all the landlord cares I never in one instance knew the landlord to either build, fence, drain, or reclaim land for the tenant. But I have in hundreds of instances known the tenant to do all these, and get his rent doubled for his pains. This is the sole cause of the Irish people living in such wretched hovels. Those that live on and bear the misery of a hovel not fit for a piostye can do so, for the landlord or I his agent in that case will not raise his rent because le sees.' no prospect of its being paid. But so soon as a tenant re- I builds for himself a comfortable habitation, and improves I his farm and place, so sure is lie to have his rent raised. I When a tenant can do this, the landlord takes in for , granted that he can pay a rise of rent. By this conduct on the part of the landlord and his agent, they foster sloth and misery, and discourage improvements and respect- ability. This state of things, however, is more to be attributed to a ' bad agent than a bad landlord. The landlord generally lives abroad, either in England or on the continent, and to keep op a position in fashionable society with cotton lords and merchant princes, he is always dunninghis agent for meney from his few miserable rack-rented tenants. The person selected as agent is generally some unprincipled lawyer, who is paid a high commission for collectingaents, so that he is sure to levy black mail on the tenant who has half a dozen bard-working sons that are able to live and ply his rent. This money helps to satisfy his landlord's cravings, and brings more commission to the unscrupulous agent, who generally screens himself for such conduct by the plea that it was the landlord's instructions for him to raise the rent. I firmly believe rents are raised in hundreds of cases, nay, thousands, on this pretext, and I don't think an absentee landlord ever gets one penny of the proceeds, or knows anything of this systematic robbery, for they never go near the estate to hear any grievance a tenant has to make. If the landed gentry and their fashionable ladies only knew how the rents had to be made up, the starvation and misery it caused, unless their conticiences were entirely seared with voluptousness, vice, and folly, they would pause ere they touched the ac- cursed thing which was the cause of so much misery. One of the greatest grievances that Ireland has to contend with, and a just cause of complaint, is the immerse amount of money that is annually sent out of the country to absen- tee landlords without any return whatever, and it is not likely that a law will be passed to compel landlords to atop in Ireland. But Government can enact laws which will tend to make the people prosperous, contented, and happy, and they will then be able to attract landlords, CA )italists, and tourists to a country that has some of the finest scenery in the world. The Governtnent.is making a most serious mistake in spending thousonds of pounds in sending their armies to Ireland to disperse, at the point of tha bayonet, a hungry Imhof ill-clad wretches that met together to cry to God and the people for justice, to be able to live in the ' homes of their fathers, for this is a uselees waste of men and money. It is like trying to stop the mountain torrent in its course, it will 019 h, burst out again with greater vio- lence, to sweep everything before it and desolate the land. To prune the evil will not remedy it, it must be plucked out by the roots. Ireland has now the sympathy of all Europe with her, and one of the greatest countries of of the worid is nearly peopled with her sons and daughters, who carry in their breasts their country's wrongs. . And I say woe to the people, or nation, that will not lend an ear to the cry of the oppressed. Deland has groaned under the oppressor for centuries, whilst the people have been coerced , at times into something like peace and quietness only to burst out again like a volcano. 1 The question naturally arises how is it that the Irish people are always dissatisfied. discontented, and out of temper? I will not answer, as Mr. Disraeli once sneeringly did, "that It was owing to the people being surronnded by a melan- choly ocean." If Lord Beaconsfield was kept with bad shoes, I. bad clothes, and an empty stomach, compelled to Work hard 1!! i'!* We to try to satisfy a never eatfshed landlord, it would not require a melandhellf ocean to make him discon- tented and out of temper: There are no peoriLO 00 earth that can bear hardships sod toil with ft. much cheerful wl.*..!ielBnl , r ds dn Irishman, But I should like to know the people who , could be contented and happy when placed in .the same 1 position as an Irish farmer. I say place him in a position to be independent of his landlord, so that by care and industy be . can make a comfortable living, and then you will entirely change the tone end spirit of the people. That cringing, ' crawling spirit, caused by years of care and toil, will leave . them, and they will rise up a people of an independent spirit, o and of loyal respect for the legislators and laws that made ' !them hsepw. This, I admit, would not now be a fair rent for some farms, owing to the land being so much improved that is of more value. But who improved the land and made it of so much more value? 'Why, the ten- ant; and it would be an act of very great inNstice to make him pay for his improvements and rob him of the produce of the labour of years. The farm of a slothful man is of no more value te-day than at the time of the Griffith valuatilms 1 nor would a valuator lay one penny more rent on it now. SINNERS AND SUNDAYS. Sir,—Mr. Samuel Rigby, as chairman of the Wycliffe tea meetingmave utterances to some statements to which I feel bound to take exception. I gather from your report of that meeting that the chairman is of the opinion that a person who takes the very sensible course of availing himself of the weekly holiday to walk into the country on the only day on which it is possible for him to do it, is on the high- way to ruin, rags, and reprobation. Mr. Rigby says he has seen it. I also have observed it, with sorrow; but the con- clusions we came to were widely different. I thought if that Iran had continued his Sunday morning walks further into the country, and not stopped at the first public-house he found outside the three mile limit, this hatelimental declen- sion would never have come to him. No, sir; I respectfully submit to Mr. Rigby that it may net be the Sunday walk, but the Sunday drinking, that has brought him so low. I ' know men who make a constant practise of this—the walk, not the drink--who consistently and conscientiously refrain frarn attending either church or chapel, and y4t are good citizens and decently clothed, and to whom I shall be glad to introduce Mr. Rigby, and give him a chance of "follow- ing them home." lam of the opinion, sir, that the mode of passing the day of rest suited to, and enjoyed by, a pastoral people is utterly unsuited to a population like ours, pursu- ing a confined and sedentary occupation. If suicide be a crime, surely that slow but sure form of it, which consists in neglecting to seize every available opportunity of healthful relaxation must be a kindred wickedness. And then, setting aside higher inducements to visit these places of worship, what example has the simple workingman set him to leave off his walks, in which he takes a real and wholesome delight, in order to attend the ministration of my friend the 124 v. Aminadab Jackletext, while expounding the

Difference there might be 'Tvrixt tweedle dum and tweedie deo. Example! Yes he will see people rolling to church in carriages and know that some one must have had unneces- sary °Sunday labour through that. While, inside the " sacred edifice," he may see people, who are calling them- selves miserable sinners,dressed in the laet extravagance of the latest mode. Seeing this, and being a hf.ter of hypoc- risy in all its forms, he prefers, as a simple man, to tender the simple worship of sincere admiration in that grand tem- ple unbuilt by hands' where robes and ritual are alike un- known. lam sorry to differ from the opinions of a gentleman for whom I have so much respect, but must beg to ask Mr. Rigby if it might not be drink and not the Sunday consti- tutional which had reduced his friend to the aforesaid stockingless condition? In common with Mr. Rigby, I deplore this state of things, with which all the churches in the world are unable to cope without recosrse .o more common sense methods.—l am, sir, yours JOHN PEERS. Warrington, Jan. 31, 1881.

div.head: WARRINGTON DIVORCE CASE.
div.p: A WARRINGTON DIVORCE CASE.

The case of Twist v. Twist which was a petition by Clara Jane Twist for the dissolution of her marriage with William Rufus Rawstran Twist, on the ground of his cruelty and adultery, was heard on Saturday in the Probate and Divorce Division of the High Court of Jnstice, before Sir James IHannen, the president. Mr. Gill (instructed by Messrs. Harrison, eolicitors, of Warrington) appeared for the petitioner, and stated that the petitioner was married to William Rufus Rawstran Twist at the parish church of St. Paul, Warrington, on the 3rd of September, 1879, she being the widow of the late William Scott, of the Grove, Rewsey-road, Warrington, and of the Fox Hotel, in the city of Manchester. At the time of the marriage the respondent had no means of livelihood, and shortly after they were married he commenced a series of acts of ill-tteatment, struck her several times, and told her he had only married her for her money, and that she would never get a penny out of him. On one occasion be struck her ea violentlythat he broke her earrin, and in consequence of that she became very unwell. This state of thing con- tinued with very little intermission down to the year 1880, when, during a serious quarrel that then ensued, he threatened to murder her. Respondent on that occasion said, "They say that I murdered my first wife, but I know beet; but I'll do the thing properly in this case. I'll be a second Charles Peace, not only with von, but one, two, three." She became so alarmed that she applied to the local magistrates for protection, and a warrant was accordingly issued against him. After the case had been stated before the magistrates they ordered the respondent to find two sureties for his good conduct towards his wife. After that the respondent dis- appeared, and it was alleged that lie had formed an ima proper intimacy with a barmaid named Hughes, in Liver- pool. In March, ISBO, however, the wife found that he had taken some kind of situation at the Rear's Paw Inn, Rutter- market-street, Warrington, and there had been guilty of acts of impropriety with a Mrs. Morgan, the landlady. At the same establishment he had been guilty of' adultery with a 1 i domestic servant named Harriet Minted), who would be I called as' 2 witness. The petitioner, Clara Jane Twist, wee called, and said that she was married to the respondent on the 3rd September, 1870. They afterwards went to live at 9, Museum-street, I Warrington. There was no issue of. the union. On the Bth 1 January, DIM, he deserted her, and had not since returned, I nor contributed anything towards her. support. Within six I weeks of the marriage he behaved most cruelly towards her, on one occasion breaking one of her earrings, causing a great swelling. On the 2nd of January he came home late, and behaved very violently towards her in the presence of her daughter. Us said, with sm oath, that a1th912,1, Abe had entered the room alive, she would not be allowed to leave it 1 I so. He also said s---" They say I killed my first wife, but I I know best. I will do it properly this time, and they shall not talk about it for nothing. I will be a second Peace, and it shall not only be you, but one, two, three," emphasising his remarks by thumping his fist violently on the sideboard. She had heard that her husband had been guilty of adultery with a girl named Dainteth at the Bear's Paw Inn, War- rington, on the 7th March, of last Year, and also with a young lady of the name of Elizabeth. Hughes, a waitress in Liverpool. Harriet Dainteth, domestic servant, in the employ of Mr. and Mrs. Morgan, of the Bear's Paw Inn, Warrington, said that on the 7th March last, at three o'clock in the morning, the respondent entered her bedroom and got into her bed. He had previously kissed her. She had also seen the res- pondent in the bedroom of Mrs. Morgan during her hus- band's absence from home. Richard Singleton, of the Warrington police, proved that the respondent was bound over to keep the peace in conse- quenca of his illtreatment to his wife. His Lordship was of opinion that no charge of adultery had been proved against Mrs. Morgan, hut the adultery with Dainteth had been proved. He therefore made a decree nisi for the dissolution of the marriage as prayed by the petitioner,

Professor Huxley, F.R.S., it, !laid to have accepted the office of Inspector of Fisheries, vacant by the death of Mr Frank Buckland. We are informed that this appointment, as it demands his entire time, necessitates the resignation by Mr. Huxley of the post of Naturalist to the Geological Sur- vey of the United Kingdom. We cannot yet learn whether 1 he will retain his lectureship in the Royal School of Mines 1 or the secretaryship to the Royal Society.—Athencrum. A horse at Faribault, Minn., turned loose in his master's dooryard, saw a basket hanging on a clothes-pole, about seven feet from the ground. It contained a pet cat belong- ing to the place. 'the horse walked over to the basket, put his nose up to investigate, and the cat put out one of its paws and gave the intruding nose a lively scratch. The horse turned round, looked back over his shoulder as though to take aim and measure the distance, kicked, and cat, bas- ket, and all shot into the air like a rocket. The horse watched the success of his thot, and then gave a low whinny of delight and walked away. TEN 31r-nrEns AT PnEscop.—Large crowds of miners lined the approaches to the Prescot Police Court on Tues- day last, during thick trial of the men summoned by Mr. Fidlerfor non-service of notice at the pit. At the conclu- sion of the case, when it was announced that the verdict was in favour of the men, the excitement became great outside. Mr. Richardson, of Bolton, who had been defending the \ men, on his appearance in the street was greeted with loud cheers, and immediately surrounded by the large assembly, Sad conducted up Derby-street to the Royal, and in the direction of the railway station, the cheering continuing all the way, Mr. Richardson repemedly taking off his hat and bowing his acknowledgments. Many people heard the ver- dict with great relief, as several disturbtog rumours had I been abroad in the town as to the disturbances which would I take place should the men be fined. Happily the magistrates' 1 wise diction dispelled all fear, and the day's proceedings we marred by no hitch.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 5. 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 5. 1881.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. The monthly meeting of the Town Council was held in the Council Chamber, at the Town Hall, on Tuesday even- ing. Present: The Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) in the chair, Aldermen Kean, Harrison, Holmes, Chandien Inrgess; Councillors Wallington, Greening, Percival., Woods, Milner, Barker, Woolfall, Taylor, Jeans, Brown, Francombe, Monks, Broadbent, Litton, Fairclongh, Greenall, Crosfield, Ridrmay, Platt, Sutton, Burgess, Dixon, Ashton, Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), Charles Chorley (borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), and J. Paterson (gas manager).

WA:ITU COMMMED. The minutes of the Watch Committee contained order for payment of accounts for £273 Bs. 4P., and a recommen- dation that the engineer of the fire brigade be allowed the sum of 9d. per hour for all work done by him after work- ing hours in washing hose, and when on duty at the fire engine station during a fire. On the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Councillor WOODS, the minutes were confirmed.
FINANCE COMMITTEE. This committee's minutes comprised orders for payment of accounts for £4,857 ITS. 5d., and orders for payment of ac- counts in connection with gas department, amounting to

£-2,887 38.10 d. The mint. tes were adopted on the motion of Councillor MILI.TER, seconded by Councillor BROWN. A STRANGE CLAIM, AND "A MONSTROUS DOCTRINE." At a meeting of the Street Improvement and Lighting Oommittee, held on the 6th January, it was resolved that the claim of Messrs. J. Pierpoint and Son, of £5 55., "half charge" for plan and valuation made for Mr. Joseph Chrimes, of property in Bridge-street, belonging to him, be refused, the committee repudiating all liability in respect thereof. Plans were approved for proposed extension of Mersey Mills for Messrs. Fairclough and Sons. At a meet- ing en the 20th January, it was recommended that the Borough Surveyor require the owners of property within the borough to cause all gates and doors now opening outwards .over footpaths to be altered to open inwards. Councillor BROADBENT moved the adoption of the minutes, and Conncillor WamNerrox seconded the motion. Councillor JEANS said, respecting the charge of Messrs. Pierpoint, he happened to know the origin of it, and he thought before refusing to pay the charge the opinion of the Council ought to be taken. The charge originated in this way: About two years ago Mr. Joseph Chrimes, of Bridge Foot, was making alterations at his shop, and at that time the Council thought it a favourable opportunity to widen the street. But instead of going directly to what they wanted, the Committee raised objections to Mr. Chrimes's plans, and that led to negotiations with Mr. Chrimes with a view to obtaining a strip of the land. He was concerned at the time as Mr. Chrimes's solicitor, arid therefore knew all about the matter. He had not had any communication with Mr. Chrinies or Mr. Pierpoint in reference to this par- ticular charge; but knowing how the matter arose, he thought it Wa3 a proper charge for the Council to pay. It was usual for corporate bodies b pay incidental charges of this kind ; and therefore he thought this should not be an exception. Mr. Chrimes, Mr. Pier- point, and himself had an interview with the Committee in respect to the strip of land, and it was stated the land was required for street improvement purposes, and a suns of money was offered. Mr. Chrimea declined to accept that sum, and the Committee thought it would be a favourable opportunity to acquire the whole of the property. At the request of the Committee a plan was prepared and a valua- tion made. The valuation was certainly not made at the request of Mr. Chrimes, but in consequence of the action of the Street Improvement Committee, and he thought if any person had to pay Messrs. Pierpoint it should be the parties by whose wish they acted. The MAYOR: Do you contend that the Corporation should wholeior j tss d m the s ieibargetisrs. Pierpoint had reduced the e? pay he c Cotun § charge to one half, and therefore he did tno say the Cor- poration should pay the whole. They certainly should r the half.

Councillor MONKS supported the Committee, and said when individuals, who were approached by the Corporation, chose to get out plans and asked extortionate prices, he did not think there was any hardship if the Corporation refused to pay for those plans. Councillor Dame stated that it was not on behalf of the Committee, but on behalf of Mr. Chrimes. that Messrs. Pier- point were employed. Alderman HARRISON thought it desirable there should be concensus of opinion on the question. Councillor Jeans had given a very fair narrative of the circumstances of the case, lat there was one little matter he had omitted, un- intentionally he was sure, namely, that in the days of Aid. Hepherd, who was then chairman of the committee, having discuseed the pros. and cons, of the claim sent in by Mr. Pierpoint, the committee were willing, if possible, to meet him in a fair and proper spirit. At the suggestion of the chairman Alderman Hepherd was authorised to see Mr. Pierpoint and arrange to pay him one half of the claim, re- pudiating any legal liability. Councillor PLATT: Scarcely authorised him. Alderman HARRISON : I hardly know how to put it then. Mr. Hepherd did make'an overture to him. Am I right? Councillor PLATY: Scarcely, but I will give my version of the matter bye-and-bye. Alderman HanntsoN (continuing) said the committee re- pudiated the claim altogether because they did not in any iraT empower Mr. Pierpoint to make the valuation for them. Their communication with Mr. Chrimes was direct, and they asked him to say what he would require for the pro- perty. He employed Mr. Pierpoint, and beyond that they had nothing to do with the trotter. lie remembered that on behalf of the committee Alderman Hepherd suggested a payment of one half of the claim, but the overture was re- jected with some indignation by Mr. Pierpoint, and tile com- mittee passed a resolution that as they were not in any way liable, either morallyor legally, for the amount, they refused to have anything to do with it. Couneillor PLATT explained that the Corporation did not employ Mr. Pierpoint, but that Mr. Chrimes was asked what he woeld take for the whole of the land, as he did not see his way to sell a portion of it; and he it was that engaged Mr. Pierpoint, who brought in an estimate so exceedingly exorbitant that the committee saw no other course open to them but to discontinue the negotiations. Councillor JEANS said he had not alleged that Mr. Pier- point was employed by the committee, but in consequence of the action of the Corporation, and therefore he thought the coremiltee ought to pay the incidental expenses. Councillor SUTTON said as Mr. Pierpoint's services were not required altogether for the bent& of Mr. Chrimes, but 1 in order to give the committee an answer to their enquiry, it seemed to him only a matter of fairness that they should meet Mr. Chrimes in the expenses which were incurred, as the matter fell through from no fault of his. (" (NI.") A man had a right to charge what he liked. If he was put le any expense in giving evaluation of his property he should expect the Corporation to bear half if not the whole of the cost of that valuation. Councillee MILF.en supported the committee, who knew all that had taken place, Councillor CROSFIELD thought he had never heard a more monstrous doctrine in his life than that advocated by Coun- cillor Sutton-(laughter)-that as Mr. Chrimes had asked for the property 15 or 20 times moo than it was worth, the corn- -mittee should pay half of the cost of his getting the property valued. He should support the committee, and should be , ashamed ef the Council if they listened io anything so ridiculous. Councillor BROADBENT said at the time the large estab- lishment was about to be erected at Bridge Foot tho com- mittee thought there was an opportunity which they should not miss of seeing whether some attempt could not be made to alter the approach to the bridge from the Cheshire side. Considering the plans laid before them by Mr. Chrimes, the committee suggested some alterations which might lead to an improvement ip the widening of the street. Further ' than that they asked Mr. Chrimes what price he would re- quire for the whole plot of land, the committee having in view the possibility of making quite a new approach into Warrington. Mr. Chrimes replied by putting on a price which the committee thought exorbitant. Of course Mr. Chrimes had a perfect right to put on any price he thought fit; but the committee thought what was asked was exor- bitant, and with great regret gave up ths, prospect of making the improvement. If the commi reasonable spirit, they were P had been met in a pared to give a liberal sum for the property. He er'ja.td not but regret that the com- mittee were not ...apprJached in a more reasonable spirit— (hear, hear)—all that a valuable opportunity had been lost .'. of beneang the town. (Hear, hear.) After Mr. Hepherd's 4'. o,cr to pay half the charge had been refused, he thought it .... ; rather strange that a person in the position of Mr. Pierpoint I should a couple of years after send in the claim again. ,Hear, hear.) The minutes were passed. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.

At meetings of this committee, it was recommended that ' the Town Clerk serve the necessary notices upon the owners of the property adjoining Victoria-street from Orchard-street to Fennel-street, Catherine-street, and Howard-street. from Priestley-street to points marked A and B, requiring them to pave, flag, and channel the streets according to plans and specifications in pursuance of the Public Health Act, 1875. It was recommended that the tender of Messrs. Beyson arid Halton for the paving of Winwick-road be accepted; and that the tender of Mr. John Chorley, for the supply of a Healey's patent pitch boiler, to hold 300 gallons, at £52 155., be accepted. Alderman KEAN moved, and Councillor WooLnkr.r. seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor BnoAnnnyr called attention to the disgraceful condition of Bakehouse-yard, off St. James's-street, Latch- ford. It was a sea of mud. Councillor WOODS said that was owing to the weather. Alderman KEAN said, in reference to the condition of the court referred to by Councillor Broadbent, if the nuisance was owing to the want of paving, the Sanitary Committee dealt with the matter first, and the Paving and Sewerage Committee after. The minutes were confirmed. SCROOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. A meeting of the above Committee was held on the 13th January, when the Inspector reported that 41 cases had been enquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed to 98 children. Seven cases had been taken before the magistrates, when five were fined, and two were whipped. The minutes were passed, on the motion of Alderman CHANDLET, seconded by Councillor BROADBMNT. The 34Avort : I am sure we all regret Alderman Webster's olssonee. I am given to understand he has had a very
severe illtviss ; but I hope he will soon recover. (Hear, hear.)

MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTER. The minutes of the above Committee comprised the fol- lowing report of the Curator for the month of December:— umber of visitors to the Museum, 1,620, a decrease of 1,035; volumes issued to subscribers, 2,428, an increase of 115; volumes issued to readers 957, and increase of 157 compared with December 1879.—The thanks of the Com- mittee were ordered to be sent to several donors.—lt was recommended that the sum of ss. be charged to all societies and persons (with the exception of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society), for each use of the lecture room; and that the attention of the Borough Surveyor be called to the defective ventilation of the Reading Room, particularly in the evening.—lt was resolved that the thanks of the Committee be sent to the donors of periodicals during the past year. The minutes were adopted, en the motion of Councillor EROADBENT, seconded by Councillor GREENING.

THE CEMETERY CHAPEL STOVES. A meeting of the cemetery committee was held on the 17th January when the Registrar reported that the interments for the past five weeks were adults 33, minors 32, and stillborn 19, and for the corresponding period last year adults 40, minors 63, and stillborn 14.—Orders were made for payment of accounts amounting to £6B us. Oil. The receipts for the past five weeks were £59 Us. hi., and for the corresponding period last year, £7B 19s. Councillor Snows moved the confirmation of the minutes and Alderman KHAN seconded the motion. Councillor DIXON called attention to a defect in the stoves fixed in the cemetery chapels, which as far as he could gather were almost useless. Alderman HARRISON said he could assure Conncillor DixoN that the committee had not been lax in their enquiries as to how the stoves were working, and Mr. Lougdin had always replied that they were answering very well. He was therefore astonished at Councillor DIXON stating that they did not answer their purpose. Councillor Crosfield attributed the defective working of the stoves to the atmosphere. Councillor PrArr : The Registrar yesterday said the stoves answered well, and that the chapels were warm and comfort- able.

_ The MAYOR: The Borough Surveyor informs me that when the stoves were put up they worked admirably, but the soot got into the flue in the one in the Church of Eng- land Chapel. It has been cleaned since, and now works as well as ever. The minutes were then passed. TOWN HALL, PARK AND BATHS COMMITTER. A meeting of this committee was held on the eth January, when it was recommended that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to prepare estimates and plans for a gardener's cottage, proposed to be erected at the north-east end of the. garden behltd the conservatory ; and that Mr. Charles Andrews be accepted as the tenant of a portion of the land behind the baths in Legh-street, at the rental of £lO per annum, payable quarterly, subject to three month's notice to suit to be given at any time, and subject to an agreement to be prepared by the Town Clerk.—At a meeting on the 20th January it was recommended, that the tender of William Winstanlev, for the colouring and painting required at the baths, at 10s. be accepted • and that a woman be engaged to assist the wife of the hall keeper in cleaning the Town Hall once a week, at 2s. ed. The MAYOR moved the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor PLATT seconded. The MAYOR, in reply to Councillor Milner, said it was thought desirable that the gardener who was responsible for the care of the gardens should live on the spot. It appeared he had some difficulty in finding a house near the gardens, and the committee who had had the matter under discussion

----- for some time, came to the conclusion to build a cottage at a reasonable price. The committee had not had the plans before them as yet but when they had been the plans would be laid before the Council. The minutes were agreed to. MARKETS COMMITTEE : THE INSPECTOR'S SALARY INCREASED. The minutes of the Markets Committee contained recom- mendations that the Town Clerk be instructed to get the draft of the new market bylaws settled by counsel according to his recommendation; that the salary of Elijah Place, as Inspector under the Weights and Measures Act, 1878, be increased by the sum of £l5 per annum, and that the Town Clerk prepare a tabulated return in accordance with the standing orders; a minute that the question of increasing the rents of the stalls under the new market shed was fully discussed when it was resolved that the consideration of the matter be deferred. It was recommended that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to provide and erect new gates at the King-street entrance to the new market shed, and that per- mission be given to erect a circus on land adjoining Sankey- street betweeh Dixon-street and Arpley-street, and that a toll of 109. a week be charged inliftspeet of such circus sub- ject to any increase or reduction' the committee may deem necessary. The income from all sources for the past five weeks was £263 s. 3d. Alderman CHANDLEY moved the adoption of the minutes, and said the committee had thought it advisable to increase the salary of the market inspector as inspector of weights and measures, for which office Mr. Place had £25 per an- num. Eleven years ago it was in the hands of Mr. Robert Stephenson, whose emoluments were £5O per annum—£lo salary, and the fees, which amounted to £4O. Now the fees amounted to £7O per annum ; and last year, which was possibly .above the average, to £7B. They considered that with increased responsibility Mr. Place was entitled to the proposed increase. Mr. Place had lately been appointed inspector under the Petroleum Act, for which no emolument was given. The committee could well afford to give the proposed increase, and they thought it desirable to encourage an efficient officer. (Hear, hear.) Councillor LITTON seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor WHITTLE objected to the proposed increase, as lie considered Mr. Place very well paid indeed. He had an assistant, and as Mr. Hunt, the chief constable offered to find an officer to do the work for nothing, be thought it was agreat mistake to give an increase ef £l5 a year. Alderman HOLMES said there was no doubt Mr. Place was a varnable servant, but at the same time he was very well paid. With the certainty they had that the rates for the ensuing year would be something like Bs. in the pound all round, he thought it high time they should be very careful indeed in increasing expenses. The Council should be much more careful in their expenses than they had been. (Hear, hear.) . .

, Councillor PLATT agreed with Alderman Holmes's remarks. Councillor SUTTON was sorry the recommendation had been entered on the minutes, as it was always an unpleasant thing to object to an increase of salary. The market in- spector's salary used to be something like 30s. per week, but his present salary amounted to about £3 a week, and the committee proposed an increase. The inspector's time was not altogether taken up by these duties, inasmuch as there were only two market days a week, and his other duties mot he very light indeed. He thought Mr. Placa was receivigg satisfactory remuneration, and agreed that they should be very careful in increasing salaries when the rates were increasing to such an extent. Councillor Warma3 thought they ought to divide to see rho were economists,

who were Councillor BURGESS said the matter had been carefully considered by the committee. Mr. Place had been in the service of the Corporation 15 years' and the committee having had returns from other towns, unanimously came to the conclusion that his salaary ought to be increased. Councillor Dizorr said if- Alderman Holmes saw the amount of labour that had to be bestowed upon the weights he would not think the salary too much. Councillor 'll/forras asked the Council to support the com- mittee, who felt that in Mr. Place they had a very effi- cient officer. He thought under all the circumstances the Council might grant the increase, Alderman CUANDLBY said the duties might be performed in a mechanical manlier, but the committee felt that in Mr. Place they had a man who exerted himself and gave his heart and soul to his work. They felt it was their bounden duty to recognise that strict integrity which they had found in Mr. Place, and which was absolutely necessary in every officer who had such large amounts of money passing through his hands. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were adopted. , Tint aANITAILY COMMITTEE AND Tjul frtterious DISBASES

vention of fairs and markets for selling fat stock, from the middle of January up to the end of February, but reserving to the Sanitary Authorities, urban and rural, power to grant licenses in their discretion for the holding of such fairs. In accordance with their powers, the committee considered it within their jurisdiction that those licenses should be granted. Referring to the proposed appointment of Mr. Lamont as general manager of the Longford depot, he said it might seem a serious item to start with £2OO for an office that had
only just come into.existence. lithe Council would give
the Sanitary Committee their confidence, and would accept from him the statement that it was not in the interests of

the public that he should go -into a further eiplanation of the subject, he should ha obliged. Councillor Monts seconded the adoption of the minutes. Alderman KEAN asked if they paid £2OO to the new manager because he was a practical man. Alderman BURGESS : Yes. Councillor TAYLOR asked whether it was necessary for him to apply again for permission to bold a sale during the prohiliited period. Councillor BROADBENT called the attention of the Chair- man of the Committee to tlie condition of Bakehouse-yard, Latchford. . .

Alderman I.lannisoN said although he was quite of the opinion that the resolution which Alderman Burgess referred to was intended in the first instance as a beneficent one, and that it was intended also to benefit a certain class of persons, _

someitow or other they had not appreciated it. He did not wonder very much at that, because they might take it for granted that any law which did not consist of an embodi- ment of common sense possessed in itself the element of its own destruction. Few persons would say that that resolu- tion, however well it might have been conceived originally, was an embodiment of common sense, inasmuch, as at. a
critical period in a child's life, it rendered compulsory the removal of the child from the control of its mother to. the

Infectious Dise‘ases Hospital. He was pleased that Alder- man Burgess lwas the one to move the rescinding of the resolution. He was sure it must give satisfaction to the public, for the Council' should remember that arbitrary authority of any kind was a dangerous power in the hands of its possessors. (Hear, hear.) And what was most singu- lar was that it was liable to grow almost imperceptibly, and nothing but the jealbus supervision of those on whose kehalf the law was brought into existence, and the moderation and wise restraint of these called upon to exercise it was likely to prevent it from degenerating, if not to a scandal, at any rate to an instrument of oppression. Therefore it was with feelings of great satisfaction that he had heard Alderman Burgess making the first move towards rescinding that resolu- tion. He was satisfied it was a wise course to adopt, and the public would appreciate it accordingly. Alderman HOLMES was glad the committee proposed to I rescind the resolution. Alderman Burgess had spoken of the unanimous adoption of the resoluti, n in September. Tkere was no doubt the resolution passed without a division, but nearly every member at the time strongly opposed it. He knew it was one of those things that could do no harm, because they could not over-ride the Act of Parliament. He might, however, tell Alderman Burgess they would never pass a similar resolution. Councillor SUTTON had no doubt that the rescinding of the resolution would meet with the approval of every mem- ber of the Council. (Hear, hear.) They need not fear that

the Conservatives would walk out of tile room and leave them in a minority, so that they could not pass it. ( Laughter.) Councillor CROSFIELD objected to the statement of CORR- cillor Sutton. He had been accused' of being one of the members who went out of the Council Chamber for political purposes. He protested against it at the time, and he denied that there was any political feeling. Both Liberals and Conservatives walked out together. It was a great mistake of Councillor Sutton to make that remark—[A Voice: It was only nonsenee]—and he differed from the grand high- flown philosophy of Alderman Harrison. He took flights into regions whither it was almost impossible for any one to follow him. He was wondering where Aldermen Harrison would land—(laughter)—and thought he would have got to the moon before he stopped. He quite agreed with what the Sanitary Committee had done during the attack of scarlet fever, ard thought the town was much indebted to the exertions of the committee in stopping the spread of infection. He did not think the powers which were given to the Medical Officer were at all exceeded in any case. There were many gentlemen in the Council Chamber alarmed themselves about the matter unnecessarily. He be- lieved they had got a medical officer who would exercise proper judgment in every individual case and that nobody need be afraid that he would be unreasonable or exacting in carrying out his duty. Mr. Hornall was a conscientious gentlemen, and nobody had any reason to complain of what he did. Councillor BURGESS said a little while ago he heard a gentleman complain OR a public platform of the annoyance caused by the Corporation carts being drawn up in front of his breakfast-room window. He lived next door to that gentleman, and he had seen carts there at breakfast time himself. He should nal say much about that, for it did not affect him much; but he had been in the poorer parts of the town, and had seen the pail carts at noon with the doors wide open. He did not think that sort of thing should be allowed. In Birmingham the whole of that hind of work was done in the night. He had made enquiries, and he had a letter from the Birmitigham Town Hall to that effect. The whole of the ordinary night soil was removed in the night. The dry dust was removed in the day In War- rington the night soil was never removed in the night. EAlderman Burgess: "And never will be."] As to the resolution it was preposed to rescind, he could never under- stand why it should have been passed at all; but it was satisfactory to find that the committee had given way on the question. But he was not quite satisfied; he should like something more. He was very undecided when he left the Council last month what course he should adopt, but after some consideration he decided not to renew the motion without getting an understanding with the Sanitary Com- mittee as to the course they intended to adopt. He believed the committee were as anxious as he was to work for the good of the town; but he did ask for an assurance that they would not act in an arbitrary manner; and that when two doctors certified that a case was already sufficiently isolated, they would instruct their officer not to serve a notice re- quiring removal. (Hear, hear.) He hoped the Chairman would give the assurance he asked for, as it would set people's minds at rest. Councillor BROADBENT thought it would have been much better if Alderman Burgess had been allowed to move his resolution without comment. The kind of discussion which they bad had, seemed rather to perpetuate than to do away with the prejudice against the establishment of the Hospital. Ile was sorry the resolution to be rescinded was ever passed, but after the feeling expressed by the Council at the last meeting, ha thought the Chairman of the committee had taken a wise course in moving the resolution. (Hear, hear.) It would have been more gracious on the part of the Council to have taken the resolution without further com- ment. What the committee desired, and what they all, he hoped, desired, was gradually to remove from the minds of their fellow-townsmen any prejudice that might exist againai sen'ling Children to the Hospital. It was very desirable thatthat should ljeslone. He hoped there would be a growth of opinion on the subject, and that people would be willing, when infectious dieease arose, to take AteiYantage of the hospital. That discussion, however, would tend to retard the progress of such an opinion. It was something new to him to hear the remarks made about the way in which some of them left the Council at the last meetieg. He left for the reason that Councillor Burgess brought forward a proposition which the Town Clerk said was out of order— (hear, hear)—and in contravention of the Act of Parliament, and therefore they were wasting their time in talking allbut the proposition. Councillor linunEss : May I ash the Town Clerk if he said it was in contravention of the Act of Parliament. The TOWN CLERK :Certainly. - Councillor BURGESS asked in what respect. Other legal gentlemen said it was not, The MAYOR : I think the Town Clerk has answered your question. Councillor PLATT thought if less discussion took place upon the matter it would be for the good of the town. After the action of the Council in remitting the charges made upon people whose children and relatives had been in the Hospital, things had gone on satisfactorily. He had been informed by medical men that that had great effect in doing away with the prejudice and opposition of the pe ,pie to send their children to the Hospital. He thought the opinion was grow- ing in town that it was a good institution, carefully and admirably managed, Councillor JEANS congratulated the committee upon the course they had taken. He thought that step was adopted in consequence of what had taken place at the last meeting, and, therefore, Councillor Burgess and one or two of them might also congratulate themselves trpon the action they took. (Hear' hear, and laughter.) In regard to the resolu- tion proposed by Councillor Burgess, and which the Town Clerk said would be contrary to the Act of Parliament, he repeated that they could not override the Act; but they could pass a resolution which would be a guide to the Sani- tary Committee as to what course they should take in certain cases. The Town Clerk said it would be void. In opposi- tion to that, he said the resolution passed in September was on' the same principle void and amounted to nothing. Whether they rescinded it or not, it had no operation in law. The MAYOR: The Town Clerk says he quite agrees with you. It was not the idea of gratify- ing anybody specially, but it was simply a sense of duty that brought the committee to rescind the resolution. At a meeting Of the Sanitary Committee, held on the sth January', it was recommended that seven blue cotton loose dresses be provided for the use of the nurses at the hos- pital when on duty.—lt was resolved that the Council be re- commended to rescind the following resolution, passed on the 7th September, 1880, and that a motion to that effect be made by the chairman at the nest Council meeting : "Resolved, that in the interest of public safety, all cases of infectious diseases such as are specified in the Warring- ton Corporation Lighting and Improvement Act, 1879, arising within the borough, be removed to the Infectious Diseases Hospital for treatment."—At a ' meeting held on the 19th Jan., It was resolved that licenses be granted under section 5 of "The Markets and Fairs Temporary Order of , 1881," to Mr. Joseph Taylor and to Messrs. Peter Harrop and I Joshua Mosscrop,, authorising sales by public auction of I certain fat animals intended for slaughter, such licenses to be granted under and subject to the conditions specified in section s.—lt was resolved, at a meeting held on the 26th January, that Mr. James Sinclair Lamont be appointed the general manager of the Longford Manure Depot, at a salary of £2OO per annum, sabject to the terms of an agreement to be prep tred by the Town Clerk. Alderman BUROESS moved the adoption of the minutes of this committee. In reference to the resolution which the committee recommended the Council to rescind, he said that 1 resolution was put upon the minutes of the committee at the; time the town was threatened with a severe epidemic of scarlet fever. The committee knew when they passed it that no resolution of theirs could over-ride the Act of Par- liament. They never dreamt of such a thing. They simply placed the resolution on the minutes as a record of their 1 opinion that received the unanimous confirmation of the Council; and it was now a matter of record that the Coun- cil thought that under certain conditions, all cases of infec- tious disease, such as were specified in the Act, arising in the borough, should be removed to the hospital for treat- 1 ment. That condition of things bad passed away, and there was no necessity for the resolution to remain upon the minutes of the Corporation. If such condition of things should again arise, in all probability the Sanitary Committee I would bring forward a similar resolution, which he had no t doubt would also receive unanimous support. div.p: Mr. Bright (to Mr. Swift) In what do you contend the Contract lies. Mr. Swift : In that book sir (meaning the book in pos- session of the witness.) Mr. Richardson: No, no. Mr. Swift: And what was given the man was a mere copy

for his information. Mr. Richardson (laughing) : You know my friend is really amusing you. (Laughter.) Mr. Swift: No, it is my friend who is amusing you, if you are capable of being amused by tactics like those. Mr. Richardson: What was the meaning of giving him that for his information. (To witness) : Has this man (the defendant) signed anything in your book. Witness: No. (Laughter.) But the man engaged has his attention drawn to the terms.

Mr. Swift: Now, then. , Mr. Richardson: No, no, no. Mr. Swift (to witness): Did you engage Thomas Smith? —Yes. Mr. Richardson: You handed him a document of the conditions.—Yes. Mr. Swift: Well, I don't know whether your worships consider I am entitled to go on, or whether I must take an adjournment and give notice. Mr. Richardson: A document they say was given to Us which they say we are bound by. Let them Produce that document in the usual way. .

Mr. Swift : Well, you keep saying that. Mr. Richardson: You have to trace it to our possession. Mr. Spencely (to Mr. Swift) : They don't admit they have got it. You see where you are: Mr. Richardson (facetiously): If it was not a material point I would:oblige my,friend, hut it happens to be so material that I cannot oblige him. Mr. Bright: You see where we are, and the question is whether without giving notice you can prove your case. Due notice has not been given to the opposite party to pro- duce the document, and are you prepared to go on. Mr. Swift: Well, if your worships rule that, I should ask for time to give a formal notice. Mr. Richardson: Very well, if your worships give it they will never appear again. (Laughter.) Mr. Swift: But they can give me an adjournment for a fortnight, and I can give Mr. Richardson as many notices as he likes. _

Mr. Richardson: Nothing would afford me greater gratifi- cation than to see the strike soon at an end, and it would not be far lack of effort on my part if it was not. I presume my client may go out without any further trouble. • Mr. Swift: No, no. Mr. Richardson: Oh he will do that whether you think so or not.

Mr. Swift: My friend thinks he is entitled to a dismiisal, but it is the practice of these courts constantly to adjourn cases for formal proofs. Mr. Richardson: Is it indeed. Mr. Swift: And this is one of the most technical of objec- _. . _

tions. He is not entitled to demand a dismissal. Jam en- titled to ask for an adjournment, and I think you would be disposed to give it. He himself is the obstructive, and nobody else, and it is only a reasonable request. Mr. Richardson; Now have you done. My friend, Mr. Swift, I may say, gentlemen is very unkind; he wants to I land me in a dilemma. All I have done to-day is what I have a right to do, and which. if I had left undone, I should be answerable for to my client for neglect of duty. But , when he says that an adjournment is the practice he forgets this is a civil proceeding. He may search Stone, or any authority on criminal law, but this is a civil proceeding of the County Court. The County Court acts as a nisi prius court, and in the sittings of a nisi Rrius he would have been nonsuited by any of Her Majesty's judges in one twentieth part of the time. He is nonsuited to all intents and pirposes. As to its not preventing him from coming again, I will offer no opinion on that. If this is an and to the proceeding an action might be started de noes. Mr. Swift: That is not law. Mr. Richardson: I say this was law when we were both going about in our perambulators. I say it is the law. Mr. Swift: Entirely wrong. Mr. Richardson: The question is, is he entitled to ask for an adjournment. I say no. He is nonsuited, this being a civil proceeding under the power of the County Court. Mr. Swift : My friend has referred to the County Court, and I can only say that it is every day's practice there in civil cases to adjourn for formal proofs. And it is quite in your discretion now whether you compel me to withdraw the summons or grant an adjournment. Is it a reasonable thing to be driven out of court upon an objection of so tri- vial a nature. My friend does not deny that he has the document.
Mr. Richardson : I may have as many as will make poste and nails for all the town.
Mr. Bright: This is really a technical matter, and we had better adjourn into the other room and ask our clerk. Mr. Richardson protested against such a course.
On their return,
Mr. Thompson said : We have considered it very care- fully, and as there is not sufficient evidence of a contract entered into, the case must come to an end.

Mr. Swift: With regard to the other cases, your Worships I withdraw them. Mr. Richardson: We are entitled to our costs, and I shall fall back upon very old statutes not yet repealed. Mr. Swift objected, as it was not the practice. Mr. Richardson: Well, if there is no precedent we will make one.

Mr. Thompson : ; we are not inclined to grant it. Mr. Richardson : Not inclined to grant it? Pardon me asking, as the smallest donation would have been thankfully received, and you even don't concede me that. (Laughter.) Mr. Richardson then left the court, and was heartily cheered by hundreds of people as he emerged from the court and proceeded along the street.

div.p: RUNCORN W ESLEY AN_ TEMPERANCE
SOCIETY. ANNUAL MEETING.

_ On Monday evening, the annual meeting of the Runcorn Circuit Wesleyan Methodist Temperance Society was held in St. Paul's Chapel. The chair was occupied by Mr. John Simpson, and there were also present on the platform—The Revs. John Nowell (superintendent), Henry Valentine, and John Colwell and Thomas Hardy (who attended as a deputa- tion from Manchester); Messrs. Timothy Simister, J. D. Jones, and S. C. Beckett. There was a fair attendance. After devotional services, The CHAIRMAN said he was very glad to take the chair at the first temperance meeting which had been held in St. Paul's Chapel. When they looked at the impoetance of the subject they had before them, it seemed to him to be a very proper thing that they should hold their meetings in the chapel. When they remembered that intemperance was the cause of nine-tenths of the crime which was committed in this country, that it desolates more homes than anything else, that it was the cause of the fall of a greater number of their ministers and private church members than anything else—when they remembered that it was the cause of more destruction than war, pestilence, and famine all put together —that it was the greatest hindrance to the spread of the Gospel and the progress of social and religious life—that without temperance education was all in vain—that religion Itself was often, alas I not sufficient to keep men right, he thought they could not attach too much importance to the Subject. Some said that religion was quite sufficient. If a man had the love of God in his heart, if he would keep it there, of course nothing more was wanted; but the mischief was that the love of drink drove out religion from a man's heart. (Hear, hear.) The other day in a town not a hun- dred miles from Runcorn, two men were noticed looking very earnestly down the street. Some one enquired what they were lookin; at, when they replied, "Look at that drunken parson. He is so drunk that I don't know how he will get home." Yes; the parson was so drunk that he could scarcely walk. That occurrence happened within the last week. Of Course they might multiply instances, sad enough to break their hearts. Almost everyone knew instances where drink had ruined the body and soul of its victims. Surely, they could not neglect the matter, when the Con- ference had arranged that ode Sunday every year should be especially devoted to the subject of temperance in their pulpits. When they remembered the importance which was attached to day school education, that sermons were preached and meetings held in chapels, Surely they could not think there was the slightest objection to holding tem- perance meetings, the influence of which would be for the good in every way of their chapels. They had had for some time a temperance society, which had proved success- ful in a certain sense. They had not a very large number of adults who bad actually become members of the society, but he was very glad to say that they had on the books 189. These were actual members—not members who had given their names some time ago, and who were now lost sight of. They were actual members at the present, and he was pleased to say of that number 53 were ladies. The influence exercised by those members of the society could not be but very great. Then in connection with their four Sunday schools they had very successful Bands of Hope, and he said it in an unqualified sense. They had in connection with Brunswick Band of Hope 471 members; at Camden, 280 • at Mill Brow, 120; and at Nelson-street, 45; making in an 916 children who were members of the Bands of Hope in connection with four Sunday schools. These were actual members, and he believed that amongst that number not one of the 189 of what they called the Temperance iSociety for adults was counted. They had reason to expect,when they saw what they, as WesleYans, were doing, and what other denominations in Runcorn were carrying out, and when they looked on what other societies not connected particu- larly with any religious denomination, were effecting in the way of promoting temperance, that many of them might eve in teeht had a tsdoe weh enae. nb e et tee Try hrs eet avr etael ewonf et trihet i nwtg swe would ladpnd oeienetthhs a tibl. ewe eheweinroe d eu would ul rinkaker enittyo- name, which ought specially ° be first was that it was their duty to anyone woUld d with h disagree w • •r k themselves, and they all toolktakkee kept care n . omf i care nd The themselves.. alll fe did took not care ei nf bodies.
