(Hear, hear.) There was- another paint to be kept before them, viz., that they ought to try and be careful not to injure those around them. They could not take drink without the influence of their example being injurious to others. They knew there were many people who had been in the habit of taking drink all their lives, and it never seemed to lead them into danger or excess. They could not tell whether that was really the case, but so far as they could judge it was so; but them were so many cases in which they knew very well it was a temptation to evil, and that if the people took drink at all i they could not help taking too much. They ought to use their example to induce such persons to refrain from taking drink altogether. If they looked at the subject fairly, they would see that both for their own sake, and for the sake of those around them, it was better to totally avoid the use of intoxicating drink. He did not blame those who differed with him ; those views were very different from what he once held, and he was a long time in getting to what he I considered a proper state of mind on the question. He did not blame anyone who did not look at the matter as he did, but he did think if they would really try impartially to judge of the question and not to be swayed by their friends, not to be swayed by their own tastes—but look it fairly in the face, and see whether they could find any good reason for continuing to take drink, or whether they could not, on the other hand, find hundreds of reasons why they should give it up, he thought some of their friends would soou agtee -with them, and think that it was better for them- selves and better for others to be total abstainers. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The Rev. Jolter Cotwata, who delivered a speech marked by much humour, and was loudly applauded, said a man ought to be a teetotaller in order to preserve his own safety. (Hear, hear.) The first business of a man was to save him- self. The superfine philosophers of the present day dealt with many questions in a somewhat remarkable manner, and somehow or other they had begun to discover that Christianity itself was a very selfish thing, because it was always teaching people to save themselves. He should like to suggest to them the very important fact that the only man who was prepared to save another, was the man who had saved himself; and therefore the great object of these philosophers was to do the unselfish work of saving humanity. The speaker narrated several anecdotes where fine promising young men who had commenced life with the Glue!. la Unapt prospects had fallen to the lowest depths of . vice and degradation. The only way for them to be safe was to leave the drink alone, neither to touch, taste, nor handle it in any way whatever. (Applause.) lie next gave an accouut of the work done in one of the Wesleyan cir- cuits where he had at one time been stationed, and in which 1,403 adults ha, signed the pledge in the course of nine mourns. He was glad to be able to Bay that the wheels of the temperance car movement were in motion, and, perhaps, , moving as fast as Was safe and expedient. They must closely study the signs of the times, and bestir t hernselves when, like one of old, they heard the sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees." (Hear, hear.) An organ- ised attack was now being made upon the temperance move 4. meut, and it Was their duty to valiantly resist it and do all that they were justified in the way of defending them- selves, rue other day a man was talking to another in a railway train cud he said that Sir Wittrid Lawson was a rat. 'lime second peisuu, who, it was hardly necessary to state, was a teetotaller, said "Yes, and you would like to be the cat.which would eat the tat!" The supporter of the drink traffic. „canewledged that he would, ou which his companion rernarkal "You mind that the British House of Commons is not the dog that eats the cat that ate time rat." (Loud laughter.) Vested intgests on the part of the publicans was a cry of modern date. Vested intetetts Yshiat about the vested interests of the thousands of men and women who were be* destroyed body and soul? What about the vested iuterests tat the poor little children who welt being injured from their very cradle by the drink traffic? Now that they had a great organisation rising up to protect the traffic—an organisation which had its ramifications ll through the country; which had the Press at its command; which haa talent both at home and abroad in its service—it was time for them, as temperance men, to take up cudgels in their own defence. (Applause.) They must not allow their opponents to have matters all their own way—(hear, hear)—for" there Was a sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees." There was another sign' which they must by no means dis- regard, viz, that the present Government was, to a large extent, on the side of temperance. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) He was not going to say anything political, buthe thought he might be allowed to remark that the late Govern- ment was one of the very worst they ever bad in power from a teetotal point of view. (Hear, hear.) He did not think the men that composed it were worse that those who com- posed the present one; but it was a" beery Goverarnent." It was rolled into powder, to a large extent on beer barrels, and they could not expect a Government that got into power that way, should turn its back upon the people who sent them there. (Laughter.) Now they had a Government in authority who, whatever might be its political merits or de- merits, were pledged to do something in the matter of licensing reform. (Hear, hear.) They had men, who by Weir speeches before they went intothe House, who by their history, and by the tendency of their intellectual and moral thought, into, who, by their pledge, and by everything that made them such men as they were, committed to do some- thing in respect of the question. (Hear, hear.) Now was the time to strike, while the iron was hot. They must not pursue a course which brought to his mind the story of two blacksmiths, both of whom were dreadful stammerers; and whilst one was trying to tell the other where to strike the iron got cold, on which the other said, "You needn't— strike—it—anywhere—now.—We cold." (Loud laughter.) They must not Wail until the golden opportunity hail passed. They might depend upon it that the arm of the law was the only capable way of dealing with the giant drink evil in their large centres of population. It was not the duty of a legislature to run before the people, but to follow them ; and when the mass of the people gave a distinct and unmis- takable utterance, to the effect that they meant to have the great evil of the traffic in intoxicating drink removed from their midst, no Government woald resist that cry, for the Voice of a united people never had been and never could be resisted. (Applause.) What they needed was to cultivate public opinion. Look at the question as it stood in connoc- tion with the Church of God. In this great movement they were striking for God and the lives of millions of English- men—it was no trifling work in which they were engaged. They must try to exert a discretionary power upon the Government; and if they could net get all they wanted, must try to get all they could. If they could only keep cutting off, little by little, some of the power of the publi- cans they would in the end find themselves masters of the situation, and able to raise a shout victory and give God Ithe glory. (Loud applause.) The Rev. THOMAS HARDY delivered a speech marked by considerable power and originality. He commenced by dealing with the objection that men who bad to perform hard physical labour could not do without strong drink, and remarked that his auswer to that was at the time when he first became a total abstainer he was hard at work in one of the coal Mines of Lancashire. He maintained nothing was in- terfering so much with the trade of this country as the great amount of money spent in drink, which, if it found its way into commercial chaunels, would produce results that would astonish the entire commercial world. Surely no one would disagree with him when he said that the drink traffic had an evil influence politically. This was clearly. proved by the reports of the Election Commissions at Chester and other large towns' which were enough to bring a blush upon the cheek of all true patriots. If the de- moralisation caused by drinking at election times were removed, their members of Parliament would be returned on a more intellectual basis, and men sent to St. Stephens who would represent the morality, the virtue, and the piety of our country. (Applause.) They were all agreed that in- toxicating drink was an evil religiously—never had the churches been so distinct in their utterance upon this matter as at present. He was not an old man, but he could remember the time when it would have been almost con- sidered sacrilegous to hold a temperance meeting in one of I their chapels. He could recollect very well a brother," , who was possibly very well meaning, declaring that he I I would rather read a play bill than the notice of a tempe- rance meeting front tie pulpit. When they considered the great change which had taken place in their own denomina- tional theological institutions and their circuits on this ire- I portant question, and that the Conference had sent forth the solierne for establishing circuit temperance societies, they could not but feel astonished at the progrest they had made. They had about 1,000 professed teetotallers, or members of Bands of Hope in connection with the Wesleyan Methodist circuits in Runcorn, and these, if only properly generalled, were capable of causing a great change in that neighbour- hood. (Hear, hear.) They rejoiced that the Methodist Church was now working energetically in connection with the movement. Then there were such men as Cardinal Manning and Father Nugent, who by their devoted efforts . had wrought a wonderful change in the Roman Catholic population of this country. The Church of England Tern-I perance Society was also doing a most able work. As to the Primitive Methodists, they had been in the van of the tem- perance mov.ment from the very first, and Hugh Bourne, ' one of the principal founders of the denomination, was the ' first man to give abstainers the benefit of unfermented wine at the Lord's table. He had a confident belief that there was a mote bright and glorious future before this country than anything it had known in the past, if we could only secure the sobriety of our people. The speaker then gave a very touching account of , the fall of a well : know missionary to China, in connection with the Methodist denomination through drink; and the unavailing efforts he had himself made to save hint. It was 'sad to relate that the very man to whom he referred was that day I one of the stonebreakers at Crumpsall workhouse! The temperance labourers might be described as the moral scavengers who were going:before the chariot of the Gospel, levelling the hills and other obsticles in the way, and pre- paring a highway of holinese on which the redeemed of the Lord might walk with safety. Mr. StarPsorr left the meeting at this part of the proceed- ings, and his place was taken by Mr. Timothy Simister. After a few remarks from the chairman and Mr. Beckett, the proceedings terminated.

div.head: RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBITING SOCIETY. THE LICENSING BILL.
div.p: RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBITING SOCIETY. THE LICENSING BILL.

- _ The House met on Tuesday evening, when, there was a ' fair attendance of members and strangers. The Speaker took his seat at eight o'clock, and the Ballet Amendment Bill was brought on in committee for the last time. An amendment to the last clause relating to the length of time the Act shall remain in force, was proposed by the member for Ncrrrureattat, namely: "That the Act shall remain in force till December 31st, 1886." The Bill as amended was then passed without a. division. The HOME SECRETARY then introduced his Bill to amend the licensing laws, and said in introducing that Bill he was pleased to think it was not a party measure, seeing that Liberals and Conservatives, abstainers and non-abstainers alike felt that the question of the liquor traffic was a subject which most come to the front. An effort must be trade to deal with the growing evils arising from the present state of the licensing laws. He believed the time had arrived when the present laws relating to the sale of drink should give place to more just legislation. It was a melancholy fact that the drinking system of the country was destroying its wealth. In a recent speech delivered by the Rev. G. M. Murphy it was stated that dining the past 25 years there bad been spent in drink, in the United Kingdom, 1.2,500,000,000, ea amount which was over three times the total of the Natienal Debt, and the Archbishop of York said it was a fact that £140,000,000 were spent annually in the country en intonicating drink. The amount was so gigantic they could scarcely realise it. It one-hatf of that sum were turned into other channels and spent upon their manufac- tures, the cry of bad trade would soon cease, and they would be able to 'held their own in the manufacturing industries; and considering the richness of the mineral wealth of the country, make it impossible for other conntries to compete with them. The drinking system produced crime and its consequent misery. M. Gladstone said, "The drinking systeni of this country is equal to the accumulated evils of warosettilence, mad famine." Mr. John Bright said, "at produces crime, disorder, and even madness." Dr. Norman Kerr stated that over 100,000 people died annually in the conatry through drink. Major Greig in his report for 1880 said that in Liverpool there were 43,059 persons proceeded against summarily, of which 1452 were for drunkenness. That state of things was not to be wondered at when they found that to every 36 houses in England there was a public- house. flay* referred to the dark side of the question, he would see if there was anything to relieve the darkness. Their opponents were fond of referring to the revenue de- rived from the drink traffic, which amounted to 40 millions annually. But when they put the cost of the crime, pau- perism, and lunacy caused by drink in the scale against the 40 millions, it would more than weigh it down. They spent on paupers alone f.. 15,140,727. He then re- ferred the House to the first preamble, which was to the effect that it was desirable to give the ratepayers a more direct and immediate control over the granting of licenses than they at present possess. Under the existing law the magistrates were the licensing authority. They were ap- pointed by the Lord Lieetenant af the County—a total stranger in most cases to the localities. They were notably party political appointments. The majority of magistrates were non-residents, and unacquainted with the requirements Of the neighbourhood, and had manifested a great disinclina- tion to listen to the ratepayers when they appealed aga nst the setting up of public-houses in their midst. The Rev. H. P. Hughes had mentioned a case where the magistrates in his own neighbourhood declined to receive a memorial signed by 95 per cent. of the inhabitants against the grant- ing of a license. The ratepayers bore the burdens of pauper- ism and crime produced by the drink traffic, and ought, therefore, to have a voice in the election of those who grant the licenses. That right was a characteristic of the British Constitution. He referred to the importance of the ques- tion of Sunday closing of public-houses. He had seen the beneficial results of the system in Scotland, where for 25 years Sunday closing had been in force. Canon Stowell had stated that in one year 15 millions of money passed into the till of the publican on Sunday. In proportion to the number of hours the houses were opened there was more drunkenness on Sundays than on any other days. Mr. B. WRITWORTII, M.P. for Drogheda, said the Irish Sunday Closing Act WAS a perfect success. Judges said that drunkenness had decreased. and it might be attributed to the Sunday Closing Act; and Judge Lawson said perhaps some gentleman will propose to extend the Act to every day in the week, and if that succeeds we shall have a millenium of sobriety. The publicans said it was destroying their trade. (Laughter. and hear, hear.) The licensing laws had been tried for 300 years, and though 300 amendments had been made and added to the statute book, vet they had the desola- tion and misery which time would fail to enumerate. It was time to try some other mode, and branch out into an alto- gether different line, and endeavour, if possible, to wipe away the stigma which clung to them as the moot drunken nation under the sun. (Applause.) The INDIAN SECRETARY seconded the second reading of the Bill, but reserved his speech. After a few remarks from the Foreign Secretary in favour of the measure, the right hon. member for &WEE rose to move an adjournment of the delapte, which was agreed to. The member for Lt-neow gave notice of an amendment to clause 2, which would disqualify any person connected with the drink traffic from acting on a licensing board. The member for WALSALL gave notice of an amendment to clause 2, to the effect that the manner of election of licensing boards be similar to that in force for the election of town councils and other bodies. The member for LEEDS gave notice to ask the President of the Council "What has been the yearly amount of Government grants which have been given for education to public elementary schools from the year 1870 to 1880 inclu- sive, and also the number of public elementary schools there were in 1870 and 1880."
The House then rose.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit (chairman) and Mr. R. M. Brooke. THE SUMMONS AGAINST Ma. BANHES, J.P.—On the pre- vious Monday, Mr. Wm. Bankes, J.P., was summoned for non-payment of poor rates.—Mr. Ashton (magistrates' clerk) said he understood that the case was settled, but that Mr. Lake (Messrs. Day and Lake) wished to make some remarks in the Way of explanation, on the part of Mr. Baikes.—Mr. Lake said the summons was taken out for the purpose of enforcement of poor rates in connection with some property at Weston. Having censured the reference to Mr. Bankes in a contemporary as "a defaulting ratepayer," he said the rates for the property were payable by the bene- ficial occupier, and not by the owner. The rates had been paid by the tenants daring the past year, and not by Mr. Bankes. The property was not in that gentleman's posses- sion, and it was on this ground that he cbjected to paying the rates. The defendant received no note whatever in regard to the rates until the summons was taken out, so that he found himself in this position—that he was asked to pay rates for which he was not aware he was rated. The pro- perty was not in Mr. Bankes's occupation, and what made the matter worse, he was then unable to appeil. If the rate had been properly laid, it was somewhat strange that the defendant did not receive the notice about it at the same time that be had the other notices. On the gronnds men- tioned, Mr. Bankes refused to pay. Though the rates had since been paid, Mr. Baakes wished it to be understood that ho had not paid them, neither had they been discharged by hie privity.—The Chairman: Who ha e paid them, then?— Mr. Lake could not say, but he presumed the tenants. So far as he could gather, the person who had received the money from the tenants te pay the rates had done so; but the money had not been received from Mr. Bankes. It was not, therefore, correct to say that the defendant was "a defaulting ratepayer," as he objected to pay en the ground of his non-liability.—Mr. W. H. Linaker asked if he might be permitted to say a word on behalf of the overseers of Weston 7—Mr. Brundrit intimated that he was perfectly at liberty to do so. —Mr. Linaker remarked that after what had been stated he thought it only right to say that the over- seers had no vindictive feeling against Mr. /Nukes. They had served him with a notice as to the rates, under the be- lief that he was the party in beneficial occupation of the land. He understood that the crops had since been sold by direction of the defendant. Mr. Lake was certainly wrong in his law, as the Chairman would know, because any ratepayer had the right to appeal to the Assessment Com- mittee against the rate, as well as against the assessment list. [The Chairman: Yes.] In what they had done the overseers had taken the only course that was open to them. If Mr. Bankes had appealed on the recerpt of his demand note, they would only have been too glad to put the matter right, if he were not the proper person liable. Under the circumstances, the overseers had no option but to sum- mon the defendant, as he was in the rate book.—The Chair- man said he supposed the matter was now settled, and that, the explanation having been given by Mr. Lake, the Bench bad no more to do with it.—Mr. Linaker: No, sir; the thing is now settled.—The proceedings in the case then terminated. TRIMATENING A LANDLADY.—Jane Jones, a middle-aged woman, was summoned for threatening to assault Mary hl lme, of the Holyhead Harbour public-house, High-street, on the 22nd ult.—Complainant said the defendant came to the house and wanted a man who was in the parlour. She told her to leave, as she did not want her nor any such characters there. Defendant then became very abusive, and threatened to kick her nose off—Defendant, who said she lived with a man named Wm. Cox, stated that the com- plainant would not allow any but married women in the house. "They had three or four servants, and did not want any women like her in." Complainant called her a dirty name, and told her to leave. She did not threaten com- plainant.—Defendant was ordered to be bound over, herself in £lO, and two sureties in £5 each, to keep the peace to- wards complainant, and she bad also 14s. 6d. costs to pay. She wept and said she could not find the sureties, on which the Bench said she would have to go to gaol for four- teen daYs• . _

- yEsTNEDAY.—Before Mr. S. B. Chadwick (chairman) an . Mr. J. Reynolds. A DISORDERmt RAILWAY Passim:int.—Samuel Nancar- row, a sailor, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at the Runcorn railway station.—Mr.- James Leach, station that on the previous evening the prisoner arrived by the 7-30 train from Chester. A passenger comef master, sMtecl pained to him that he had been annoyed by the man, who, on getting out of the carriage, pulled off his coat and waist- coat and expressed a desire to fight with anyone upon the platform. lie gave the prisoner in charge of the police.— Prisoner now pleaded guilty, and he was fined 10s. and 78, 6d. coats, or in default of payment 14 days' imprisonment.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. DRui. 11„"Dss"._'"Iheofttrase mGrOlGdiengrgweasrifilknengthd ss. and c0.t,c9,1. on the evidence of P.C. Graham, for this offence, eit the 27th ult. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. E. Gibbon and Mr.F. ll.Gossage. CHIMNEY ON FIUE.—For being guilty of this offence, Ellen Glynn, widow, Catherine-street, was ordered to pay ss. —The case was proved by P.C. Brydges. Caution ow AOORAVATED ASSAULT AGAINST AN AMLE- 'TON PUBLICAN.—Mr. Harrison Turton, landlord of the I Railway Hotel, Appleton, was charged, under a warrant, with assaulting his wife.—Mr. MOOPO, of Warrington, appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Beasley defended.—ln opening the case, Mr. Mame said it was one of the most painful with which he had ever had to deal. The complainant and defendant had not been married quite twelve months. A week ago the prisoner was summoned to that court for a similar offence to that with which he was charged that day. but the wife, being willing to give him another chance. asked that the case might be allowed to stand over. Both himself and Mr. Beasley had come to the conclusion that it was absolutely necessary for the safety of the wife that she should live away from her husband. Not only had defen- dant been drinking heavily, but he was scarcely responsible for his actions. The complainant was afraid , that it she went to live with her husband again, she would not leave the house alive. He had to ask for an order of separation under the Matri- monial Calms Act. If the Bench declined to grant a jUdicial separation, it would result is putting the wife to extra law charges in the Divorce Court- Tie persons in the case held a respectable position in society, and the com- plainant did not desire that her husband might be sent to gaol. On the night of the 31st ult., defendant came home from Widnes, and complainant get his supper ready, after Ohich be went to bed. In the bedroom he seized the poker, broke the castors of the bed with it, and then threw it into the bed. Complainant became alarmed, and ran with her child into the servant's room. Defendant then seized her, knocked her against the wall, and otherwise so conducted himself that she was afraid of living with him again.—Mr. Beasley agreed with his friend Mr. Moore that it was neces- sary there should be a separation. He was of opinion that at present it would not be wise for the wife to live with Mr. Turton, who had not for some time been quite responsible for his actions. The complainant's relatives were people of means, and he hoped the Bench would not come to any de- cision to send defendant to gaol.--The Chairman scarcely thought it would be to the interests of the wife to grant a separation at that time.—Mr. Moore said that since Whit- suntide his wife had lived in a perfect purgatory.—The Bench retired for half an hour, with the Deputy Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. Lewin) and on their return into court, the Chair- man said they had decided to remand defendant until that day week, in order that he might be examined by a com- petent medical man as to his state of mind. CHARGE AGAINST THE MANAGER OF A BOOT AND SHOE SHOP.-Wm. Holland was brought up, on remand, charged with having, on the 2nd ult., embezzled 3e. 3d., the money of his employers, Messrs. Henry Garner and Sons, who have a shop in Victoria-road, Widnes.—Mr. Beasley appeared to prosecute, and Mr. Husband for the defence.—Mr. Beasley said that owing to certain circumstances the suspicions of the firm had been excited, and they bad an examination made of the defendant's books, which were not found in a proper condition. His (Mr. Beasley's) friend, who appeared for the defence, had been to him that day, and offered a reasonable explanation of the charge of embezzlement. From the facts , placed before him he was of opinion that there was some . chance that Holland was not criminally culpable. If such , proved to be the case, he was sure his clients would have no , desire to proceed with the case. It had been agreed that the Bench should be asked to grant a remand for one week, in order to give the defendant a chance of establishing his in- nocence.—Mr. Husband felt every confidence that the defendant would be able to establish his perfect trustworthi- ness.—The magistrates remanded the prisoner for one week, and admitted him to bail?himself in £2O, and two sureties in £lO. • DISCI:JAW:MD.—John Riley, a lad, brought up on remand, charged with stealing a bucket of slack from the Mersey Copper Works, on the 20th ult., was discharged. ALWIED JUVENILE SHOPIIREARERS. Two youths named Martin Mulvey and James Dwyer were charged, on remand, with breaking into two lock-up shops belonging to James Haynes, boot and shoe maker, and Thos. Cook, a sweet dealer, both in Victoria-road. On going to hissbop on the previous Monday morning, Mr. Cook missed a number of cigars, sweets, and matches, value about 88. Entrance had been obtained by breaking the windows. Mr.i Haynes told a somewhat similar story, and said the only articles be had missed were some leather laces. On appre- hending and searching Mulvey, P.C. Ross found upon him boxes of matches and a fusee box containing sweets. He admitted having six cigars, and said that Dwyer broke the glass to gain an entrance. On the latter being charged, he denied being concerned in the offence, but Mulvey told him that he was there at the time.—Prisoners, who have been for trial on another charge, were committed to the Quarter Sessions. NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN. PRIMITIVE METHODIST MISSIONS —On Sunday last a series of sermons and evangelical services were begun at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Leigh-street, Earlestown. The services were conducted by the Rev. G. Warner, of the evangelical connection, London, and will be continued every 1 evening up to, and including Thursday, February 10th, I 1881. So far the services have been of an earnest character and are fairly attended. Collections are made each evening in aid of the expenses incurred in the mission work.

INTERMENTS IN THE WARRINGTON CEMETERY. —The interments in the Warrington Cemetery for the week ending yesterday, were: Adults, 11; children, 11; total, 22. IlaianTor's Dv:manta IN RIINCORN.—Last (Friday) night, Mr. Hamilton commenced an exhibition of their new I pictorial entertainment entitled "Past sad Present," at the Public Hall, Runcorn. The views embrace the principal cities in Great Britain and Ireland, and the continent of Europe, and pictures of the comparatively recent events in Zululand, including the defence of Rorke's Drift, by Lieu- tenants Chard and Bromhead, with their little band of 90, against 5,000 Zulus. It is now a long time since there was a good entertainment of this description in the town, and we hope it will receive the patronage it deserves. NATIONAL UNITED ORDER OF FREE GARDENERS.— The balance sheet, of the Sandbach district of the above order has justbeen issued from which we quote the following items :—Sick and 'funeral fund receipts, £305 Os. Bd.: ex- penditure, £2OB 19s. id.; management receipts, £4O 35. 4d.; new members entered during the year, 29; expelled, 3: suspended, 1; dead, 4; present number of members 275; being an increase of 25 since the last annual return'; total, worth of the district £3,310 15s. We congratulate the mem- bers and the order in Sandbach district on the fact that, not- withstanding the unfavourable state of trade during the past year, the order is making steady progress. WARRINGTON LEAGUE OF THE CROSS. —A concert was given in the League Hall, Bewsey-street, on Monday' evening, for the purpose of clearing off the debt incurred by the alterations in the hall. There was a good attendance, and the concert passed off successfully. The "A BC" duet and " Flow on, thou shining river" duet were well Tendered by Mss K. Marsh and -Mr. J. Mullins, and also "Come back to Erin," by Mr. J. Wilkinson; "The cottage by the sea," by Mr. A. Boyle; "We come to thee, Savoy," duet, by Miss K. Marsh and Miss J. Molyneux ; and "Pull away chesrily," by Mr. P. Walsh. Mr. T. Mather presided at the piano. •

WILMINGTON PETTY SESSIONS.—There were no cases for disposal at this court on Wednesday morning, and the presiding magistrate, Mr. Artingstall, was presented, as is the usual custom, with a pair of white kid gloves. Mr White (the magistrates' clerk), in making the presentation, remarked that it was the first time in his recollection, which extended over 20 years, that there had been no business to transact at that court.—Mr. Artingstall said he hoped there would be many such occasions in the future.—The reason assigned for this immunity from detected crime is that almost all the constables in the division have been for the last fortnight amongst the colliers in the Wigan and Tyldesley divisions. ANCIENT OMER Or FORMTERS WARRINGTON DIS- TgieT.—The annual returns of Court Jaaziel, No. 138, of the above order, held at the Crown and Sceptre Inn, War- rington, have been issued to the members. The receipts for sick and funeral fund last year were £ll5 85 2d; expendi- ture for 46 weeks' sick pay to 13 members, £2l 15s; tune- rtls, £2B; levies to district, £3O is 7P; management fund balance for last year, £1 185 7d; receipts, £26; expenditure for medical attendance an/ managetnent, dtc., £27 12s 71d Total worth of Court, £llB 8s sd. Increase of the funds for the year, £34. Present number of members, 80; admitted during the year, 7 • dead, 1. It is pleasing to notice that this old-established Court, during a time of trade which has militated very much against the prosperity of friendly societies, has been enabled last year to add to its funds a sum equivalent to 8s 6d per head on its present number of members. - -

Mr. Swxyr : I know it was una-nswered that day, and I was surprised at that answer last Council meeting. I think it is most important that the Act of Parliament should be observed, because it is only becoming that members should not vote upon matters they are interested in. Mr. FILKINGTON: But does this not refer to partner- chips? Mr. SWIFT: My impression is that it applies directly to any one who has any pecuniary interest in any limited liability, or joint stock company. With regard to the elec- tion of a town councillor the Act of Parliament has re- moved the difficulties, and enables a member of a liability company, to be a member of the Council, but not to vote on matters in which he is interested. Mr. MASSEY : My object is simply to avoid difficulties in the future. I have no wish to embarras the Town Clerk or any member of a liability company. Mr. Swlrr : Personally I am quite satisfied with the ob- servation as I think it is quite enough. Alderman GAMBLE: Well, are members interested en- titled to speak, or are they not? I don't pretend to know the law, but I have been advised, on many different occa- sions, that a shareholder does not become subject to this. It would be very inconvenient to many and (laughing) to some of those who are interested in the London and North- Western Railway Co. The minutes were then confirmed. THE STAMPING OF WATER TAPS. The minutes of the Water Committee contained the fol- lowing :—" Resolved, that the suggestion of the Water Engineer, that a water fittings stamping office be estab- lished in this borough, be not adopted." Councillor WILCOCK asked why they should go to Liver- pool, as ever since they had done so they had to keep regularly repairing their taps. Alderman GAMBLE explained that a great number of taps used in the town were very defective. The builders fre- quently put in taps and Attiop willch were really thc rig use of other town!, which would hot be ACCeptea oy the water engineers; and Ito, thought it was only advantageous to the community to have them of good quality, and to ensure this they bad them examined at Liverpool. Bad fittings also caused a waste of water, and by ensuring good taps they not only prevented a great deal of inconvenience, but saved the Corporation a great expense. The question now came before them whether they should have a stamping office of their own and if they did, they would require an officer who would have to be not only perfectly competent, but entirely free from any suspicion of being tampered with. The Chairman of the Liverpool Water Committee said that gave them a good deal of anxiety, and they had to raise the salaries of their officials, not because they could not otherwise get efficiency, but they were obliged to have them entirely above suspicion. Every maker could send his stamp to Liverpool, and there was no favouritism he was sure, and the charge was about 21. a tap. Mr. BROOK was in favour of having a stamp office of their own. It seemed strange to him that they could not find a man in St. Helens able to judge of the quality of taps. It was a great inconvenience and involved great expense in going to Liverpool as they had sometimes to wait for weeks before they could get their fittings stamped. Surely the water engineer was capable of judging of the quality of the taps. Alderman GAMBLE said the cost of stamping was 2d., and it would cost them much more to have a stamping office of their own. They would have a swami of people continually round the office of the water engineer, and some would say that he had no business to stamp such and such stamps. Mr. BROW said he had sent hampers and taps and had to wait a fortnight, though he would guarantee Ley were heavier and of better make than what they had at Liver- pool. Mr. FOSTER said he was talking to a plumber that very morning, who said that he had had to wait three months. It was the general rule to have to wait,and, as a matter of fact, they only tested for pressure, and did not examine as to quality or workmanship. It was a well known fact there difficulty were a great deal of inferior taps at Liverpool, because they particular about their quality. He could see no them pa ymi nt establishing a and dn eoxffipceenosef tihne irg going n, andt,e it would savewie reffi n Liverpool. They stamped their own weights and measures, why not their water taps? If they had a place behind the Town Hall it would not cost them above £5O.

The frost had gone, and many of those men who had been prevented from working would now be in employment. Mr. MASSEY : But, of course, he means strikes as well. Alderman Joineson : But that does net say that if em- ployment were found for those they would accept it. Nothing was done in the matter. BACK YARD SPACE. The minutes of the Paving Committee, containing the following, were confirmed :—Back yards. The committee having visited certain of the back yards referred to in tke notices served by the Surveyor in pursuance of resolution of this Committee of the 22nd November last, resolved, that all such notices be allowed to stand in abeyance, and that the Surveyor be and he is hereby instructed to require for the future a strict compliance with the provisions of section 125 of the St. Helens Improvement Act, 1869. and the by- laws of the Corporation, as to back yards and back yard Space.

TRB TRAMWAYS. A meeting of the Tramways Committee was held on January 17th, Alderman Cook (in the chair).—ln Parlia- ment, Session 1881, St. Helens and District Tramways Bill. —The Town Clerk submitted a copy of this Bill, whereby it is sought to extend by two years the time limited by the St. Helens and District Tramways Act, 1879, for completion of the tramways specified in the Bill—Resolved, that this committee see no reason for recommending the Town Council to oppose the Bill. Alderman CooK proposed the confirmation of the minutes. The Council would be aware that the Tramways Company were applying for an extension of time, and their Bill was laid before the Committee With the teSlitit SA stated. Mr. WacocK seocnatied the motion. Alderman (lemma was sorry that the' Company were tjg that action. It would be remembered there were two other companies with whom they had the chance of making a bargain, but they choose the present one, and something had occurred to stop the tramways being carried on as they ought to have been. It seemed that the Council should op- pose the Company in getting an extension of time. He did not want to put anything in their way, but it appeared to him that that application was attempting to do every- thing that the Corporation did not want them to do, and they had neglected the principal matter which the Corporation insisted upon which was to nuke tramways from St. Helens to Prescot, to Flaydock, to Marshall's Cross, and to Denton's Green. The other companies were perfectly willing to do that work. He proposed the following resolution, which should be insisted upon, or their alternative would be opposition to the Bill : " That they insert a clause in their Bill to take no dividend from their shares until all the tramways are open." That would oblige them to open all the tramways. If they mean to do that it would therefore do them no harm. Mr. W. W. Punisorow seconded the motion. Alderman JOHNSON said if Colonel Gamble would with- draw his resolution he would move that they oppose the Bill in Parliament, as that would answer the same purpose, and they could endeavour to get what clause inserted they liked. Two years was a long time, and if they got the Bill passed it might have the effect of throwing the tramways further off completion than they otherwise would be. Alderman GAMBLE said he would withdraw his motion. Mr. WALKER seconded Alderman Johnson's motion. Mr. BROOK ; What is the objection against the company that they should not be allowed to go on. Alderman COOK: There is no objection. We are certainly not obstructing them. If they will only comply with the requirements of the Act it would be all right. We want to get them completed. Mr. BROOK: I am much obliged to you for the informa- tion. (Laughter.) . Mr. MASSEY : I should like to ask if the application for an extension of time applies to all the tramways. I have been told by the solicitor to the company that this extension of time merely meant for the purpose of completing the line of tramway frona St. Helens to Haydock. Alderman COOK: I understand that the Act of Parlia- ment refers to the whole undertaking. Mr. FosrEn would like to know what was the probable cost of opposing the Bill in Parliament. Mr. W. W. PIJ.KINGTON : I should like to know the pro- bable cost of not opposing them, Mr. Mayor. (Laughter.) Mr. Fonme : I think the people should know what the Coat BM be. lilt is to come out of the ratepayers' pockets I shall oppose it. Alderman Joirtmotir : Well, I should say £.5. (Laughter.) Mr. Swum.: You won't get much law for 45. (Renewed laughter.) Alderman JouNsow : You can get a barrister for £5. Mr. SWIFT: As a friend of Mr. Hanson says, in his line of business you don't see much for M. Mr. Hart baying been sent for, Mr. BREWIS said: The Council want to know if the Bill includes the whole of the tramways. 1 Mr. HART: The whole of the tramways in the borough. Alderman COOK: That is outside the borough ? Mr. HART: I don't know, sir.

Mr. COOK could hardly accept the statement of Mr. Foster as to the taps being only stamped for pressure at Liverpool. He had always understood, and had reason to believe, that they took quality and efficiency into considera- tion. • Alderman JOHNSON said that as it had been stated the time of stamping would only be about two hours a week it I would scarcely be advisable to go to the expense of a build- ing, and of keeping an officer. Mr. FOSTER moved that that minute be referred back to the committee. Mr. BROOK seconded the motion. Mr. McKEctrsrrs thought it was rather too much to go to the expense of having a stamping office in order to accom- modate a few manufacturers in the town, and also run the risk of the work not being done well.
Alderman GABLE: Is it not all the tramways ?

Mr. MASSEY : There must be some mistake somewhere; I don't think I misunderstood my friend. The Councillors having examined the plans and Bill, the conclusion was come to that the Bill included all the lines except Prescot, which is partially finished. The minutes were not confirmed, and it was decided to oppose the Bill.

A PROPOSAL TO HAVE BOROUGH MAGISTRATES. Mr. MASSEY rose to move the resolution, of which he gave notice, "that it is desirable that a Bench of Borough Magistrates should be appointed for St. Helens, and this Council hereby resolves to forthwith petition the Crown to make such appointment." The benefits of such an appoiat- ment were so self evident that he expected very little op- position from that Council. It seemed to him that the appointment of a borough Bench would be nothing more nor less than fulfilling the spirit of the Local Act of Parliament of 1809. That Act of Parliament gave them powers to cover their own affair, and that motion if carried would give them something no less important than the other government of their town. The administra- tion of justice in St. Helens was done by county magistrates, and he for one could not refrain from paying his small tribute of the efficiency and impartial manner in which they had conducted the duties of their office. But he would remind the Council there was a great deal of inconvenience arisim to suitors and advocates in the police courts from there

being a suffiaent number of cOunty magistrates attending: They found that the magistrates who were down on the rota for a particular day did not turn up, and anyone would readily see that the absence of magistrates imposed on suitors great inconvenience, and added additional cost. They had in St. Helens a lare,e number of gentlemen well quali- fied to discharge the duties of such office—men of position, ability, and integrity, and if it were necessary to name any gentlemen who were capable, one might very readily turn to those gentlemen who had occupied in previous years that position which the present Mayor filled—Aldermen Radley, Cooki,and Johnson. If they had a borough court they might, too, have a court sitting daily, and they could thus have a cheap, efficient, and speedy administration of justice. Owing tb the absence of ,nagistrates, cases had to be con- tinually adjourned to the great cost imposed upon suitors, whereas if they had justice administered at once suitors would be benefited every way. It might also obviate the necessity of a stipendiary. It would also give to the town the control of its own affairs, such as licensing the sale of intoxicating drink. He saw no reason why they shnuld not license their own public-houses, and thus it would give them a sort of local option virtually. The ratepayers might make their own opinions felt and regarded by the Bench through representatives in the Council. Under the present system the fees charged by the county were much larger than those charged under the borough magistracy, so that cheaper justice would be given, and quite as efficient, He did not wish St. Helens to be behind other townS, which, with less population, area, and rateable value, had thought it necessary, at all events, advisable, to have a borough bench. .Crews, for instance, had a population of 15,000, and an acreage of 1,318. Accrington, with a population of 30,800, acreage of 3,425, a rateable value of £112,000; Bootle, their neighbour almost, population 25,000, rateable value £105,000, had their borough bench; but St. Helens, with a population of 60,000, acreage 6,586, and a rateable value of £221,199, had not yet its borough bench. He had been in communication with the town clerks and magistrates of other towns, and they were all unanimously of opinion that they would not change their present system if they had the chance. He would remind them of what an eminent member of the Government recently said in a speech de- livered at Birmingham on municipal life—" The greater the responsibility of the ratepayers and the greater the dig- nity they attached to those offices, th, more efficiently , would the affairs of the town be discharge a by those to whom they were entrusted." Mr. BROOK seconded the resolution. Mr. MASSEY: I have been asked if this involves borough police, and I say—no, it does not. Mr. ALLEN said it was an important matter, brought for- ward very suddenly, and he thought they ought to have a little more time to consider the question. Mr.T. COOR said Mr. Allen echoed very much his senti- ments. He was quite ignorant of the relative merits of the two systems, and he thought snore detail should be given in order to form a correct judgment as to the advantages or otherwise of the proposed new system. As to the bad attendance at court, he thought that was as likely to arise in the case of a borough magistracy as in the county, and there were other matters which he would like more information about.

Alderman JOHNSON agreed with the remark that there wanted some rectification in the attendance of magistrates at court. He had had some experience, and there were great reasons for finding fault. Why there had not been more county magistrates appointed he could not understand. The Mayor, they would find, was appointed for almost every Friday in the year to sit in court two or three hours, and he thought that was too much to be called upon to do. Mr. SWIFT could see no objection to the matter being disposed of at once. Personally he had no interest in the matter, but he had a very strong impression that there ought to be a borough bench, and the Act of Parliament contemplated that state of things. It was certainly anomalous that the Mayor of their borough, and the alder- men, during the first year after their mayoralty should sit upon the Bench,—and it was sometimes felt they were not well received by the county magistrates—and after they had performed their functions for a certain time to be cast off like an old shoe. It was a reflection upon the towns- people when they had to go up and down the county to Woolton, Garston, and West Derby for men to administer justice, while they had in St. Helens men with plenty of ability, integrity, and willingness to do everything to be useful to the community. To hold the Queen's Commis- sion of his native borough was an honour, and if St. Helens men were said to be not fit to have that honour, and were allowed•to go without it, it was casting a slur upon their town, and laid them open to the charge that while they might have good and prosperous business men amongst them, there was not a man in the place fit to be a magis- trate. He then compared St. Helens with other towns, re- marking that all the principal towns rco_nd St. Helens every way had borough benches, while St Helens with a large population had justice administered by country men. In the absence of a borough bench the chief men of the town were stigmatised and dishonoured. If there was anything to be said as to the relative merits of the two systems, why did all the other towns round about throw up the county magistrates and form a borough bench of their own. He had never complained of the county magistrates, and he had got on very pleasantly with them. He gave them the highest possible credit. The only two county magistrates living in St. Helens were Dr. Twyford and Mr. Blinkhorn. As to the fees they were certainly very much leis in a borough magistracy. Dr. TWYFORD: He says no one has heard him complain of the county magistrates, yet he says that the fact of there being no bench was owing either to the apathy of the in- habitants or the jealousy of the county magistrates. Ishould like that to be explained. Mr. Swirr : Alderman Johnson has given you a chance of vindicating it by suggesting that a list et men be nomi- nated.

Alderman JOSINSON moved that the question be adjourned for consideration. Mr. MclCEcnxix seconded the motion. Nine voted for this amendment, six voting for the motion of Mr. Massey, amongst Wil9nl were Colonel Gamble and Dr. Twyford,
A BARIVIIIPTCY COURT. Mr. BREIVIS said he had drawn up a petition to Lord Se!borne praying him for bankruptcy juisdiction for St. Helens.
The seal was ordered to be affixed. TUB PARK. ... _
Mr. BROOK: Is there anything to report about the park? The Mavou : It is probable that a special Council meeting will have to be called to censider the report of the committee.

Mr. MASSEY asked if any idea could be given when such a meeting would be called, as he did not think it was cour- teous to Colonel Taylor in treating the offer in that manner. He thought the offer ought to have been either rejected Cr accepted before now. There was a great feeling in the town that some Information should be given. It was now two -months sine the committee was appointed, and almost three since the offer was made. He would move that an extra- ordinary meeting of the Council be called for that day fort- night. The MAYOR: In answer to Mr. Massey I may say that the committee have had several times to meet the railway corn- pang. There was no want of courtesy on the part of the committee as the Town Clerk had seen Mr. Taylor, junr. There was some difficulty in getting the landscape gardener to give his estimate. Mr. MassEv : Well, if Colonel Taylor doesn't care,l don't, only it is to my surprise that he has not withdrawn be- fore now.
The subject then dropped. The minutes of the rest of the committees were confirmed.

PIANOFORTE RECITA.L. —We would draw the atten- tion of our readers to the announcement contained in our advertising columns that a pianoforte recital will be given on Thursday evening next, in the Assembly-room at the Lion Hotel, by Miss Kate Ockleston. Miss Ockleston, who is a young local pianist, recently made her first appearance before a Manchester audience, and our Manchester contem- poraries in their criticisms of the performances speak in unqualified terms of praise of the abilities of which she then showed she was possessed.

RECHABITE TEA MEETING, AT WARRINGTON.—The an- nual tea meeting in connection with the Union Tent of the r Independent Order of Rechabites, was held on Monday evening, in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom, Legh-street. There was a fair attendance of members and their wives. After tea Mr. Thomas Hall was called to the chair, and short addresses were given by the secretary (Mr. John Green), Messrs. J. Dodds, W. 11. Chapman, J. Shaw Green, and others. In the course of his remarks, Mr. J. Shaw Green entered into details as to the state of the Tent, showing it to be in a b;ghly flourishing condition with a reserve fund superior to that of most other sick and benefit societies. He strongly advised all who were present to use their in- fluence to prevail upon young men to join the order, the advantages of which, he said, were at least erimal if tot superior to any other sick society in the world. He also informed the meeting that during the time the Tent had been in existence, now over 40 years, there bad never been a levy upon the members, nor a call for sick pay that had not been met out e the funds of the society. Selections of music were given at intervals, and a pleasant meeting was brought to a close with the usual votes of thanks.

Skrunnay.—Before Alderman Charadeley and Alderman Burgess. WILFUL DAMAGE.—Sarah Riley, a married woman, was charged with having on the 22nd January, done wilful damage to the Cross Keys publichouse, by tweaking a win- dow. The prisoner entered the house on the day namett and behaved in a very disorderly manner. The landlady, Mrs. Laithwaite, advised her to go home, and she then smashed the window.—Prisoner was fined ss. and His. expenses. A DEFAULTBD.—WiIIiam O'Shaughnessy, a private in the Army Reserve, was charged with failing to report himself at Liverpool. He had, it appeared, been imprisoned at the Barracks since the 7th December. vvaitisg instructions from the authorities, and the Bench thought an additional month's imprisonment would be sufficient to meet the case. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) Alder.

Tun BLACK LlST.—James Higham was charged with being drunk in Bold-street, at 6-50 p.m. on Saturday night. He was fined ss. including costs.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed on Patrick Reegan for being drunk and dis- orderly in SaLkey-street on Saturday night.—John Johnson was fined ss. and 6s. costs for being drunk in Crossley-street on the 22nd January.—John Ward, and Julia Ward, man and wife, were charged with being drunk and riotous in Butter- market-street on Saturday. P.C. Astbury and two other constables gave evidence in support of the charge, but the woman denied being drunk and she callled a witness whe confirmed her statement. The Bench discharged the female prisoner and fined her husband ss.—John McKenna was mulcted in a similar sum for being drunk at Market Gate on Saturday night. The offieer said he was very noisy.—The Mayor: He was what they call "Pot valiant.' (Laughter). AN INDISCREET CORSTABLE.—MichaeI Connor, a man well known to the pelice, was charged with being drunk in Horsemarket-street on Saturday, and also with assaulting P.C. Neill. The latter officer said the prisoner when taken into custody, was very violent and struck him several times and then threw him to the ground. • When at the police station he would not be searched, and caught hold of the officer's beard and behaved very roughly.—Prisoner denied 1 the assault and charged the officer with illusing him when in the act of searching and said he would have allowed P.C. Trickett to do so quietly.—P.C. Trickett said the prisoner would have allowed him to search him and lock him up quietly but he would not allow Neill.—Mr. Hunt said it was the duty of the constable who brought in a prisoner tosearch him. Connor wee well known by the police to be a violent man in drink and Neill when he saw the man would not be quietly searched should have kept away. Neill had brought this on himself by his indiscretion, andiit would be a matter for him(Mr. Hunt) and the Watch Committee to deal with. He wodid, if the Bench would allow him, withdraw the eiarge of assault.—Prieoner was ordered to pay the costs 2s. for drunkenness.

ROBBERY FROM THE Pio-Km—Daniel Connor, a tailor, was charged with stealing from the person of Rd. Walters, in Arpley-street, on Saturday night, a felt hat and muffler, value 9s.—Mr. Hunt said the prisoner was very well kaywn at the police court, that being his 39th appearance. At a quarter-past eleven en Saturday night P.C.' Bowen and Illingworth were passing up Arpley-street, better known as Slutcher's-lane, when a man, whom they afterwards found to be the prisoner, walked quickly passed them with some- thing under his coat. The officers stopped him and asked him what he had got under his coat, and he said, "I picked it up from a chap that's lying down there drunk," bringing out the hat produced. The officers took the prisoner back, and found, as he had stated, a man laid on the ground. Whilst there the prisoner endeavoured to pull the muffler from his pocket and drop it on the ground, but he was detected. —The prosecutor said he had worked on Friday, Friday night, and Saturday, and he fell asleep in Arpley-street be- sides some reeds. The hat and muffler produced were his property, and he was wearing them on Saturday, the muffler being fastened to his waistcoat.—P.C.'s Powell and Illing- -1 worth and a man named Evans corroborated the statement lof the Chief Constable.—Prisoner said he found the bat on the footpath, and that he never took the muffler at all.—He was committed to gaol for two months with hard labour.

THE Forriern Ttiam.—Mary Ann Babbitt, a bad character, I was charged with stealing from the person of Henry Evans, in Arpley-atreet, on Saturday night, a purse containing £4O in bank notes and about £l2 in gold and silver.—Mr. Hunt said the complainant in this case was a stonemason bailing ; from Frodshein, and the defendant was the wife of Thomas Babbitt, who is now in gaol serving a term of six months. The defendant one or two nights a week dressed herself up and turned into the dark places about the town, and on Saturday night she was seen in Bridge-street. About nine o'clock the complainant went to the police station, and com- plained that he had been robbed by a person who, from the description he gave, the police suspected to be the defen- dant. She was met with at Market Gate about a quarter to ten and taken into custody. The complainant said he was accosted by the woman in Bridge-street, who said, "How are you? I know you are in want of a sweetheart. Come this way." She forced him down Arpley-street ; and after they had been there a short time a little man came in sight, and defendant ran away, saying "There's my husband." Evans shortly after missed his money. The defendant had been very minutely searched, but all that could be found was 3s. ad. In silver and one penny in copper.—The com- plainant confirmed the statement of Mr. Hunt.—Prisoner stated she had not seen the prisoner before.—Mr. White said this was the fourth charge of that kind there had been against the prisouer, and she had been discharged each time. —Mr. Hunt: She does her work very clean indeed.—The Chairman said it was a very suspicious case, and she would he hound over in her own recognisancee of £2O to appear when called upon. Scwooe ATTENDANCE CASES. John Kelly was sum- moned by Mr. Riley, the school attendance officer, for not sending his son, John Henry, to school. Defendant said he could not manage the lad, and he had tried his best to make him go to school. The lad said that when he went to school Mr. Riley caned him. Mr. Riley wished the Bench to send for the schoolmaeter. It was not likely that he would go into the school, get the schoolmaster's cane, and beat a boy. Mr. Crosfield said the lad deserved punishing for telling such a lie. The Bench asked the father if he was willing that the boy should receive 12 strokes with the birch rod, and he said he was. The Bench made the order. —John Hill was summoned for not sending his sons, John and Joseph, to school. The defendant said the lads were beyond his control. He had whipped them very often, es- pecially John, who had frequently spent the school money. Mr. Riley said the children had not been at school since September. Defendant was fined 58. in each case.—John Bandies was fined Sc. for not sending hie daughter regularly to school.—Peter Kenwright, a butcher, was summoned for not sending his children, Alice, Elizabeth, and Mary to school. Defendant said he had had the measles in the house, and thought it best to keep his children at home. They web ° going to school now. Case dismissed. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A TRADESMAN. James Tetley, provision dealer, summoned for having of Bewsey-road, Warrington was unlawfully assaulted Elizabeth 'Tim- mins, on the 12th De'cember, and with baying, on the 18th January, used language calculated to cause a breach of the peace.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the defendant —Mr. Moore said he had only had the brief put into his hands that morning. Mr. Harrison should have taken the case, bet he Was away in London, and he asked for an adjourn- ment as he could not do full justice to the case. The Bench refused to adjourn the case, and Mr. Moore then threw up his brief.—The complainant said that on the 12th December she went into the shop to fetch some whitening to clean the hearth, and Mr. Varley followed her. She knelt downbehind the counter and he came and assaulted her. In the scuffle he dragged her round to the other side of the counter, and she managed to get away.—Cross-examined by Mr. Davies: It was about three o'clock. There were only two children In the house; Mrs. Varley had gone to Padgate. Witness did not go to the Sunday school on that day. She had not told Mrs. Yates it was all a lie. When he Fot hold of her she screamed loudly. She remained in his service until January 18th. She told Mrs. Bibbington and Mrs. Byfield of the occurrence but not Mrs. Varley. She did not go home and tell. Mr. Varley said the same day that he would not interfere with her again if she would not tell. On Sun- day, the 18th January, he got her on his knee. He had only joked with her on previous occasions before Mrs. Varley, who had told her to take no notice; be meant no harm. She had been in his employment about five months. She had no nights out. She kept company with a man named Kilter. She knew a man named Neilton, but had never kept company with him. He took her home from the Christmas tea party. She had been servant for Mr. Clayton, grocer, Buttermarkee. street. She had made charges against him, but he had not gone as far as Mr. Varley. She did not take proceedings as Mr. Clayton begged her father not to do—Mrs. N. Hum- I phreys, aunt to the complainant, said she went to see her neice on Tuesday the 18th inst., and she asked Mrs. Varley if she was aware that her husband had bevejeuniting Elizabeth and she said she was not. Elizabeth was out taking milk, but when she came in Mrs. Varley asked her to tell her what the master had been doing. She did so, and the defendant said "I was only wrestling with her," avid added that if he had done any harm he would pay for it. After that he jumped up to strike her niece, but witness pre- vented him. She brought her niece away and defendant said "If you will leave her here I will not interfere with he... again."—Mrs. Bebbington, Mrs. Byeeld, and Margaret Jones were called, but each other stated they knew nothing of their own knowledge; only what the girl had told therre—mr. Davies, for the defence, said the defendant was unques- tionably a most respectable man. If the wife of the defen- dant had been able to give evidence she would have told the Bench that the complainant on the day in question left the house at two o'clock to go to Sunday school, and that she did not return until 5 o'clock. How then could Mr. Varley have taken these liberties in the shop? The girl after the alleged assault took place still remained in his service and did not go home to tell her parents. A very strange proceeding..--7. Mrs. Bebbington, who was recalled, said it was through her e advice that the girl stopped at the shop and did not tell Mrs. a` Va e larley.—Jobn Williams, wireworker, said he was 1 at the Bank Quay Sunday school. NOTICE is HEREBY GIVEN, that a PETITION for the WINDING UP of the above-named Company by the High Court of Justice was. oh the 3rd day of February, 1881, presented to the Master of the Rolls by Parr's Banking Com- pany, Limited, whose registered cffice is at Warrington, in the county of Lancaster, creditors of the said Company: and that the said Petition is directed to be heard before his Lordship the Master of the Rolls, on the 12th day of February, 1881, and any creditor or contributory of the said Company desirous to oppose the making of an order for the winding up of the said Company under the above Acts should appear at the time of hearing, by himself or his counsel. for that purpose, and a copy of the petition will be furnished to any creditor or contributory of the saki Company requiring the same, by the undersigned, en pay- ment of the regulated charge for the same. FIELD, ROSCOE, & Co., Of 36, Lincoln's Inn Fields, London, W.C., Agents for BIICKTON & GREENALL. of Warrington, Solicitors for the Petitioner.

IVOTICE is hereby given, that the PARTNERSHIP _LI heretofore subsisting between us, the undersigned, JOHN TOULMIN and HENRY HUNT BARKER, in the trades or businesses of Newspaper Proprietors, Publishers, and Letter- press Printers, at Warrington, in the county of Lancaster, and in the trade or business of Newspaper Publishers at Runcorn, iu the county of Che6ter' and at Widnes and Stint Helens, both in the said county of Lancaster, under the style or Arm of "TOULMIN and BARBER," was, on the first day of Decem- ber, one thousand eight hundred and eighty, DISSOLVED by mutual consent; and in future the several BUSINESSES will be CARRIED ON by the said JOHN Touratur on his separate account, and he will PAY and RECEIVE 911 DEBTS owkng from and to the said partnership in the regular course of trade. As witness our hands this twentylninth day of January, one thousand eight hundred and eighty-one. JOHN TOULMIN, HENRY HUNT BARKER. Witness to the signature of the said Henry Hunt Barker: JAMES E. WOESLEY, Solicit or, Warrington, Witness to the signature of John Toulmin: T. J. RIDGWAY, Solicitor, Warrington.

MAKINSON AND WILCOCK, in returning their sincere thanks to their numerous patrons and the public generally for the very kind and liberal support they nave hitherto received, hope, by strict attention to the interests of their clients, and the prompt and faithful discharge of their duties, to continue to merit the same; the more so, as they are able to offer ad- vantages not generally enjoyed by those engaged in the same business, Mr. Makinson having had from early youth practical experience of the English Timber, Stone and Building Trades, and of Farming in all its branches, being at the present time a farmer himself on a large scale; and, in addition, having served his apprenticeship to the ENGINEERING and MILLWRIGHT busi- ness, besides having had, during the last TEN years, consider- able practice ha Valuing and Belling Colliery, Quarry, and other Machinery and Working Plant, Growing and Fallen Timber, Farming Stocks, Growing and Gathered Produce, Stocks-IA- Trade, Household Furniture Innkeepers' Effects, Houses, Buildings, Landed Estates and Property generally, and also in cases involving Damage and Trespass. Mr. WILCOCK, also, has had the advantage of being brought up to Farming, together with that of having served an appren- ticeship to an eminent Veterinary Surgeon, combined with the experience he has had since his connection with this firm, enables him to give judicious and valuable advice in all cases in which he may be consulted. In conclusion, M. and W. beg their friends and the public generally to note that they have a trustworthy and efficient staff of assistants in their employ, who have been carefully trained to watch over the interests of those who favour the firm with their patronage; whilst last, but not least, their system of advertising, and the facilities they possess of ensuring an extensive circulation, enable them to offer the utmost pos- sible publicity to any sales entrusted to their management.
